World.title: Best outdoor adventures near Memorial Stadium for Ohio State vs. Indiana football fans
World.content:
Week 7 | No. 4 Ohio State at No. 5 Indiana | Saturday, Oct. 17 | Memorial Stadium, Bloomington, IN | 12 p.m. ET | FOX

Indiana has won 22 games in a row, owns the national championship trophy, and is hosting Ohio State in Bloomington with both teams ranked in the top five. The last time these two met, the Hoosiers upset the Buckeyes 13-10 in the Big Ten title game, ending Ohio State's unbeaten season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Now the 5-1 Buckeyes are coming back as 3.5-point favorites against an undefeated Indiana team that has plenty to prove all over again.

I'm biased on this one.

Sure, I went to the University of Tennessee. But Indiana is my home state, and I grew up spending my summers on Lake Monroe. But Southern Indiana in mid-October — with the hills lit up in red and gold — is hard to beat.

Bloomington sits right in the middle of it. Brown County, in particular, is a little slice of heaven.

Let's get into it.

About 40 minutes from Memorial Stadium | $7 per vehicle with Indiana plates, $15 out of state | Easy to moderate

Indiana's largest state park covers roughly 16,000 acres of rugged hills and ridges, and people call it the "Little Smokies" for a reason. Hike to a scenic overlook like Hesitation Point, climb the fire tower, or just drive the park roads and pull off at the viewpoints if you'd rather stay warm.

The park gets busy on peak foliage weekends and the entrance can back up, so get there early. Nashville, Ind., is right outside the gate, which makes it easy to turn this into a full day.

McCormick's Creek State Park

About 25 minutes from Memorial Stadium | $7 per vehicle with Indiana plates, $15 out of state | Easy to moderate

Indiana's first state park is also home to one of the few waterfalls in a state not exactly known for them. The Wolf Cave Trail is a roughly 2-mile moderate loop through a wooded nature preserve to a small cave, rated 4.6 stars across more than 1,200 AllTrails reviews. If you're short on time, the waterfall is just a short, easy walk from Trail 3. It's the closest of the big state parks to Bloomington, which makes it a good fit for a shorter window.

Hickory Ridge Fire Tower & Deam Wilderness

About 30 minutes from Memorial Stadium | Moderate

The 110-foot Hickory Ridge Fire Tower has 133 steps and is open to climb, with views over the forest and Lake Monroe.

6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK

It's the last fire tower standing in Hoosier National Forest. The surrounding Charles C. Deam Wilderness, Indiana's only wilderness area, covers nearly 13,000 acres and about 36 miles of trails.

Lake Monroe

About 6 miles from campus | Canoe or kayak rental from about $42 for four hours, plus a state entrance fee

Indiana's largest lake is nearly 11,000 acres, and in October the fall color reflects right off the water. Lake Monroe Boat Rental at Paynetown State Recreation Area rents canoes and kayaks that seat one or two people for $41.73 for four hours or $53.50 for eight.

A state entrance fee applies at Paynetown. Call ahead to confirm hours this late in the season, and keep in mind the water is cold, so dress for it.

There are also hiking trails along the lake if you'd rather stay off the water.

Griffy Lake Nature Preserve

Under 2 miles from campus | $12 per hour

The closest option to the stadium, and a nice one for a lower-key day. The city's boathouse rents canoes, kayaks and stand-up paddleboards on a 109-acre lake, with hiking trails through the surrounding preserve.

There's a two-hour limit on weekend rentals, and you'll need a photo ID. In October the boathouse is open Saturdays and Sundays only, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., so it won't work for a pregame paddle with a noon kickoff. Plan on it after the game or on Sunday.

Or, again, just go for a hike.

Nashville and the Get Lost ATV Tour

About 40 minutes from Memorial Stadium | Strolling is free, ATV tour is $70 per person (21+)

If you've got an extra day, or even an extra afternoon, spend it in Nashville. The small downtown in the heart of Brown County is made for wandering, with art galleries, craft shops and homemade fudge packed into a few walkable blocks. There's a couple of wineries, too, if you're into that sort of thing.

I'm into that sort of thing.

For something a little more adventurous (and super fun), Hard Truth Distilling Co. sits on 325 wooded acres just outside town and runs its Get Lost ATV Tour. Staff drive you through the property in an off-road vehicle with stops for tastings along the way.

The tour runs 45 to 60 minutes, costs $70 per person, and you have to be at least 21. It is weather dependent, though, so rain can cancel it.

So there you have it.



Even if the football game doesn't go your way, you'll still get to see a corner of Indiana that doesn't get nearly enough credit.

Because as that animated crow in a commercial from my childhood always said, "There’s more than corn in Indiana!"

Every week this season, OutKick OutDoors is finding the best ways to touch grass before you touch down at the tailgate. Got a favorite spot near your campus we should know about? Hit us up on Instagram and TikTok.

World.title: Billy Joel says he can't drive, unsure about touring future after brain disorder diagnosis
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Billy Joel's touring future remains uncertain due to his ongoing health issues.

Joel, 77, revealed in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter that he's also not allowed to drive a vehicle after being diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) in 2025.

"What the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion," Joel said.

'PIANO MAN' BILLY JOEL'S PRIZED MOTORCYCLE COLLECTION HITS THE AUCTION BLOCK

When asked about his current status, Joel said that his "health is good," but still isn't sure when he'll be able to tour again.

"I have this thing called hydrocephalus," he told the outlet. "It used to be called water on the brain, so it affects your balance, it affects your memory, it affects your vision, your hearing. But I’m OK."

"They call it a brain disorder, but it’s not that serious. It’s just something that affects your balance mostly."

LIONEL RICHIE HOSPITALIZED IN ST LOUIS AFTER SUMMER OF HEALTH SCARES AND CANCELED CONCERTS

As far as going back on the road again, Joel admitted he can't perform quite like how he used to.

"I have to take a series of tests before I know, but I can’t drive right now," he said. "I’m not allowed to drive. And I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion."

He added, "So they have to test me further to see if I can go back and do performing again, which I would like to be able to do."

The "Uptown Girl" singer underwent brain surgery after revealing his normal pressure hydrocephalus diagnosis in May 2025. NPH affects his vision, hearing and balance, according to a statement Joel released on social media at the time.

He delved more into his recovery process during a recent appearance on his self-titled SiriusXM show, "The Billy Joel Channel," and said doctors told him that performing loud rock 'n' roll music caused damage to his brain nerves.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Joel remembered his medical team saying, "Well, we drill a hole through your skull, and we stick a shunt inside your brain."

"I didn't want to do that, but then I read up on it and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory," he noted. "You know, I don't want to lose my marbles. It's hard to tell what's age and what's a condition, so I agreed to do the shunt and I had a surgery. And they implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things."

"My memory got better. My balance got a little better. My ability to function was better, and I realized, and the doctors told me this, because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show."

Joel shared more about his diagnosis ahead of the sale of more than 70 lots from his personal collection of motorcycles heading to the auction block next month with Gooding Christie's.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Well, I ended up having over a hundred motorcycles, and the truth is you can only ride one at a time. I’m into my 70s now, and I realized I can’t ride as much as I used to," he told the outlet. "I don’t want to die like a bug on a windshield. So I thought I’d put a lot of them on auction."

"And also I have a condition called hydrocephalus, which makes driving a little bit iffy. So I realized it’s time for me to turn it over to somebody else."

The collection includes a number of his most cherished motorcycles, in addition to Ducati, BMW, Moto Guzzi, Harley-Davidson, Yamaha, Triumph, Honda, Kawasaki, and more.

"One of the stars of the sale is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville that was gifted to Billy Joel by Madison Square Garden to commemorate 150 sold out shows," Gooding Christie's founder David Gooding explained to Fox News Digital of the bike, which is expected to retrieve anywhere from $10,000 - $15,000.

"He still holds the record for the most sold out show of anyone ever at Madison Square Garden. And this bike is painted with a keyboard on the tank. It's really, really a special, special item."

Motorcycles from the auction – which is slated for Nov. 20-21 – will be on display at the Javits Center in New York.

World.title: Houthis emerge as global threat beyond Iran control amid Saudi strikes, former envoy warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Houthis are increasingly operating independently of Tehran, posing a "clear and very present danger" on the international stage as the terror group rearms and sharpens its strike capabilities, a former U.S. envoy warned Thursday.

The warning came amid deadly missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days and growing threats to global shipping routes and critical Middle East infrastructure in the run-up.

Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, also confirmed Thursday that Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had killed 17 and injured 333 others from Oct. 7-11.

Speaking at a news conference in Riyadh, al-Maliki said the Oct. 10 attack involved 10 drones, missiles and other projectiles.

"King Khalid International Airport has been subjected to 20 attacks since (Oct. 1)," he noted.

Tim Lenderking, who served as U.S. special envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2025 and was posted to Saudi Arabia from 2013 to 2016, said Saudi officials had warned more than a decade ago that the Houthis would become a major threat, a prediction he says has now materialized.

SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE

"The Saudis were very clear to our leaders that they viewed the Houthis as a major threat," Lenderking said of his time in the kingdom a decade ago.

At the time, he said, the group was "quietly building up their capability, burnishing their narrative of why they sought to lead Yemen as a messianic group, as a group from northern Yemen, with an agenda, with a mission."

The Houthis had emerged as a religious and political movement in Yemen in the 1990s, but their ties to Iran developed into a military partnership after 2014, when Tehran expanded its assistance and training during Yemen's civil war.

"The Houthis don't really need the Iranians anymore," Lenderking, a former acting assistant secretary for Near Eastern affairs at the U.S. State Department, continued, adding it was still "a very important relationship that "enabled the Houthis to become the powerful force that they are."

Lenderking, now a distinguished diplomatic fellow at the Middle East Institute (MEI), said, over time, the Houthis had developed their own "homegrown indigenous capability" as they capitalized on any disunity across the Gulf region.

Saturday's missile and drone attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh raised concerns that President Donald Trump could be drawn into a broader regional conflict as Saudi Arabia seeks U.S. assistance.

Asked whether the U.S. would defend Saudi Arabia against further attacks, Trump said, "You'll find out soon."

NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

Speaking at an MEI briefing, Lenderking said the Houthis' sophisticated weapons and targeting capabilities have transformed the group from a regional insurgency into an international security threat.

"They have the capability to hit around the region, including up into the northern reaches of the Red Sea. So, this is a regional problem, and given the fact that the Houthis control the west coast of Yemen," Lenderking said.

"It's an international problem now."

Lenderking cited the precision of the Riyadh airport attack as evidence of the Houthis' growing capabilities compared with earlier strikes during the Gaza conflict.

"They can hit things better. Now, they are hitting Terminal Four of Riyadh Airport, very specifically. It's a clear and very present danger," he said.

The Houthis reportedly launched multiple drones followed by cruise and ballistic missiles that traveled more than 620 miles to Riyadh, prompting an investigation into possible Saudi air defense failures, according to The Associated Press, citing regional officials.

Saudi forces intercepted two more ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh on Monday. On Tuesday, a Houthi strike caused damage to Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, sparking a fire that spread across several floors, Reuters reported.

Lenderking said the Houthis have built extensive weapons supply chains, smuggling networks and domestic financing operations that allow them to sustain attacks without relying solely on Tehran.

HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS

"They get a lot of supplies off the open market through the internet, through commercial exchanges. They have a very well entrenched smuggling network, from big boats onto small boats, onto tiny boats, on the pack animals, on people's backs.

"They are able to move things undetected through government terrain, even through various borders and with a lot of wide open space there. They are constantly moving, building, resupplying, restocking, innovating."

The group's self-sufficiency also extends to financing. Lenderking said the Houthis generate revenue through black-market oil sales, taxation and extortion while also forcing families to provide recruits, allowing the group to continue fighting even if Iranian assistance is cut off.

"They have had support from Iran over the years, so they have money in the bank from that," Lenderking said.

"They relied on sales of black market oil in the past. They extort Yemeni transport companies, businesses. They tax people in areas that they control. They force many families to offer up a son to fight on the front lines."

The Houthis' expanding arsenal has raised concerns about potential Chinese involvement in their weapons supply networks.

OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES

Yemen's government has accused the rebels of seeking Chinese components for medium-range ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the group's access to advanced military technology.

"There is a Chinese connection here that's very detrimental," Lenderking warned, adding that front companies have helped the group obtain weapons through commercial channels.

Lenderking warned that the Houthis could also target Saudi energy facilities, pipelines and desalination plants, infrastructure critical to the kingdom's economy and water supply.

"The Houthis have hit pipelines," he said. "They have diesel plants and other energy infrastructure in their sights."

Attacks on such facilities could disrupt global energy markets, maritime commerce and regional stability.

The Houthis also control Yemen's western coastline along the Red Sea, a vital shipping corridor connecting Europe and Asia.

With the rebels now capable of striking targets hundreds of miles away, Lenderking warned that the threat extends far beyond Yemen's borders.

"One blast at Riyadh Airport is a huge statement," the expert said.

"That's why I come back to the fact that this is an international conflict," he said, adding that "immediate action is required."

World.title: Feds investigate suspicious letters sent to lawmakers and election officials
World.content:
The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to “various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices,” according to a notice that senior staff in Senate offices received Thursday morning.

“Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations,” the notice said, according to two people who received it.

The offices of several Democratic senators were targeted, including that of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., NBC News confirmed. Two law enforcement sources briefed on the matter confirmed that “dozens of letters” were sent, but because law enforcement continues to intercept the letters, they declined to put an exact number on how many have been received or seized.

The notice included an image of one of the suspicious envelopes and said that the letters “may contain different variations of postage stamps.” It also warned that suspicious letters, packages or substances “should be treated as potentially hazardous and handled in accordance with established safety protocols.”

The notice outlined how staff should handle the items and noted that mail and packages delivered to Senate offices or the Capitol complex are screened and tested for potential threats.

Three law enforcement sources briefed on the matter told NBC News later in the day that preliminary testing of the white powder substance showed that the contents are not hazardous.

However, additional testing will continue to take place at law enforcement labs around the country to ensure the letters do not contain anything dangerous.

A similar notice was sent to House lawmakers and staff Thursday from the House sergeant at arms. The notice said that while mail and packages delivered to the House offices in the Capitol are rigorously screened, district offices should use safe mail handling procedures, including the use of “mail hoods” — screening equipment that allows the handling of mail without exposing staff to danger — provided by the sergeant at arms, according to two congressional offices who shared the message with NBC News. The notice said no House members had been identified as intended recipients of the mailings.

The U.S. Postal Inspection Service and Capitol Police referred questions from NBC News to the FBI, which confirmed in a statement that the agencies are investigating “a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” The agency did not specify the locations of the offices targeted.

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”

The notice sent to Senate staff did not say whether the congressional offices involved are the ones in Washington, D.C. or local and regional offices. Congress is on recess leading up to the midterm elections, so most lawmakers are back home in their districts as they campaign in the final weeks of the races. Congressional staff, however, are still on the Capitol campus.

One of the letters with a suspicious substance inside was addressed to Schumer, which was intercepted by authorities, according to a spokesperson for the Democratic leader.

An office for Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., was among those targeted, a spokesperson for the senator told NBC News in a statement. “We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS. Follow up questions should be directed to the FBI.”

A letter with a suspicious substance was also sent to Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy’s Hartford, Connecticut, office, his spokesperson, Josh Sorbe, said in a statement. The FBI, Capitol Police and sergeant at arms informed the office about the letter, Sorbe said, adding that the senator and his staff “were not in immediate danger.”

NBC News reported Wednesday that state election offices in Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma were sent packages this week containing mysterious powders. Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.

These offices oversee and manage the election process in their respective states, and these incidents come just weeks before Election Day on Nov. 3.

Threats against election workers have increased in recent years, including incidents of suspicious substances being mailed to their offices. It happened in 2023 and just weeks before the presidential election in 2024.

CORRECTION (Oct. 15, 2026, 5:23 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified which Oklahoma office received a package. It was the state election board, not the secretary of state’s office. The article also mischaracterized election oversight in Oklahoma. That’s carried out by the election board, not the secretary of state.

World.title: Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues on whether Fed will raise interest rates this month
World.content:
When Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh strides onstage in Bangkok on Friday morning, it will be after 11 p.m. on Thursday in New York. But investors, economists and politicians in the United States will be awake and hanging on his every word.

Any speech by a Fed chair is closely scrutinized. This week’s talk has an extra dose of urgency, though, after two government reports showed inflation heating up for consumers and businesses — spurring speculation about how soon the Fed will raise interest rates to handle soaring prices.

Warsh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where he will be interviewed by IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. The Fed chairman has repeatedly said he will not use public speaking engagements to intentionally steer the expectations of investors and markets, but his comments could nevertheless signal whether the central bank will hike rates before, or after, the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

It will also be the last speech from a Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.

“Broad based” inflation “strengthens the case for an October hike,” Bank of America analysts wrote on Wednesday. “The data continue to underscore two key sources of inflation pressure: AI and Iran.”

Those two factors aren’t likely to be going anywhere soon, either.

The price of politics

Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.

But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.

Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”

“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.

Asked what the president’s expectations are for Warsh’s appearance, the White House pointed to a Truth Social post from September in which Trump had written, “Interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”

Diesel and the damage done

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.

“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”

Her warning came to fruition in September, according to the consumer price index and producer price index reports this week. With diesel prices remaining solidly above $6 per gallon so far in October, and with no sign that the Iran war is near an end or that attacks on energy assets in the Ukraine-Russia war will be paused, it could keep fueling overall inflation for months.

Big Tech is also fueling inflation. Trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components that will be used in data centers. That’s caused price spikes across the economy.

Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.

A consequence of that, Warsh noted recently, is that there’s a “competition for capital” driving up interest rates on government debt, too.

“This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury,” Warsh said. “It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.”

Without referencing the Iran war, he also said yields were being driven by “geopolitics” and the strength of the economy.

World.title: ICE agent driving vehicle that struck and injured Houston man is placed on administrative leave
World.content:
The ICE officer accused of running over an immigrant in Houston on Saturday has been put on administrative leave while the incident is investigated, a senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News.

As NBC News has reported, a senior DHS official said that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras and that ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation.

The DHS official said no decision has been made about sharing the video with the public or with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office, which is conducting its own investigation.

District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News on Thursday that he has interviewed a key witness who was handcuffed in the back of the ICE vehicle when it hit Miguel Parra Hernández. The witness “had a front-row seat to the incident and everything that led up to it,” Teare said. “We did get a significant amount of relevant details from him.”

The witness was interviewed at the Port Isabel Processing Center, about 35 to 40 miles from the U.S.-Mexico border in South Texas, according to the district attorney’s office. The Port Isabel facility is historically known as the last stop before an immigrant is removed from the U.S.

Teare said his office is compiling all information it has gathered or is still gathering, and “in very short order we’re going to come to a point where we present this to a grand jury.” He said that could happen as soon as next week.

Security video shows the moment an ICE vehicle struck a man in Houston. KPRC

Teare and Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant civil rights group, identified the witness as José Presa Cañada.

“It’s very troubling” that Presa is in Port Isabel, Espinosa said Thursday. “We want to know why he’s there and why he hasn’t been released yet and why they are trying to deport him so expeditiously.”

Teare declined to comment on what was said during the interview with Presa. Teare also has interviewed Parra.

The auto-pedestrian collision Saturday, which left Parra hospitalized with multiple injuries and needing surgery, triggered the investigation, which could result in charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, according to Teare.

The district attorney’s office said it notified ICE soon after the incident that it wanted to interview Presa. In an email, ICE responded that Teare should get to Port Isabel fast because the agency planned to deport Presa, according to the district attorney’s office.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for information about its detention of Presa and whether it plans to deport him.

ICE has said Parra was not its arrest target on Monday. An agency spokesperson said Parra ran into the ICE vehicle’s path.

The other potential witness who was handcuffed in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra is Luis Delfín Martínez, who is being held in the Montgomery Processing Center in Conroe, north of Houston, according to advocates and relatives.

Miguel Parra Hernández. Courtesy FIEL

The district attorney’s office has issued subpoenas for Parra’s medical records, as well as for records of emergency medical personnel who responded when Parra was struck.

Teare, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno and advocates have been pressing the Trump administration not to deport Parra and the two men in the vehicle and have asked the district attorney and others to protect them.

Teare said in an interview this week that his office had been in touch with consulates for the countries of origin of all three men to let them know it was ready to assist with their applications for visas for witnesses key to criminal cases, known as U visas.

“We’re working with the powers that be in a really significant effort to keep them here in this country,” he said then.

Teare told NBC News that it’s “pretty obvious” from videos his office has collected, including drone video, that ICE intentionally hit and ran over Parra, an allegation ICE has said is reckless and false.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck facing the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.

At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction. The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center.

When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

Teare sought to download data from the ICE vehicle while it was still at the scene, but an agent drove the car away. Driving the car may have automatically erased critical data, said Teare, who led the district attorney’s office’s vehicular crimes division for several years.

World.title: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market, as doubts grow about AI investments
World.content:
Just one week after hitting fresh all-time highs, U.S. stocks are showing signs of strain as investors begin to fret about returns on the trillions of dollars that have been put into AI.

For U.S. consumers, it could mean a shakier economy moving forward.

After trading closed Thursday, the S&P 500 was off 1% from its week-ago record, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen more than 3% below its peak last week.

Driving the declines: Quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic has slowed, the Financial Times reported Wednesday. The AI giant is expected to be worth more than $1 trillion when it goes public, and at nearly $17 billion, its revenue is still massive and the company said it is profitable.

There are also rising concerns about whether China-based memory technology companies could undermine, or even overtake, their Western rivals. And even though the AI data center buildout has created a global shortage of processing chips, there are fears that Chinese mass production of memory chips could flood the market with an oversupply.

Meanwhile, investors have begun selling off the bonds backing some data centers, primarily over fears that AI revenues won’t be sufficient to cover the massive sums that have been borrowed to finance the building of the centers.

On Thursday, economist Ed Yardeni, a widely respected market commentator, lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 target to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates. The S&P 500 currently sits at about 7,600.

Most Americans don’t directly own tech stocks, let alone work in AI, which a growing number of studies show may have begun to limit job opportunities. Still, the AI buildout has been a massive part of what’s bolstering the economy, at least on paper.

Nearly half of all U.S. economy growth this year is attributable to tech-related spending. Those investments have also lifted the stock market even as a growing swath of other companies have experienced sharp declines in their share prices.

The tech-driven gains have in turn created a wealth effect that has helped propel steady U.S. consumer spending and, by extension, the job market. The result has been sturdy economic growth, even as lower-income and even middle-income households have continued to struggle under stubborn inflation and declining earnings.

“While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said earlier this week.

But other economists say consumers are already contending with a host of stressors that stand to weaken their position. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that inflation among businesses reached its highest rate since December 2022 — price growth that could eventually trickle down to consumers.

If tech spending — and stocks — show any sign of sustained declines, broader U.S. economic growth would likely be at risk.

“Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices, slow job growth and the sell-off in equities (if it continues) are all downside risks to consumer spending,” analysts with Citi wrote in a note Thursday.

World.title: Cornell president faces contentious faculty senate meeting over Jane Doe allegations
World.content:
Cornell University’s president was met with scrutiny and sharp questions from its faculty senate on Wednesday, when the group convened to discuss a no-confidence vote over the university’s handling of an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording obtained by NBC News.

Discussion of a no-confidence vote comes after serious concerns were raised by students and staff over how the university responded to the allegations.

University President Michael Kotlikoff defended himself and Cornell’s administration as he took a series of pointed questions from the school staff.

At the meeting, most speakers were heard identifying themselves before speaking. Risa Lieberwitz, a professor of labor and employment law, said the issue of sexual assault “is a systemic problem. It deserves systemic attention.”

She told Kotlikoff that thus far it appeared he had “simply reacted to pressure.”

“It feels that the administration is considering more about how do we respond to pressure rather than the kind of leadership, which should have been doing systemic work and prioritizing these issues all along,” she said.

Kotlikoff argued that replacing its leadership was not the solution.

“We need to be able to work together to be able to change the culture, educate our students, and try and address this problem,” he said at the meeting. “I want Cornell to be a leader in this area, and we have plans to really invest in this area. But the idea that you can somehow, because an event has occurred, eliminate it immediately — it’s just unrealistic.”

Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.

In 2024, Cornell shut down the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at the university and expelled two students after Doe reported the incident. Others were suspended or faced lesser disciplinary action. The university also said it launched the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault shortly after the incident and implemented recommendations to address sexual assault on campus.

No criminal charges were brought at the time, and the investigation has been reopened following Jane Doe’s lawsuit. Four of the men, through their attorneys, have denied coercing Jane Doe with drugs or sexually assaulting her. NBC News was not able to reach the other three men named in the lawsuit.

While the faculty senate does not have the authority to remove the president, the move would greatly increase the pressure on Cornell and its administration.

Darlene Evans, a senior lecturer emerita, asked Kotlikoff why he was only taking steps now “towards serious systemic change” when he had been in leadership roles at the university for more than a decade.

Evans noted that more than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a Cornell University poll conducted last year, a figure that was up from 23% in 2023.

“It wasn’t until a no-confidence vote was introduced that Cornell’s administration announced any real steps to prevent sexual assault on this campus, or to seriously support survivors,” she said. “So saying what we’re going to do now kind of rings hollow here. Why haven’t you taken these things more seriously until now, when there’s a firestorm of press looking at Cornell?”

Kotlikoff announced on Tuesday that all parties at fraternity houses and events would be banned through the rest of the academic year.

“We don’t have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe and so for the time being we will stop that activity,” he said during the meeting on Wednesday.

He also addressed calls from some over whether Greek life at the university should be banned altogether.

“If at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment, and we can’t be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision,” he said. “But we should make it based on data and study and expertise, not on emotion.”

After a question-and-answer session, the faculty senate began debating the no-confidence resolution, with another meeting scheduled for later this month. Many spoke in favor of the resolution, while others wanted to delay the vote until the results of an upcoming independent investigation.

Earlier this month, the university announced that Sally Yates, the former deputy U.S. attorney general and acting U.S. attorney general, would lead an independent review on how Cornell University responded to the allegations and, more broadly, how it responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”

After the meeting, music professor Ariana Kim said she was “really inspired by everyone who spoke and was brave in favor of the resolution — it takes a lot to stand up in front of the president and ask direct questions of him.”

Kim said she has received some 200 emails from alumni saying they support the no-confidence resolution and want the administration to be held accountable.

The professor said some at the meeting held up signs that read, “I stand with Jane Doe,” “How many more?” and “We demand accountability.”

“Some people broke down and held each other after the meeting,” she said.

Political history professor Richard Bensel said that so far the central administration “has not responded in a way that is going to diminish faculty and students’ despair over the way that the university has treated the issue.”

Bensel said he was unsure if he wanted the president to resign, but said he thought university leadership “will not reform itself without passage of the no-confidence resolution.”

“I can imagine a way the trustees through the president can reconcile their relations with the Cornell community but that requires a real change in governance style and I don’t think that is possible under this administration,” he said. “There are real problems in the way the university is run.”

World.title: Feds probing suspicious letters to election officials, lawmakers
World.content:
Washington — Federal investigators said Thursday that they are looking into "suspicious" letters mailed to state election officials and congressional offices, some of which contained unknown substances.

At least five Democratic Senate offices were sent the letters, most of which were intercepted before they were delivered. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was one of those targeted, CBS News has learned.

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the "suspicious mailings," according to Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the USPIS. Donahue told reporters earlier in the day that some letters have contained an unknown substance and that they were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue said. "Our partners, including the FBI and we at the Postal Inspection Service, will bring all of our resources to bear on these investigations."

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. The message, which was obtained by CBS News, said congressional offices were among those who received the suspicious letters.

A spokesperson for Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told CBS News that the senator's office in Dover, Delaware, received a suspicious letter that contained a white powder. The letter was not opened in the office, the spokesperson said.

A letter meant for New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was found at the senator's office in New York City and postal inspectors were on the scene to investigate, an aide for the senator said.

A spokesman for Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut also said his office was "sent a letter with a suspicious substance."

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," said Josh Sorbe, a spokesman for Murphy. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger."

A letter was also sent to Sen. Alex Padilla's office, according to a spokesperson for the California Democrat.

"We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS," the spokesperson said.

The House sergeant at arms sent a notice to the lower chamber's offices stating that no House members were known to have been targeted.

Federal officials are working to identify the responsible parties and have intercepted some of the letters, Donahue said. Donahue declined to provide an exact number of incidents or discuss possible connections, citing the ongoing investigation. He added that investigators would bring their full resources to bear on the cases.

The development comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Federal investigators also probed a series of suspicious letters ahead of the 2024 elections.

In addition to the congressional offices, top election officials in at least eight states have reported that their offices were sent suspicious packages in recent days.

Delaware's Department of Elections said in a post on X that it "received and opened a letter which was discovered to contain a white powdery substance" on Thursday. "Staff members followed security and USPS instructions on handling suspicious mail," the post said.

Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said Tuesday that an employee in her office's Elections Division opened a package and found a white powder.

"Law enforcement responded to today's incident and conducted tests that found no evidence of harmful substances," she wrote on Facebook, adding that no one was injured.

The Oklahoma State Election Board said it received an envelope containing "suspicious" white powder Tuesday morning, and its office was evacuated.

Paul Ziriax, secretary of the election board, said no one was hurt as a result of the incident, and law enforcement is investigating.

The Wisconsin Elections Commission said it received a "suspicious mail piece" on Wednesday, but "field testing confirmed no hazardous material was detected."

The secretaries of state in Pennsylvania, New Hampshire, Ohio and Mississippi said their offices were also sent suspicious mail, but the deliveries were intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service or law enforcement before they arrived.

World.content:
Vice President JD Vance told CBS News on Thursday that anybody who is "selling access to the White House" should "suffer consequences."

Vance spoke with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil during a one-hour town hall in Michigan that is set to air on Saturday evening, less than three weeks before the midterm elections.

Dokoupil pointed to a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's staggering cryptocurrency earnings, and the ousting of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle over allegations she asked a man who was seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000.

"First of all, if somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences," Vance responded.

He went on to say, "I want to make those judgments based on the facts and not based on a random news media report that I read."

Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.

Congressional Democrats have vowed to investigate the Trump administration if they win control of the House or Senate, which would grant them control over committees and allow them to issue subpoenas to administration officials.

Asked if the administration would comply with any subpoenas, Vance said: "Of course I will. Look, I mean, we follow the law."

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.

World.title: Justice Department sues California over noncitizens getting ballots
World.content:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.

"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."

In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.

Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."

Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.

In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.

"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.

"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.

In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.

CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.
