World.title: Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric
World.content:
Social Security benefits to get a boost. And, Hasan Piker defends his rhetoric

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Consumer prices in September were 3.7% higher than they were a year ago, according to a Labor Department report. A spike in energy prices linked to the U.S. war with Iran drove up the cost of living. Excluding energy and food prices, core inflation reached 2.6% in September, up from August. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for next year after the release of the inflation report. This annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices from July, August and September. Some recipients say the increase is not enough.

toggle caption i Isabelle Souriment/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

🎧 Social Security may run out of money to make full payments to retirees as soon as 2032. NPR's Planet Money examines possible solutions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced he will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries, despite President Trump's request to refrain from doing so. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that he had ordered commanders to stand down earlier this week, but wouldn't anymore. But Ukraine's ability to conduct these long-range attacks may be limited, as it has seen sudden crippling restrictions to Starshield, the satellite communications system provided by the U.S.



Sponsor Message

🎧 The U.S. is seemingly trying to limit Ukraine's ability to fight Russia, though that has not been announced outright, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. Ukraine's defense ministry said today that operations are back to normal. The country relies on the Starshield system for offensive and defensive drones to protect against Russian strikes. Elon Musk, who developed the system for the U.S. government and military, says the U.S. government sets its speed and usage limits.

A man shot and wounded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in New York last week says he didn't know the men who shot him were ICE agents until after he woke up in the hospital. A new petition filed in Brooklyn federal court says the agents — many of them masked — didn't identify themselves before approaching Oscar Belgal's vehicle with their firearms drawn. The filing contradicts the Trump administration's version of events.

Watch this

Nickolai Hammar/NPR

Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

California-based Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has emerged as a key target for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections. The president recently labeled him a "terrible liability" and a "communist." In Michigan, political ads attempting to link him to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayef repeatedly play Piker's most controversial statements, including the infamous "America deserved 9/11." Piker remains confident that he won't hinder Democrats this November. In a conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, he reflects on his past remarks, the loneliness young men feel and his critique of Tucker Carlson.

Sponsor Message

Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.

Picture show

toggle caption i KT Kanazawich for NPR

Australian DJ Lenny Pearce is taking over venues with his toddler rave world tour. Yes, it's is exactly what it sounds like: techno dance parties for families. Most of the dance floor is filled with little ones under the age of five. Around 5 p.m., the speakers blast nursery rhymes like "Bingo" and "The Wheels on the Bus," while the bar offers a refreshing house specialty: apple juice. Pearce kicked off the North American leg of his tour in Baltimore, but has sold-out shows in cities such as New York and Los Angeles and has already captivated audiences in Bahrain, Singapore and India. Take a look at these photos of the young ravers at his events.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Claire Harbage/NPR

Coral reefs worldwide face rising threats. On a remote Pacific island, scientists discovered that seabirds can help them. The New York City Council and Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced plans to ban carriage horses in Central Park. (via Gothamist) NPR's Eyder Peralta takes readers to a Mexico City park in the latest installment of Far-Flung Postcards. There, people still practice bullfighting, even though it is banned.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back
World.content:
After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back

toggle caption i Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.

Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.

Sponsor Message

A fix for widespread fraud?

Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.

Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don't respond to outreach efforts by "around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections," said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.

He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.

Few details

Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.

Sponsor Message

"It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it's almost impossible to tell," said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. "That they are not being very transparent is telling too," she said of the administration.

The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.

At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children's Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.

Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants' providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.

Even so, how the move will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden's presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only states that use Healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.

Sponsor Message

"To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active," said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

How it played out

According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:

The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.



A broker was involved in the sign-up process.



The plan had no monthly premium payment.



The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.

Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers' outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn't respond.

Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting "an all-hands-on-deck" effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.

"Getting them to answer the phone isn't easy," he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.

Additionally, his team has been asked by insurers to help contact those targeted in the second phase of CMS' review. A recent case involved a client who needed to upload his new green card after his previous one expired, but language barriers meant that he had to take time off work to come in for agents to help with the process.

Sponsor Message

Information from a financial filing

CMS would not provide a list of the insurers it contacted, but publicly available documents show that New York-based Oscar Health was one.

In an August earnings call with analysts and investors, CEO Mark Bertolini said the company was reviewing the files and that "there are a number of cases where we've actually had contact" with people on the list. In other words, the company reached enrollees CMS had targeted over fraud concerns.

He did not specify how many it had reached. The company declined to comment for this article because it is in a voluntary "quiet period," when publicly traded companies limit disclosing information before the release of an earnings report.

Still, in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Oscar Health estimated that 250,000 to 300,000 of its members might be disenrolled because of the CMS effort. Nationally, the company had about 3 million members in the second quarter and reported strong profits.

Overall ACA enrollment has declined sharply, falling by nearly 3 million in the first few months of the year, due in large part to the expiration at the end of last year of the enhanced subsidies. The Trump administration has also taken some credit, saying its focus on weeding out improper enrollments and other changes, such as eliminating a special year-round low-income enrollment period, led to the decline.

CMS has also suspended some brokers for improper activity and barred new brokers from enrolling clients in ACA insurance on the federal exchange during the upcoming open enrollment period.

CMS did not respond to requests for data on the reasons it canceled enrollments. What percentage of enrollees were deemed ineligible due to incorrect income reporting or because they had other health coverage, such as through their jobs? How many because their ACA applications lacked immigration documents or Social Security numbers?

Sponsor Message

"Currently, there is no additional data to share," the agency's press office said.

But people outside the administration have been vocal.

"This was clearly phantom enrollees," said Paragon's Blase. He thinks more than 99% of the cancellations are of zero-premium coverage that people were signed up for by rogue call centers without their knowledge, or for people who don't exist at all.

Blase said the carriers had a big incentive to get hold of the enrollees because they would lose the subsidies they were being paid if the plans were canceled.

And for any people unfairly caught up, Blase and Trump administration officials say all they have to do to be reinstated is call the marketplace and provide their Social Security number or other missing information.

"Everyone has the political incentive for that process to be that easy," Blase said. "We're a month before the election."

But, as prior reporting has shown, it isn't always a quick process to get an ACA plan canceled or reinstated following an unauthorized sign-up or switch, even when a consumer discovers it themselves and reaches out to the marketplace.

Brokers and policy analysts note that some of the factors used to question enrollments — such as a plan's having no claims filed in a year — are not that unusual. Many people, for example, don't visit a doctor or hospital in a given year.

Insurers "want those healthy people in the insurance pool to help bring down the rates," said Ronnell Nolan, president and CEO of Health Agents for America, a trade group for health insurance agents. "We're against fraud, and CMS has allowed a lot of fraud to happen. But we don't want people who just didn't go to the doctor to be canceled."

And even with the outreach required by CMS, not everyone answers phone calls from unknown numbers or opens their mail or emails.

Sponsor Message

A recent marketing report found an average "open rate" on emails of 28.6%.

Policy experts also note that, while lack of a Social Security number on an ACA application could indicate a fake enrollee, it might also be an oversight, or the number might not be required, like for a child if the person applying is an adult who is not seeking coverage for the child.

"There will be legitimate people who don't have a claim or don't respond to an inquiry from an insurer," said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. "If the goal is to target fraudulent enrollment, what CMS did is better than tossing people at random, but is likely to miss the mark."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
World.content:
Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce

toggle caption i Alberto Pezzali/AP

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.

The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.

Zelenskyy complains about U.S. behavior in recent days

The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.

Sponsor Message

Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.

The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.

Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.

Sponsor Message

"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."

He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."

Starlink speed limits affect Ukraine's ability to defend itself

In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.

He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."

Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."

The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.

Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.

The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians

Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.

Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."

Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.

"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."

Sponsor Message

Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

World.title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
World.content:
Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training

Eyder Peralta/NPR

They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.

"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.

"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.

Sponsor Message

"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."

The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.

As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."

Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

Police are responding to a fatal fire involving a bus in Calgary’s northeast Saddle Ridge neighbourhood.

Police are reporting at least 10 people were injured as a result of the incident involving a City of Calgary bus. Three people have been declared dead. One person has sustained life-altering injuries and one person suffered serious injuries, according to police.

World.title: Carney says Albertans should vote 'No to the Nine' in referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Albertans should vote against the nine referendum questions focused on immigration and constitutional reform as he visited Calgary on Thursday.

"I just wanted to come here, thank you for what you've already done, thank you what you're going to do in the next few days," Carney told the crowd in the city's northeast.

"Make sure everyone's out there marking their ballots ... including, 'No to the Nine.'"

"No to the Nine" is a prominent federalist advertising campaign that urges Albertans to reject the nine ballot questions on Oct. 19, in addition to voting to remain in Canada.

Carney was meeting with volunteers and others at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park in Calgary.

Earlier, he appeared to discuss the campaign with a person holding a sign tied to a campaign from Public Interest Alberta, an education advocacy group.

"'No on the Nine' … that's good," Carney said.

WATCH | Carney says 'No to the Nine' while campaigning in Calgary: Carney says 'No to the 9' while campaigning for Canadian unity in Calgary | Duration closed caption 3:06 Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Calgary Thursday to rally Albertans to choose Option 1 to stay in Canada in Alberta's referendum on Monday. While here, he also voiced his support for the 'no' side on questions 1 to 9 that deal with immigration and constitutional changes.

In a response posted on X, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith wrote that she and Carney have found common ground on many things over the last 18 months.

"However, it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were," Smith wrote.

"Those policies caused Canada’s cost of living to skyrocket, overwhelmed our social services, and made homes and jobs unattainable for thousands of young Canadians.

"That’s why I’m encouraging Albertans to vote ‘yes to the rest’"

The prime minister has previously spoken out on the separatism question. In a Thanksgiving message delivered from a classroom in Edmonton, Carney highlighted various federal initiatives, such as the Pacific Link pipeline.

"We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines," Carney said.

Carney is scheduled to join former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for his Forever Canadian group Thursday evening, while Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver a pro-unity message at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Friday.

Carney is also expected to attend a rally on Friday at a Red Deer brewery with Smith, as well as make a stop in Edmonton the same day.

Volunteers at Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park hold placards for Alberta's referendum during a visit by Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on Oct. 15. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)

Smith, while saying she has voted to remain in Canada, has advocated for Albertans to vote "yes" to the other nine questions.

Speaking to CBC News' chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault during a one-on-one interview in Calgary last week, Smith said the nine questions are those which she "wants a mandate" on.

"I haven't been neutral on that," Smith said. "I've been persuading people that this is what we need to do."

Earlier this week, three former Alberta premiers urged voters to say "no" to the five immigration-related questions on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot.

In a statement, a spokesperson in the Prime Minister's Office wrote that Canada's government "believes in co-operative federalism that can deliver for Albertans on the issues that matter to them."

"We work continuously with the Province of Alberta on shared priorities addressing areas of concern through established processes — without needing to have a referendum that divides us at a time when we need to be strong, and we are stronger together."

Carney was also asked about his position on the nine questions while speaking on Thursday with Rishi Nagar, a host on the Calgary radio station Red FM.

"Well, the first thing is that we don't need a referendum to make progress on taking control on immigration. We've taken control on immigration," Carney said.

CBC News has requested additional comment from the Alberta premier's office.

Liberal MP says he's voting against questions

Liberal MP Corey Hogan, who represents a Calgary riding, spoke to CBC Radio's Calgary Eyeopener on Thursday about the nine other questions.

Hogan said he was voting "no" to the entire process.

"We should be asking ourselves: do we want to reward this kind of behaviour? And I don't think that we should," Hogan said.

"I don't think that we should use our country as a bargaining chip … I think the questions are quite manipulative — they're written in ways to get certain answers."

LISTEN | Liberal MP Corey Hogan talks to the Calgary Eyeopener ahead of the referendum: Calgary Eyeopener 10:05 Referendum 2026: Corey Hogan While Prime Minister, Mark Carney, is in town tonight for a pro-Canada rally at the BMO Centre, Calgary-Confederation Liberal MP, Corey Hogan, joined the show to voice his own thoughts ahead of Monday's referendum.

Although he said he'd vote "no" to all nine questions as a sort of protest to the process, he was most open to Question 7, which involves abolishing the federal Senate.

"With all love to my senator colleagues: I love senators; I don't love the Senate," he said.

World.title: How did a P.E.I. cold case fall apart just before it was set to go to trial?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

All charges related to the 1988 murder of Byron Carr were dropped after police finally revealed what they've known for years: key evidence in the case had gone missing. A well-known criminologist and cold case researcher questions why police kept that information to themselves for years. CBC's Steve Bruce reports.

There are still unanswered questions about how Charlottetown Police Services handled a high-profile P.E.I. cold case after all charges against the accused were dropped just before the case was set to go to trial.

The provincial Crown Attorney’s Office announced Tuesday that the charges against Todd Joseph Irving in connection with the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr were being withdrawn after it came to light that Charlottetown police had lost "extensive crucial evidence" in the case.

CBC News first learned about that missing evidence — which includes the knife found at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr — at a bail hearing in July. The Crown confirmed that’s when they first learned about it, too. But Charlottetown police later told CBC News they knew physical evidence was missing as far back as 2007 when the case was reopened.

Interim Charlottetown police Chief Darren MacDougall believes police did tell the Crown at some point that some items were missing, but not the full picture of how much physical evidence or exactly which items were lost.

He acknowledges that information should have been provided to the Crown sooner.

"There was likely not enough transparency with regard to the evidence as it relates to the Crown and the investigators. So there was certainly a breakdown there. I think that the investigators clung to the hope that they would be able to interview some of the people involved in 1989 to determine where they might have put these exhibits," MacDougall said.

"It’s the responsibility of the police, for full disclosure, to move that disclosure to the Crown."

But MacDougall was quick to point out that the DNA evidence collected from the items wasn’t lost — that material was processed and stored appropriately. It was the items themselves, after they’d been processed and sent back to Charlottetown police, that were misplaced.

WATCH | Calls mount for investigation into how crucial evidence was lost: Calls mount for an investigation into how crucial evidence in P.E.I. murder case was lost | Duration closed caption 2:59 Members of P.E.I.'s 2SLGBTQ+ community are calling for an independent investigation into how Charlottetown Police Services lost crucial evidence related to the 1988 murder of Byron Carr. Charlottetown's interim police chief says he welcomes an investigation, and believes one is necessary. CBC's Wayne Thibodeau reports.

Michael Arntfield is a professor and criminologist at Western University who heads up the school’s cold case research group. He’s also a former police detective.

"It’s both unusual and unfortunate because this was a great solve using state-of-the art investigative genetic genealogy, IGG, to track down the still alleged or once alleged offender in a very infamous cold case," he said.

"However, it turned out to be sort of an exploding cigar in that once, sort of, the novelty of the solve subsided … the two key pieces of evidence seem to have disappeared, which sort of pulls the rug out from underneath the whole case."

'It contaminates the whole investigation'

Arntfield believes police were hoping the DNA evidence was incontrovertible. And police have said as much.

Todd Joseph Irving walked out of court on Tuesday a free man after the charges against him in connection with the death of Byron Carr were dropped. (CBC)

"With the evidence that we relied upon, and we had significant forensic DNA evidence, we believed the evidence met the threshold to believe that [Irving] committed the offense," MacDougall said in an interview with CBC News after the charges were dropped.

At the July bail hearing, police testified that Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.

His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind, according to police testimony.

The entirety of the missing evidence isn’t clear, but the Crown described it as "the overwhelming majority of the critical physical evidence," going on to say that included "key exhibits central to the prosecution."

With that, Arntfield said, the credibility of the Charlottetown Police Services is lost — along with whatever remaining evidence they had.

"It contaminates the whole investigation because a judge or jury or both … would be left wondering, 'OK, if they have slipshod record-keeping and no chain of custody for key exhibits, what else don’t we know? What else was overlooked? What other corners were cut?'" he said.

"This isn’t corruption, this isn’t malicious. What I think it is is they were fixated on solving this, they cut corners and ultimately at the end of the day they were motivated by getting an alleged killer off the streets and ensuring justice for the family decades later."

WATCH | What happened to missing evidence? Police chief explains: What happened to missing evidence in the Byron Carr murder case? Charlottetown's interim police chief explains | Duration closed caption 9:03 All charges against Todd Joseph Irving related to the 1988 murder of Byron Carr have been dropped. The case unravelled after Charlottetown Police Services revealed the evidence crucial to securing a conviction was missing. Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, joins CBC News: Compass host Louise Martin to explain what happened.

If police had been forthcoming with the Crown about what physical evidence they did — and didn’t — have in their possession, Arntfield said the outcome could have been much different.

"You would think in a case like this — a high-profile historical homicide using a state-of-the-art and still somewhat controversial technology, IGG — that, even just as a courtesy, some senior officer or the case manager might have notified the Crown that a complex, high-profile case is coming down the pipe, apprise them of the strengths and weaknesses of the case, what witnesses are still alive and locatable and exhibits are still intact," he said.

"There’s other things that could have been done based on what police knew in order to shore up those deficiencies.… I think they would have had probably more evidence to incentivize maybe a quick guilty plea, which is I’m almost certain what police were relying on here. They were expecting a quick guilty plea and none of this suspicious disappearance of evidence would have ever seen the light of day."

Police, Crown look through different lenses: MacDougall

In Ontario, Arntfield said, cold cases get what he calls a "concierge approach," where the Crown is brought in early to weigh in on the strength of the evidence.

MacDougall acknowledges that, in this case, investigators were perhaps weighing the strength of the evidence differently than a prosecutor might.

"Perhaps the Crown, who views this through a different lens — the weight that existed with the missing exhibits measured with the weight of the DNA evidence, the forensic DNA evidence that was very compelling, I would say — [the Crown], again viewing it through a different lens, they came to the conclusion that they were unable to provide the accused with a fair trial."

Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, says he would welcome an independent investigation. (Barry Acton/CBC)

While Arntfield called the outcome of this case a rare and regrettable snafu, he said it shouldn’t erode public confidence in police.

"The investigation was solid, there was a chokepoint along the way where something happened and I wouldn’t even call it a coverup, I would say they strategically omitted that information at the last minute," he said.

"The question will be: who made the determination to suppress this glaring deficiency and suspicious disappearance and proceed at great time and expense?"

There have been calls for an independent review of how the case was handled, which MacDougall said he would welcome.

It’s up to P.E.I.'s justice and public safety minister to call such an investigation. In a statement to CBC News, the department said it was communicating with Charlottetown police about the Byron Carr case, saying " government has various options to consider in terms of a review and scope, so a particular path is not set yet. It's still under discussion."

World.title: Think you'll win the $90M Lotto Max? Here's a primer on your odds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Friday's $90 million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada — may the odds be ever in your favour.

(Even though, statistically, they're very much not.)

Draws take place every Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 p.m. ET. Tuesday's previously record-setting $85-million jackpot rolled over after no one claimed it, which allowed the prize pool to keep growing.

Lotto Max, a national lottery, announced in April that it was increasing its jackpot cap from $80 million to $90 million, but this is the first time it's actually happened.

So, what are the odds of winning? And how does this compare to past jackpots?

Let's break it down.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by two friends in London, Ont., last December. At the time, the men said they were still overcome with shock that they'd won. (OLG)

What are the odds of winning?

Don't quit your job in anticipation just yet.

The odds of winning the main jackpot are one in 33 million per $6 play, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG), the Crown agency that manages and conducts gaming and lottery operations across the province.

Let's put that into perspective.

You're almost exactly as likely to flip a coin 25 times in a row and have it land on "heads" each time — an extremely rare probability of one in 33.5 million, according to the scientifically developed coin flip probability calculator.

Meanwhile, the odds of being struck by lightning in Canada are less than one in a million, according to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.

And we're sorry to say that you're actually far more likely to be killed by an asteroid's impact on Earth on your way to buy the ticket than you are of winning the $90-million jackpot.

How does the $90M compare?

However, despite these odds, people do win the lottery. And the prizes keep growing.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by a pair of long-time friends in London, Ont., last December. They won the $80-million Lotto Max jackpot and the $403,285.40 s econd prize in the combination play option.

At the time, the men, identified only as Greg S. and Krys P., said they weren't sure how they would spend the money.

Before that, the top prize was claimed by a B.C. man who won the $80 million Lotto Max jackpot in May 2025. Justin Simporios of Surrey quit his job hours before the news conference where he claimed his cheque.

Lotto Max's first $80-million draw in September 2024, was split between two winning tickets sold in Ontario and Quebec. The first $70-million prize was in 2020, and the first $65-million draw was in 2019. (It was actually the second time the $65-million winner, a family in Montreal, had won the lottery).

The first Lotto Max draw for $60 million was in 2015, after the lottery changed the rules previously capping the jackpot at $50 million. Two years before that, however, a record-breaking $63.4 million Lotto 649 prize was split between four tickets.

Some may also recall 2005, when 17 oil and gas workers from Alberta split Canada's biggest jackpot to date, a whopping $54 million. Before that, the previous lottery record was $37.8 million, split between four tickets in a Super 7 draw in 2002.

Canada's first national lottery dates back to 1974, when nine women from Quebec City split the $1-million prize in a lottery held to raise money for the Montreal Olympics.

World.title: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia didn't pass the bar exam
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is defending her legal background, while acknowledging that she did not pass the bar exam.

In an interview with the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia said she was preparing to take the California bar exam at a time when she had just gotten married and was preparing to move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing.

"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Zacharia said.

She said the results of the bar exam, which she did not pass, were "somewhat inconsequential" because she would not need to be a barred attorney while living in China.

Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny for calling herself a "lawyer," said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.

"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."

Zacharia said she will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House role.

Showed 'ample deference' to Trump

Zacharia also spoke to Human Events about her start to her new job as press secretary — including her truncated inaugural press briefing on Tuesday.

She said she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing and that the plan had always been to keep it short because U.S. President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.

WATCH | Zacharia makes her debut: New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:00 Donald Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia took only three questions in her first briefing.

"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Zacharia said. "So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."

The initial briefing materials were given to Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed on Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps. She had been up since 3 a.m. preparing, Zacharia said.

"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.

Trump called her about job

She also revealed details about how she secured the White House press secretary job. Zacharia stressed that she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, which became vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.

Zacharia, who was a communications adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, said she closely monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.

"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job. I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."

Zacharia says that U.S. President Donald Trump called about the press secretary position on Oct. 7. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Then on Oct. 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.

She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.

World.title: Arizona university to 'part ways' with coach who oversaw training where Matthew Mayich collapsed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Arizona State University (ASU) says it will "part ways" with the hockey coach who oversaw the training at which Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout on a hot day this August.

ASU has “reached a mutual agreement to part ways with hockey coach Greg Powers,” officials said in a statement Thursday, adding that former NHL coach Dave Hakstol will replace him.

Mayich, an NHL prospect drafted by the St. Louis Blues, remains in hospital in serious condition, his family’s lawyer, Robert Carey, said Thursday.

In an initial review released last month, ASU official James Rund wrote that Mayich collapsed at a training at ASU’s Tempe campus just before 8:30 a.m. Aug. 20. The review also said coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

ASU then said it would commission an independent review, to be conducted by former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales.

Mayich's family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances around the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to his collapse. Mayich's parents say he was healthy prior to the workout. The family's lawyers said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

WATCH | Mayich family demands answers: Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout | Duration closed caption 2:26 The parents of Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old NHL prospect from Stoney Creek, Ont., speak to CBC News after their son collapsed after 'military style' training at Arizona State University. Mayich is in critical condition and unlikely to recover, says his lawyer.

Family says Powers should cooperate with investigation

"Our focus remains where it has been since August 20, on Matthew, and making sure what happened to him is fully understood and never happens to another player," the Mayich family said in a statement through Carey Thursday.

They said Bales's investigation must continue "with its full scope, gathering all digital evidence and covering everyone involved in that morning’s workout and in approving it, and its findings must be made public."

"Coach Powers’s departure should not limit his cooperation or anyone else’s, and the players who have spoken up must be protected," the family added. "We wish Coach Hakstol, his staff, and the players a safe and successful season."

Seven of Mayich's teammates anonymously sent a letter to ASU's president Michael Crow on Sept. 28, disputing some findings from the school's review of the workout that led to his collapse. Players alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

It urged that the team's coaching staff be replaced "for the period of the investigation if the facts set out in this report, together with what the investigation finds, indicate that step is appropriate."

Powers had been ASU’s head coach since 2015 and, in 2022, signed a five-year contract extension through the 2026-27 season. He was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 30, ASU said in a statement. ASU assistant coach Mike Corbett was appointed to lead the team.

University hires Colorado Avalanche assistant coach

Before ASU announced hiring Hakstol on Thursday, he had been working as an assistant coach for the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche. He previously worked as a head coach with the Philadelphia Flyers and the Seattle Kraken, as well as an assistant for the Toronto Maple Leafs.

In a post to X on Thursday afternoon, ASU said the staffing shakeup was a "new chapter of Sun Devil Hockey" and shared a statement from Hakstol which said, in part, "I couldn't be more excited to return to college and bring a winning culture to Arizona State Sun Devil Hockey."

ASU Athletics Director Graham Rossini also announced that former NHL player Matt Greene, who played for the Los Angeles Kings and Edmonton Oilers, would join the team as an assistant along with current assistant, Jimmy Mullin. Corbett’s status was not announced.

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

World.title: Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with her third child: 'This one releases in December'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hilary Swank may be 52, but it's not slowing down her family — the Yellowjackets star has announced she's pregnant with her third child.

The two-time Oscar winner is already mom to two children with her husband, Philip Schneider. After freezing her eggs at age 37, she welcomed twins Aya and Ohm in 2023 when she was 48.

Swank dropped the news on Wednesday with a light-hearted Instagram video showing her family dancing in a dark room with glow sticks on their bodies to make them look like stick figures. In the video, Swank turns around to reveal a tiny glow-stick-figure in a circle on her belly.

"A lot of people have been asking what project I'm doing next," she wrote in the caption. "This one releases in December," she added, with an emoji of a baby angel, suggesting this is when the baby is due.

Swank has previously spoken about how happy she is to have waited to have children, telling Women's Health in 2025 that she feels she's a different parent than she would've been even in her early 40s.

"I'm much more patient. I'm much more understanding," she said. "And I have my career that's already established, so I'm not divided. I'm able to really sink in and be present with them and be a hands-on parent."

The American actress won her first Oscar at 25 years old with her starring role in the 2000 film Boys Don't Cry, following it up with a second best actress Oscar for the 2004 film Million Dollar Baby. Most recently, she appeared in the Netflix series Away and Showtime's Yellowjackets.

She's also spent the past few years lobbying the California government to pass bills requiring manufacturers to disclose ingredients in diapers and in prenatal vitamins.

Swank isn't the first celebrity to welcome kids in her 50s. Pop icon Janet Jackson and supermodel Naomi Campbell both had children at age 50, in 2017 and 2021 respectively, with Campbell welcoming a second child at age 53. Brigitte Nielsen, of Beverly Hills Cop II fame, gave birth to her fifth child and only daughter in 2018 at the age of 54.

Late pregnancies a growing trend

Advanced maternal age pregnancies — defined as occurring past the age of 35 — are becoming more common in North America.

In 2021, a quarter of mothers were 35 or older when they gave birth, compared with just 16 per cent 20 years earlier, according to Statistics Canada. In the U.S. , federal data shows 21 per cent of births in 2023 were to those aged 35 or older, up from nine per cent in 1990.

Those who can get pregnant are born with a set number of eggs, which drop in number and quality as we age. This drop gets "more dramatic after your mid-to-late 30s," said Dr. Prati Sharma, a reproductive endocrinologist in Toronto, and the past president of the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society.

Natural pregnancy is possible at any time before menopause, but as eggs reduce, the odds get steeper.

Anne Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child, telling Access Hollywood in July she was "overjoyed" that it had happened.

"When you get to a certain age, that hope looks like it's about one per cent to two per cent," she said. "It's a blessing that we do not take for granted."

Anne Hathaway, 43, seen on the red carpet last month in New York City, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)

The vast majority of pregnancies as late-in-life as Swank's are possible through modern technology such as egg-freezing, implanting donor eggs and in vitro fertilization (IVF), which can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

"If you freeze your eggs or embryos at a younger age … you can use those later on in life because the uterus does not age at the same rate that ovaries do," Sharma said.

"The uterus can carry a pregnancy even upwards of 60-plus years old."

Egg-freezing allows families to press pause by extracting and preserving eggs from the ovaries at a younger age. The eggs can be stored at fertility clinics for decades, if desired, before being reimplanted when a person decides they're ready to try to conceive a child.

Swank and husband Philip Schneider attend the 80th Annual Golden Globe Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2023, prior to the birth of their twins. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

But while developments in medical care have made pregnancy and birth safer over the years, medical experts caution that the risk of complications with pregnancy still increases at an advanced maternal age.

"Yes, science can make it possible for a woman to have a child at 52. That being said, it's not without risk," Sharma said. "The fertility clinic and the doctor has to assess each patient, make sure that they're safe enough to get pregnant."

World.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate accused of making comments about Hitler
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A B.C. Conservative candidate has been dropped after he was accused of posting offensive remarks on social media.

The party says Jordan McIntosh is no longer its candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona and that if elected, he will not sit in caucus.

The Conservatives announced his removal from the slate less than an hour after Callista Ryan, the NDP’s candidate for Vancouver-Quilchena, posted screenshots on social media platform X, showing what she said were McIntosh’s posts.



"Looks like Lorne Doerkson's candidate in Strathcona Jordan McIntosh thought he could use a nameless twitter account to say many awful, offensive things," Ryan said.

Looks like Lorne Doerkson's candidate in Strathcona Jordan McIntosh thought he could use a nameless twitter account to say many awful, offensive things, including claims that Hitler didn't "specifically" hate jews and that the holocaust may not have been "the goal". https://t.co/xsxsvuQiob —callistaryan

A post under the account @DeathNight771 made claims that Hitler didn't "specifically" hate Jews and that the Holocaust may not have been "the goal."

McIntosh is a university student working toward a BA in geological engineering, according to his biography, which has since been removed from the party’s website. His LinkedIn page says he attends the University of Waterloo in Ontario.

A party spokesperson speaking on background says McIntosh was informed he was no longer a candidate shortly after Ryan's social media post. McIntosh is 18 years old and the party says it appears the posts were made when he was 15.



The Vancouver-Strathcona riding was previously held by Joan Phillip, who died on Aug. 28.

Amanda Burrows, who has served as director for First United in the Downtown Eastside, is the NDP’s candidate in that riding. It’s considered one of the safest NDP seats in the province.

This is the second time the B.C. Conservatives have dropped a candidate over offensive social media posts.

Last week, the party fired Joachim Agou in light of social media posts targeting Palestinians and Pakistanis that came to light.

WATCH | B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts: B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts | Duration closed caption 2:47 Joachim Agou was running for the Conservatives in the Victoria-Beacon Hill riding before the B.C. NDP highlighted some of his past offensive social media posts.

Doerkson has also faced calls from the Unified Muslim Associations of B.C. to drop Katy Merrifield as the party’s campaign director over anti-Islam posts.

Merrifield posted on X in June in response to a U.K. inquiry about child sexual exploitation: "F--k Islam. Defend Western civilization." The post was later removed.

During Wednesday night's B.C. leaders' debate, Doerskon defended Merrifield, saying she made the comments and has since apologized for them. He says he will not remove her.

Doerkson could not be reached for comment on McIntosh’s removal or the party's vetting process.
