World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Argentina’s bill toughening sanctions over Sea Lion stalls in Congress
World.content:
Argentina’s bill toughening sanctions over Sea Lion stalls in Congress

15th Thursday, October 2026 - 20:59 UTC Full article

The bill, sent to Congress in September, has 133 articles. The first 40 repeal the 2011 law penalising hydrocarbon exploration not authorised by Argentina and create a broader regime with fines

The National Sovereignty Defence bill, with which Javier Milei’s government seeks to toughen sanctions against those involved in exploiting resources in the Falklands, failed to secure committee approval in the Chamber of Deputies and will not reach the special session planned for October 21, according to the Argentine press. The opposition is demanding that the text, which besides sanctions reforms security, defence and intelligence, be split.

The fourth joint meeting of the Defence, Criminal Law and Foreign Affairs committees ended on Wednesday without agreement, on the same day Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to halt the Sea Lion oil project. The ruling La Libertad Avanza party refused to break up the bill.

The bill, sent to Congress in September, has 133 articles. The first 40 repeal the 2011 law penalising hydrocarbon exploration not authorised by Argentina and create a broader regime with fines, disqualifications, a public register of offenders and prison sentences of up to 20 years. According to the British newspaper The Guardian, it extends sanctions to affiliates, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers of the companies involved, and includes clauses that could reach the islands’ fishing industry. The Presidency’s Legal and Technical Secretary, María Ibarzábal Murphy, told Congress that current legislation “does not provide for fishing-related offences”.

That first part has partial opposition support, but the rest of the text is contested: the creation of a National Security Council chaired by the head of state and a protocol authorising, as a last resort, the shooting down of aircraft or sinking of vessels deemed hostile. Several blocs propose approving separately only the sanctions linked to resource exploitation.

The United Kingdom announced on Tuesday measures under its protection of trading interests legislation to prevent British companies and citizens from having to comply with Argentine rules outside Argentina’s jurisdiction.

World.title: Brazil approves a 40-hour week and two days off ten days before the runoff
World.content:
Brazil approves a 40-hour week and two days off ten days before the runoff

15th Thursday, October 2026 - 20:54 UTC Full article

Lula’s campaign hopes the reform will help him overturn the nearly two-point deficit with which he ended the first round

Brazil’s Senate on Wednesday approved, by 75 votes to one, a cut in the maximum working week from 44 to 40 hours with no reduction in pay, ending the so-called 6x1 schedule of six working days and one day off and extending to two the days off for formal-sector workers. The reform, which according to Reuters benefits some 37 million people, comes ten days before the presidential runoff between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.

“The end of the 6x1 schedule is more than a change in working hours. It is more time to live, to rest, to be with family, to watch your children grow, to take care of yourself,” said Lula, who made the shorter working week one of his legislative priorities and a pillar of his campaign. The measure will take effect 60 days after its promulgation.

Bolsonaro, who had expressed reservations and whose Liberal Party backed an alternative proposal, voted in favour remotely from Porto Alegre, where he was attending a campaign event. His party, the largest in Congress, has not ruled out making changes in the next legislature. The only vote against came from senator and retired general Hamilton Mourão, vice president under Jair Bolsonaro.

The initiative, championed in the lower house by deputy Erika Hilton of the Socialism and Liberty Party, began in 2023 with a TikTok video by Rick Azevedo, then a pharmacy worker, complaining about the exhaustion of working six days a week. Azevedo founded the Life Beyond Work movement and was elected a federal deputy on October 4.

Lula’s campaign hopes the reform will help him overturn the nearly two-point deficit with which he ended the first round. The latest Quaest poll gives Bolsonaro 47% and Lula 45%. The two candidates will face each other on Sunday in the campaign’s first debate, hosted by the Band network, the same day Bolsonaro has called his supporters to São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista. Lula, for his part, has promised 5,000 reais to every micro-entrepreneur.

World.title: Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Badenoch accuses Farage of trading Chagos for Trump’s silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch

British Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called “humiliating” a proposal by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage to offer US President Donald Trump the Chagos archipelago in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating,” she told The Telegraph.

“There is no pride in our country in the way he talks about us. This is careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security,” added Badenoch, who said it was “mad for someone who wants to be prime minister to say we should give away one piece of British territory just to stop an American president talking about another”. “The Chagos Islands are British. And the Falklands are British and will remain British, irrespective of what the American president says. When Donald Trump is right, we should say so. When he is wrong, we should have the confidence to tell him.”

On the US podcast The Benny Show, Farage had suggested offering Trump Diego Garcia “in perpetuity” in return for his silence on the Falklands. “I give him something. I ask for something back. He’d get that. He’s a businessman,” he said. A Reform UK spokesman said he was referring to US use of the base, “not the Chagos Islands as a whole”, and noted that Farage has opposed handing the archipelago to Mauritius.

The deal to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius while retaining the joint Diego Garcia base was paused in April following opposition from the US administration, although Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to see it through. According to The Telegraph, the White House even considered buying the archipelago as an alternative.

The same newspaper notes that Trump said in August he was reviewing the US position on British sovereignty over the Falklands, amid a dispute over defence spending. Burnham assured him in September in New York that the United Kingdom would defend “the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British”.

World.title: US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly
World.content:
US lifts sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 22:02 UTC Full article

The US Treasury Department on Wednesday removed from its sanctions list Jorge Rodríguez, president of Venezuela’s National Assembly and brother of acting president Delcy Rodríguez. The Treasury did not explain the reasons for the decision.

Rodríguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was taken off the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, which entails the blocking of assets in the United States, a ban on entering the country and a prohibition on transactions with US citizens and companies. He had been designated in September 2018, along with his sister, former first lady Cilia Flores and then defence minister Vladimir Padrino. At the time, the Treasury said Nicolás Maduro had given them “high-ranking positions” in the government to help him “remain in power”.

Rodríguez was removed from the list in April, which allowed her to travel to New York in September for the UN General Assembly, where she met US President Donald Trump. Rodríguez took power after Maduro and Flores were detained in a US military operation in Caracas in January; both face charges in New York of drug trafficking and, since last week, of torture and repression.

Since then, the Rodríguez government has negotiated an oil agreement with Washington, announced in August, which according to El País gives the United States majority control over a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, the largest in the world. According to Reuters, the Rodríguez siblings pushed legal changes to further open the energy and mining sectors to foreign companies.

Presidential elections remain without a date. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio received in Washington Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in talks with the Venezuelan government, with no announcements. Opposition leader María Corina Machado is not taking part in that dialogue and has been unable to return to Venezuela.

World.title: Farage proposes offering Trump Diego Garcia in exchange for his silence on the Falklands
World.content:
Farage proposes offering Trump Diego Garcia in exchange for his silence on the Falklands

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:53 UTC Full article

“I’d have gone in and said, ‘Right, you know what mate? Chagos, it’s yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world’,” Farage said

Reform UK leader c has said that, if he were prime minister, he would offer US President Donald Trump the use in perpetuity of the Diego Garcia military base, in the Chagos archipelago, in exchange for him to stop talking about the Falklands. The proposal sparked a clash with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who called it “humiliating”, and prompted the White House to come to Farage’s defence.

“I’d have gone in and said, ‘Right, you know what mate? Chagos, it’s yours. Diego Garcia, in perpetuity, the most strategic American military base in the world’,” Farage told the US podcast The Benny Show. “In return, just please stop talking about the Falkland Islands. I know you like Milei, but this really matters to us. And there’s a trade, you see.”

Badenoch responded in The Telegraph: “Giving away British territory in return for someone keeping quiet is not a deal. It is humiliating.” She added that “the Chagos Islands are British, and the Falklands are British and will remain British, regardless of what the American president says”, calling Farage’s remarks “careless, loose talk from a man who wants to be responsible for Britain’s national security”.

Farage didn't say that Trump/USA could use the Chagos Islands in perpetuity. In his interview he literally said he would trade the Chagos Islands for the Falklands. Reform officials and Farage can deny it all they like, but the evidence is right there and cannot be altered. https://t.co/84HYJw12sf — Thomas Evans @Renewal2030 (@ThomasEvansAdur) October 14, 2026

Farage replied on X that Badenoch “is lying again” and said he would offer the United States the use of Diego Garcia, not sovereignty over the archipelago, in return for America going “quiet on the Falklands”. A White House official quoted by The Times agreed: “He was obviously referring to the use of the Diego Garcia military base, which is critical to countering threats from China and Iran,” and accused Badenoch of peddling fake news and undermining the Anglo-American relationship.

The agreement signed by the British government in 2025 to transfer sovereignty over Chagos to Mauritius, with a 99-year lease for the base, is on hold following Trump’s opposition. The row comes amid an escalating dispute over the Sea Lion oil project: on Tuesday, Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran told the House of Commons that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had raised with Trump the islanders’ wish to remain British.

World.title: What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion
World.content:
What are the red notices Argentina has sought from Interpol over Sea Lion

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:45 UTC Full article

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat

Argentina has requested Interpol red notices against individuals linked to the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, and the United Kingdom has asked the organisation to reject them as “politically motivated”, according to the British newspaper The Guardian. Interpol responded by reaffirming Article 3 of its constitution, which prohibits any intervention or activity of a political character.

A red notice is a request to police worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. It is not an international arrest warrant: Interpol reviews each request before circulating it, but each state decides whether to act. According to the newspaper, British officials are concerned that Argentina could persuade other countries that its requests are based on domestic law rather than political motives. It has not emerged how many people are affected or whether any notice has been issued.

The chief executive of the islands’ government, Andrea Clausen, acknowledged that the use of Interpol poses a threat. “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action,” she said. “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.” Workers in the oil and fishing sectors fear being detained if they travel, particularly to South America.

Argentina has launched criminal proceedings against Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, the project’s partners. British officials quoted by The Guardian describe Argentina’s campaign as the most serious since the 1982 war. On Tuesday, London announced measures to shield its companies from Argentine sanctions, and Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion.

World.title: HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol
World.content:
HMS Protector breaks down and leaves UK without an Ice Patrol

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 21:10 UTC Full article

HMS Protector at Devonport Dockyard, Plymouth

Britain has been left without its Ice Patrol after HMS Protector on Tuesday suffered engine problems and had to be towed back to Plymouth, according to reports in the media. This could speed the Royal Navy’s assessment as to whether the vessel originally built in Norway and now with 25 years of rough seas in both poles has to be replaced.

The breakdown comes at a critical moment, when world powers are rushing to take advantage of navigation opportunities in the Arctic, particularly Russia, and in the southern seas, with as ever aggressive Argentina threatening the Falkland Islands development of its resources.

The Telegraph reports that Royal Navy sources admitted the situation as a “catastrophic failure”. And Commander Tom Sharpe, who commanded HMS Endurance, Protector’s predecessor, said it would be “poor timing” to remove the ship from service.

In March, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, admitted that the Navy was not ready for war. It has five active frigates, six destroyers and two aircraft carriers, alongside a submarine fleet of six Astute-class attack boats and four Vanguard-class subs, which carry the UK’s nuclear weapons.

Both carriers, HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth, have reported mechanical problems since their maiden voyages.

Military chiefs are waiting for the spending review for details about how the Government will meet a long-term Nato pledge of increasing the core defense budget to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035.

HMS Protector underpins the UK’s presence in the British Antarctic Territory, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

In 2008, HMS Endurance, the Navy’s previous icebreaker, suffered a flood caused by “poor engineering standards”. At the time, the Navy insisted that she would be repaired and returned to sea. However, she was not and was eventually replaced by HMS Protector after around three years.

HMS Protector was originally named MV Polarbjørn, meaning Polar bear in Norwegian, before being leased in 2011 by the Navy for £8.7m a year. The UK government paid £51m to own the ship outright in 2013. Later refurbished, HMS Protector should expect to have another decade of use before being withdrawn from service.

With a crew of 88, she is typically lightly armed carrying machine guns, but often carries a detachment of Royal Marines. Although classed as a Royal Navy warship, the vessel has retained her original red and white paint scheme. The Royal Navy website says she is affectionately referred to as the “Swiss army knife – red, versatile, and always there when you need her!”

Last month, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, described HMS Protector as an “essential presence” and confirmed she would be replaced at the end of her service life. He said the Ministry of Defense would replace HMS Protector with “a more modern variant” to ensure support for government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory would continue.

A Royal Navy spokesman said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place. As part of the defense investment plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability.

World.title: A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile
World.content:
A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 07:01 UTC Full article

An electrical storm with hail, unusual in the middle of spring, flooded streets, homes and businesses in Santiago, Chile, on Tuesday and produced a tornado that the Chilean Meteorological Directorate preliminarily classified as EF0, the lowest intensity category. The national disaster prevention and response service declared a red alert in the Metropolitan Region, five days after the mudslide that hit the Las Condes district.

The tornado struck a bus terminal in Estación Central, in the west of the capital, where the gust lifted dozens of zinc sheets into the air. The storm began around 3:30pm, as students and workers were leaving schools and offices, and within minutes flooded avenues, underground car parks and buildings, in some cases with water coming through the roofs. According to regional governor Claudio Orrego, around 20 millimetres fell in about two and a half hours, and districts such as Independencia and Providencia recorded some 18 millimetres in one hour.

Some 22,000 homes were left without electricity, according to the Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels. Classes were suspended at municipal schools in Santiago, Providencia and Ñuñoa, and Las Condes extended its restricted-movement perimeter because of the risk of further landslides. Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said “all emergency institutions” had been activated and that the rain was expected to ease overnight.

“Because of global warming, weather processes are intensifying. And we have just had an electrical storm like none ever seen in Santiago,” climatologist Alejandro Vial told the newspaper El País, linking the episode to El Niño.

Last week, an atmospheric river intensified by El Niño made this the wettest October on record in the Chilean capital and caused the October 8 mudslide in San Carlos de Apoquindo, which left six people injured and around 2,000 homes damaged.

World.title: 2,500-year-old astronomical observatory discovered in Puebla is the oldest in Mexico
World.content:
A pre-Hispanic solar observatory has been discovered in the municipality of Teteles de Ávila Castillo in the Sierra Norte region of Puebla.

According to research carried out by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), a monumental architectural complex named “Grupo E” that dates back more than 2,500 years functioned as a solar astronomical observatory and is the oldest of its kind in Mexico.

Researchers believe the settlement’s inhabitants incorporated astronomical observations into the planning of their ceremonial buildings more than two millennia ago.

Heritage Daily —a digital publication specializing in archaeology, anthropology and palaeontology — says the discovery “provides remarkable evidence of sophisticated astronomical knowledge among ancient Mesoamerican civilizations.”

INAH says it is the first discovery of its kind outside the Maya region and is comparable to the observatory at the archaeological site of Uaxactún in Petén, Guatemala, which has been identified as the first and defining archetype for ancient Maya astronomical observation complexes.

While both the Uaxactún and Teteles complexes are believed to date to the Middle Preclassic (from 1200 to 400 BCE.), the Uaxactún structure is approximately twice the size of the one in Puebla.

Researchers have confirmed that the original layout of the “Group E” settlement (also known as Tetelihtic) and the orientation of its pyramidal structures are based on an understanding of celestial bodies.

Archaeologist Alberto Diez Barroso said the ancient settlement is an outstanding example of pre-Hispanic urban planning — shaped by the observation of the surrounding landscape, such as the nearby mountain peaks, as well as the astronomical horizon — making it “a significant point of reference for Mesoamerican studies in this field.”

Tetelihtic consists of a quadrangular courtyard flanked by two platforms at its eastern and western ends. The eastern platform is elongated (90 m from south to north by 40 m from east to west), while the western structure is smaller (46 m from north to south by 27 m from east to west) and served as an observation point.

The elongated platform does not mark the equinoxes at its center, however.

“It apparently served to establish the beginning of the pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican calendar in February and the harvest period in October, making it a complex and unique feature,” Diez said.

However, the eastern platform did function as a solar calendar; observations have confirmed that, from its front, one can track the sun’s path at dawn during the equinoxes and solstices.

Archaeologists believe the finding could provide insights into the cultural relationship between the Huastec and Maya groups during the early stages of human settlement in the Sierra Norte as it serves to confirm the Maya ethnolinguistic roots of the Huastec groups.

A Maya presence at Teteles may date back as far as 3,000 years — a possibility suggested by the Puebla observatory.

With reports from INAH, Heritage Daily and Ambas Manos

World.title: Mexico targets cheap Chinese bicycles with six-month anti-dumping duty
World.content:
Mexico has imposed a provisional anti-dumping duty of US $68.60 per unit on adult bicycles originating from China, after the Economy Ministry preliminarily determined that Chinese bicycles were being sold below fair market value, harming domestic manufacturers.

The measure, which took effect on Oct. 13, will remain in place for six months and will apply to adult bicycles with a wheel size larger than 20 inches, including urban and mountain models, with or without gears, as well as unassembled units. Electric bicycles and racing or road bikes are excluded from the measure.

The decision traced back to an anti-dumping investigation requested in April 2025 by the National Association of Bicycle Manufacturers and the companies Mercurio, Veloci, Benotto and Línea Siete. The investigation formally began in August of that year.

According to preliminary results, Chinese bicycles accounted for 95% of Mexico’s imports of adult bicycles in 2024. Apparent national consumption of Chinese bicycles rose from 53% in 2022 to 61% in 2024, while the average price of imports fell 35% during that period.

In 2024, Chinese bicycles cost 27% less than their domestic counterparts. According to the Economy Ministry, this difference pressured the Mexican industry to reduce prices by 4% to stay competitive.

As more low-cost Chinese bicycles entered the country, Mexican manufacturers saw a significant drop in business. The Economy Ministry found that between 2022 and 2024, adult bicycle production fell by 34% and domestic sales declined by 32%. Meanwhile, employment dropped by 29%.

Sales revenue in the domestic market fell by 36% in the same period, while the industry’s operating profits swung into the red, a 111% drop. These figures led investigators to conclude that low-priced Chinese imports caused material harm to Mexican manufacturers.

During the six months that the preliminary duty will remain in effect, interested parties may submit evidence for or against the measures, while the investigation continues to determine whether to establish more permanent duties.

The provisional anti-dumping duty is part of a broader trend toward increased trade protection in Mexico. According to data from the Economy Ministry, imports falling under the 1,463 tariff classifications subject to new levies — approved in December 2025 — declined by 23% between January and May 2026, compared to the same period the previous year.

China, the primary supplier of the goods subject to duties, was the hardest hit, as its tariffed goods fell by 28% — from $10.1 billion to $7.2 billion.

With reports from Milenio and Diario de Tabasco

World.title: American Airlines is the latest carrier to drop service to Tulum
World.content:
American Airlines is dropping flights from Miami to the Yucatán Peninsula destination of Tulum as part of its cutback of several international routes, including its Charlotte-Los Cabos service.

American (AA) — the largest U.S. airline by passenger numbers — joins other major carriers, including Aeroméxico and Volaris, in dropping or pausing routes to the resort town on the state of Quintana Roo’s Caribbean coast.

AA had already announced that its Miami-Tulum route would be on seasonal pause through Nov. 19, after which it would continue again until Dec. 1. The current plan is to then resume service one last time from Dec. 17 to January 5, 2027, before stopping it completely.

Los Cabos is also slated for service cuts

AA ended its service to Tulum from Charlotte, North Carolina, in February, 2025, less than a year after its launch. Next year, the only AA route from the U.S. to Tulum will be from or through the Dallas/Fort Worth hub.

American has also announced plans to remove its Charlotte-San José del Cabo route from its future schedule, after its current seasonal pause. The route was originally planned to return to normal operations in November, but the schedule now reportedly shows only sporadic operations.

That limited service will end in August of 2027. A possible motive for the discontinuation is that the route’s flights on average were just 73.69% full between June 2025 and June 2026.

With reports from Simple Flying

World.title: Rachel death toll rises to 8 in Baja California as newly formed Hurricane Trudy heads for Jalisco coast
World.content:
While Pacific Coast residents are still reeling from the passage of Polo, Rachel and Simon, the newly formed Hurricane Trudy threatens to bring more chaos and disruption to the region.

Eight deaths have been attributed to Hurricane Rachel, while at least four people remain missing and the military has been actively carrying out search and rescue operations. And Simon, lurking near the Jalisco coast south of the tip of the Baja California Peninsula, is expected to remain a Category 1 hurricane through Friday.

In light of the devastation, President Claudia Sheinbaum on Thursday activated the Defense Ministry’s DN-III emergency protection plan and the Navy’s “Plan Marina.”

Sheinbaum also ordered the Interior Ministry to stay in close contact with the Baja California governor in order to provide any support that may be needed, especially as Simon is expected to move toward the peninsula on Saturday.

Last month, Polo — the second most-intense Pacific hurricane on record — made consecutive landfalls on the peninsula and then mainland Mexico on Sept. 29.

Now comes Trudy, which became a hurricane before dawn Thursday.

The storm system was located about 300 miles (480 kilometers) southwest of Acapulco and 445 miles (720 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo, Colima, while registering maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h), with gusts of 93 mph (150 km/h).

According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC), Trudy is undergoing a period of rapid intensification as it moves northwest at 9 mph (15 km/h) and is expected to bring heavy rains to Oaxaca and Guerrero today (Thursday).

Forecast models project it will become a major hurricane as it approaches the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico this weekend, bringing rainfall of 4 to 8 inches (101 to 203 millimeters) through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco states.

Meanwhile, Simon remains virtually “frozen” a few hundred kilometers west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, and is expected to continue orbiting in place with sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km/h) and gusts of 95 mph (150 km/h).

Sustained winds were about 130 miles (210 kilometers) per hour as the week began, and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the Jalisco coast.

The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper Simon’s intensity and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC said. Still, as the storm system weakened from a Category 4 to Category 1 it delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, Colima.

With reports from La Jornada, The Associated Press, El Economista, Meteored and CNN en Español

World.title: International tourist spending grows 8% in August despite a dip in arrivals
World.content:
International tourist arrivals in Mexico declined year over year in August for the first time in almost a year, according to official data, even as total expenditure by international tourists increased by over 8%.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported Wednesday that 3.76 million international tourists came to Mexico in August, a decline of 0.5% compared to the same month of 2025.

International tourists are classified as foreign residents who spend at least one night in Mexico during their visit to the country.

In August, 1.39 million of the 3.76 million international tourists flew into the country, a decline of 6.5% compared to a year earlier. International tourist arrivals by air declined during every month between February and August.

The remainder of the international tourists in August entered Mexico by land, with most of that cohort staying within the northern or southern border region. INEGI’s data shows that two-thirds (67.1%) of the tourists who came to Mexico in August and traveled beyond the border regions are residents of the United States.

The year-over-year decline in international tourist arrivals in August was the first annual decrease since September 2025.

Humberto Molina, an expert in tourism economics at the consultancy firm Grupo Empresarial Estrategia, attributed the decline to a range of factors, including the presence of sargassum on Mexican beaches, insecurity and a lack of tourism promotion.

International tourist expenditure increased 8.1% in August

While in Mexico in August, international tourists collectively spent US $2.16 billion, an increase of 8.1% compared to the same month of 2025.

Each international tourist spent $573.30 on average, up 8.6% from August 2025.

Individual expenditure by international tourists who flew into Mexico was more than double that amount at $1,269.60, an increase of 15.2% compared to August 2025.

International tourists who flew into Mexico collectively spent $1.77 billion while in the country, a figure that accounts for 82% of total international tourism expenditure.

Despite decline in international tourists, international traveler numbers reached a record high in August

While international tourist numbers declined 0.5% year over year in August, international traveler numbers increased 1.3% to reach 7.98 million, the highest figure on record for the month of August.

INEGI’s international travelers category includes international tourists and international day-trippers (excursionistas internacionales). The latter enter Mexico by land or sea but don’t stay the night. International day-trippers include cruise ship passengers and people who spend a few hours in Mexico after entering the country via border crossings with the United States, Guatemala and Belize.

Just over 4.2 million international day-trippers came to Mexico in August, an increase of 3% compared to the same month of last year. Around 81% of the international day trippers (3.43 million) entered Mexico by land, while 785,558 came into the country by sea. Sea arrivals increased by 12.3% compared to August 2025, while land arrivals rose 1.1%.

Total spending by international travelers in Mexico in August was $2.4 billion, a 7% increase compared to a year earlier. International tourists spent 90% of that amount, while international day-trippers contributed the other 10%.

While expenditure rose in dollar terms, it declined 5.51% annually in real peso terms, according to Banco Base analysts, who took inflation and the USD:MXN exchange rate into account. The USD:MXN exchange rate was 17 at the end of August compared to 18.66 a year earlier.

More than 32 million international tourists came to Mexico between January and August

INEGI data shows that 32.68 million international tourists came to Mexico in the first eight months of 2026, a year-over-year increase of 3.9%.

International traveler numbers rose 6.3% annually in the same period to reach 67.69 million.

In a statement, Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez said that data from the first eight months of the year indicates that “Mexico could end 2026 with a record in international tourist arrivals.”

“Mexico is in vogue and we’re continuing to work so that more people visit us, get to know our cultural and natural wealth and contribute to the well-being of communities,” she said.

Total expenditure by international travelers in Mexico was $24.15 billion between January and August, an increase of 0.9% compared to the same period of last year.

Mexico is one of the world’s 10 most visited countries, ranking sixth or seventh in recent years. One of the goals of the federal government’s Plan Mexico economic initiative is to make Mexico one of the world’s top five tourism destinations by 2030.

With reports from El Economista, La Jornada and Reporte Indigo

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Brugada’s big plans, a sinking city and methane mitigation
World.content:
In this week’s MND Local for CDMX, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada touted her administration’s accomplishments and outlined future priorities during her second annual “state of the city” address. Meanwhile, new research highlights the capital’s ongoing sinking problem, and officials are pursuing efforts to reduce the city’s methane emissions.

Let’s get into it.

Mayor Brugada delivers 2nd ‘state of the city’ address

Earlier this month, Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada delivered a “state of the city” address, touting her administration’s accomplishments across various sectors, including social services, security, infrastructure and healthcare. It was Brugada’s second such address since she assumed office on Oct. 7, 2024.

The theme of Brugada’s speech was “utopias,” which she said are the cornerstone of her administration’s policies.

“We want to build the city of Utopias, the city where all possible utopias fit: the utopia of well-being, democracy, social justice, fraternity and freedom,” Brugada, who belongs to the ruling Morena Party, said.

She touched on several future priorities and projects the administration intends to carry out, including criminal justice reform that centers on reintegration, establishing three new public universities outside Mexico City’s core, and constructing five new high schools that serve the city’s Indigenous population.

Utopian visions

Meanwhile, she touted myriad accomplishments over the past two years, such as a 48 billion peso (US $2.6 billion) investment in the city’s metro system, resulting in 100 kilometers of electric bus routes. She also pointed to 1 million square meters of public space that have been reclaimed, 600 new public women’s spaces, a 1 billion peso (US $54 million) investment in agriculture, and an 85% increase in social programs, which now cover 2.6 million people across the capital, among other things.

“Let’s continue building all possible utopias,” Brugada said during her address, per La Gazzetta DF. “Let’s strive for more, for much more. With the memory of those who fought before and the hope of those who will come after. This is our city, this is our time, this is our history, and we are writing it together.”

While Brugada’s approval rating currently stands at 60%, according to the most recent polling from El Financiero, her tenure has not been without controversy.

During her speech, Brugada touted a significant reduction in crime over the past two years, including a 24% dip in “high-impact crimes” and four consecutive months with homicides at historic lows. However, her administration’s failure to hold anyone accountable for the assassinations of two of her deputies in 2025 continues to dog her legacy.

Mexico City is sinking … still

A new study published Oct. 12 in “Nature Cities” suggests that areas of Mexico City are sinking as much as 8.5 inches per year, while the citywide average sits somewhere around 0.3 inches per year.

The study, led by Shengli Tao and Xie Hu of Beijing’s Peking University, used high-resolution satellite data collected over nine years, from 2014 to 2023. Of the 465 cities across 107 countries that were surveyed, Mexico City recorded the fastest localized sinking.

The 8.5-inch figure hovers around a similar analysis published in May, which found that Mexico City is sinking by nearly 10 inches (about 25 centimeters) a year and has sunk by nearly 40 feet over the past century.

That study relied on NASA satellite data from NISAR, a joint U.S.-India satellite project. NISAR uses advanced radar imaging — effectively a microscope in space — to measure changes in Earth’s land, ice, sea level rise and groundwater.

It’s a different approach from Tao and Hu’s team, which used satellite interferometric synthetic aperture radar, which basically functions like a ruler that measures ground movement over time.

Mexico City details methane mitigation efforts

Meanwhile, Mexico City is attempting to tackle a significant driver of global warming — methane emissions.

Earlier this month, the city hosted Mexico Climate Week, which included a session dubbed “Accelerating Methane Action in Mexico City.” The event brought together domestic and international stakeholders representing government, academia, civil society and the private sector.

According to Ricardo Cepeda of the U.S.-based nonprofit C40 Cities, methane mitigation efforts are one of the best, most demonstrable ways to slow climate change in the near future.

“The objective is not to create more strategies, plans or projects,” Cepeda said. “The objective is to reduce methane emissions.”

Despite Cepeda warning governments off endless strategy meetings, Maritza Florez, who works with Mexico City’s Environment Ministry, did just that, detailing the capital’s methane mitigation strategy. It includes preventing food waste, expanding composting infrastructure and developing four additional treatment facilities for organic waste.

While much of the infrastructural onus lies with city leaders, residents are encouraged to develop composting and food waste prevention initiatives in their own communities.

“Methane mitigation is the brake for climate change,” said Mexico City Environment Ministry Secretary Julia Álvarez Icaza, adding that better waste management and separation systems are key to controlling the capital’s methane emissions.

“When waste is not mixed, it can be valued and utilized. When it is mixed, it becomes garbage,” Icaza said.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Which states have the most welfare beneficiaries?
World.content:
In her second annual report speech on Sept. 1, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that federal welfare, social and employment programs would benefit almost 43 million Mexicans in 2026.

In other words, about one in three Mexicans was slated to receive money from a federal program, among which are pension schemes, employment initiatives and scholarships for public school students.

Sheinbaum held up the reach of the various programs as a major achievement of her government, which, like its predecessor, has embraced the motto, “For the good of all, the poor come first.”

“Me dediqué a servir al Pueblo. Me siento muy orgulloso, muy contento, de que atendimos a todos, escuchamos a todos, respetamos a todos, pero les dimos preferencia a los más necesitados. ‘Por el Bien de Todos: Primero los Pobres’”. Última Mañanera del presidente @lopezobrador_. pic.twitter.com/reAmS0qjgR — Michael Oviedo (@Mike_Oviedo) September 30, 2024

Spending one trillion pesos on government welfare, social and employment programs — as the government is doing in 2026 — not only allows the Sheinbaum administration to provide monetary support to millions of disadvantaged Mexicans, but also shores up political support for the president and the ruling Morena party, according to analysts.

Three weeks after Sheinbaum delivered her Sept. 1 speech, the national statistics agency INEGI published a report on the results of its 2025 Intercensal Survey, which contains a wealth of data, including national and state statistics on the percentage of households that receive income from government programs.

Four of the five states with the highest percentage of households with at least one person receiving monetary support from federal and/or state authorities are among the five states where Sheinbaum obtained her highest vote shares in the 2024 presidential election. They are Guerrero, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco — poor southern states whose residents have benefited in large numbers from the federal programs launched by the government of former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador and continued by the Sheinbaum administration.

In this “Mexico in Numbers” article, we present the INEGI data on households that received payments from government programs in 2025.

World.title: Human rights commission investigates alleged police brutality in Guadalajara: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

Of the revenue, 57% would go to the Ministry of National Defense, 15% to the National Migration Institute and 28% to the federal treasury.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Thursday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum weighed in on two significant events in recent days: Abuses allegedly committed by police at a protest in Guadalajara on Sunday and the release of a man identified as a criminal leader just hours after he was captured on Monday in the state of Morelos.

A day after saying that her government “cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum acknowledged that the nation’s human rights watchdog is investigating the conduct of Jalisco state police at Sunday’s protest against water contamination in the Guadalajara metro area.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the government’s confirmation that it is proposing to increase the fee non-resident foreigners pay to enter Mexico by 17.8%.

CNDH investigating possible human rights violations at Guadalajara protest

Sheinbaum told reporters that the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) is now investigating alleged police abuses during a protest against water contamination in Guadalajara on Sunday.

Police used water cannons and tear gas against protesters and allegedly tortured some of 39 people who were detained during the demonstration.

On Wednesday, Sheinbaum said that the CNDH has to conduct a “very thorough investigation” into allegations of torture.

“The issue of torturing young people is something that has to disappear in our country,” she said.

“… How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” Sheinbaum asked.

On Thursday, she said that the CNDH will investigate “the use of water and gases in the march” and “the arrest of some young people, who were primarily beaten.”

“CNDH is now doing its work in Jalisco,” Sheinbaum said.

The CNDH said in a statement that it was investigating “possible violations of human rights during a protest for access to potable water in Guadalajara,” where water contamination is a long-running problem.

“The objective is to guarantee an expeditious and impartial investigation … into the alleged acts of repression committed by state security officers,” the commission said.

‘The important thing is the protection of citizens,’ Sheinbaum says after alleged crime boss is freed

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about the decision by Morelos authorities to release an alleged criminal leader captured hours earlier. State authorities freed José David Vergara, an alleged leader of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group, on Monday to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers.

Sheinbaum said she didn’t want to create controversy about the decision, but added that “the important thing is the protection of citizens.”

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that the decision taken by Morelos authorities was motivated by the desire to “save lives.”

“There were a lot of civilian people in the streets,” he said, suggesting that their lives could have been endangered by a violent reaction from the Pueblos Unidos criminal group if Vergara wasn’t released.

The capture and subsequent release of Vergara was reminiscent of the capture and release of Ovidio Guzmán López in Culiacán, Sinaloa, in 2019. The capture of Guzmán López, a drug trafficker and son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera, triggered a hostile response from the Sinaloa Cartel, leading authorities to release him in an attempt to quell the violence in the Sinaloa capital.

Tourist fee to increase by 175 pesos in 2027

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez confirmed that the government is proposing that the Derecho de No Residente (DNR) — an entry fee charged to non-resident foreigners entering Mexico, with some exemptions — increase by 175 pesos next year, from 983 pesos to 1,158 pesos (about US $63).

She noted that the proposed increase — subject to congressional approval — is 50% lower than the hike that was originally put forward.

According to a bill that proposes the DNR increase, 57% of the revenue raised will go to the Ministry of National Defense, 15% will go to the National Migration Institute (INM) and 28% will go to the federal treasury.

According to a Tourism Ministry statement, “173.70 pesos of the additional 175 pesos would be allocated to the INM to strengthen technological infrastructure, border security, and immigration control systems.”

SENEGAL · BUDGET

Key Facts — The country Senegal is a West African democracy and new oil and gas producer that uses the CFA franc, a currency pegged to the euro.

— What happened Senegal sent its draft 2027 budget to parliament, planning a deficit of 4.7% of economic output, against 7.6% in 2026.

— The numbers The deficit is about US$2.3 billion, on revenue of about US$10.2 billion and spending of about US$12.6 billion; interest alone costs about US$2.2 billion.

— Why it matters Senegal is negotiating with foreign bondholders and awaiting a US$2.2 billion IMF programme, and this budget is the plan both will judge.

— The catch Almost the whole deficit is interest on past debt, and the plan assumes growth of only 2.4% and a return of cheap foreign loans.

— Still open The date of the Assembly vote, the IMF board decision and the terms of any deal with bondholders are not known.

The Senegal budget deficit would fall to 4.7% of economic output in 2027, from 7.6% in 2026, under a draft bill before the National Assembly. That is FCFA 1,351.7 billion (about US$2.3 billion), against FCFA 1,735.2 billion (about US$3.0 billion) this year.

For US readers, the bill is the yardstick for Senegal’s foreign bondholders and the International Monetary Fund, known as the IMF. Dakaractu, Seneweb and Le Soleil published the figures on Wednesday 14 and Thursday 15 October.

What the Draft Budget Says

The bill counts on revenue of FCFA 6,012.1 billion (about US$10.2 billion), up 2.8% on the adjusted 2026 budget. Spending would fall 2.9% to FCFA 7,363.7 billion (about US$12.6 billion), a cut of roughly FCFA 220 billion (about US$375 million).

Seneweb, a Dakar news site, reported the Senegal budget deficit figures on Wednesday 14 October from the main lines of the draft law. The Senegal budget deficit plan rests on growth of 2.4% and inflation of 2.7%, according to the Ndarinfo news site.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where the Savings Come From

The Senegal budget deficit shrinks mainly because general spending is cut, not because the state collects much more, Seneweb and Dakaractu wrote. Domestic revenue outside oil and gas is planned to rise only 0.2%, against a long-run trend above 8%, Dakaractu reported.

Energy subsidies, the state money that keeps fuel and power prices low, are on the cutting list, according to Ndarinfo. The cost is to fall to 1% of output a year by 2029, while small butane cylinders stay protected.

Interest Eats Almost the Whole Budget Deficit

Interest and debt fees come to FCFA 1,303.9 billion (about US$2.2 billion), about 96% of the planned deficit and about 22% of revenue. Before interest, the gap would be only FCFA 47.7 billion (about US$81 million), down from FCFA 450 billion (about US$767 million) in 2026.

The state also needs FCFA 6,608.7 billion (about US$11.3 billion) of financing in total. Of that, FCFA 4,552 billion (about US$7.8 billion) repays old debt and FCFA 480 billion (about US$818 million) clears arrears owed to domestic firms.

The IMF Programme Behind the Numbers

IMF staff and Dakar agreed on 1 September on a three-year credit facility of about US$2.2 billion. The Fund’s board has not yet approved it, and the money depends on Dakar fixing the misreporting of its debt.

The finance ministry expects over FCFA 800 billion (about US$1.4 billion) of cheap, long-term loans and budget support in 2027. The bill calls the return of such concessional financing the key to covering the budget.

Hidden Debt and the Bondholder Talks

The pressure traces back to a 2025 audit by the Court of Auditors, which found far more public debt than the previous government reported. The Fund later said the underreporting was deliberate, and Senegal’s earlier programme was frozen.

Dakar wants to rework its foreign debt, including Eurobonds, and a group of bondholders holding about US$2.2 billion warned against a haircut. A haircut means creditors accept less than they are owed.

Support for Poorer Families and New Taxes

Ndarinfo reported that family security grants for poor households double to FCFA 140 billion (about US$239 million), from FCFA 70 billion (about US$119 million). The programme would reach 1,000,649 households.

New stamp taxes are planned on sugary drinks, alcohol and tobacco, along with a tax on foreign digital services and a phone registration platform. The tax burden is put at 17.5% of output, according to Seneweb.

What It Means for US Readers

Holders of Senegal’s dollar bonds will read this budget as the starting point of the talks, since the deficit shapes the relief Dakar can seek. The United States is the IMF’s largest shareholder, so a failed plan could delay the Fund’s money.

Interest takes almost the whole Senegal budget deficit, so a small miss on revenue or growth would reopen the gap. The CFA franc is fixed to the euro, and on 15 October it traded at 586.7 per US$.

What Is Not Known

The date of the National Assembly vote and any changes to the Senegal budget deficit target are not known. The IMF board has not set a date to approve the programme.

Dakar has not said whether it will ask bondholders to take a loss on principal, or how large any cut would be. The growth forecast of 2.4% and the revenue gains are government assumptions that have yet to be tested.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Senegal’s planned budget deficit for 2027?

The Senegal budget deficit is set at FCFA 1,351.7 billion (about US$2.3 billion), or 4.7% of economic output. That compares with 7.6% in the adjusted 2026 budget.

How does Senegal plan to cut the deficit?

Mostly by spending less, with total spending down 2.9% while revenue rises 2.8%. Energy subsidies are on the cutting list.

Why does debt interest matter so much?

Interest and fees of FCFA 1,303.9 billion (about US$2.2 billion) equal almost the whole Senegal budget deficit. Without them, the budget would be close to balance.

What is the IMF’s role?

IMF staff agreed on 1 September to a three-year credit facility of about US$2.2 billion, but the Fund’s board has not approved it. The budget is the fiscal plan behind that deal.

Is the CFA franc tied to the dollar?

No, the CFA franc is fixed to the euro, so its dollar value moves with the euro. On 15 October the rate was 586.7 per US$.

Is the budget final?

No, the bill is a draft that the National Assembly must still debate and vote. The date of the vote has not been announced.
