World.title: JC appeals ISSA sanctions over Jamone Lyle, says procedure was unfair
World.content:
Jamaica College forward Jamone Lyle. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica College (JC) has appealed sanctions imposed by the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) over the eligibility of footballer Jamone Lyle, with the school’s Board of Management Chairman Lance Hylton describing the penalties as “unsupportable, extreme and excessive”.

In an update to the school community, seen by Observer Online on Thursday, Hylton said JC lodged its appeal within 24 hours of the disciplinary hearing on October 13 and is awaiting the outcome ahead of Friday’s Walker Cup final.

The sanctions followed a ruling that JC fielded an ineligible player after Lyle was found to have a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

JC was subsequently removed from the Walker Cup, banned from next year’s competition and ordered to forfeit its Manning Cup second-round match against St Catherine, which it had won 3-2. The result was reversed to a 3-0 victory for St Catherine.

READ: JC booted from Walker Cup for fielding ineligible player Jamone Lyle

The decision also paved the way for Kingston College (KC) to face Mona High in Friday’s Walker Cup final, after Mona lost to JC in the semi-final on penalties.

Hylton said the school received a letter from ISSA on October 12 informing Principal Wayne Robinson that a complaint had been made concerning Lyle’s eligibility. The hearing was scheduled for the following day at 2:00 pm.

According to Hylton, the letter provided no prior notification of the complaint and did not identify the complainant or provide further particulars of the charge.

He said the school’s leadership, football management and coaching staff immediately mobilised to prepare written submissions for the hearing, with assistance from the Jamaica College Public Relations Committee.

Hylton added that ISSA’s rules did not permit the school to have a lawyer or anyone other than the coach or his replacement to accompany the principal to provide representation or support.

“ISSA’s harsh ruling followed with blinding speed…We consider the sanctions unsupportable, extreme and excessive,” he said.

Hylton said the school intends to address aspects of the hearing as part of its appeal, although he did not disclose the details of its submissions.

JC is challenging both the application of ISSA’s rules and whether Lyle’s purported contract with Waterhouse constitutes a valid and enforceable agreement.

Hylton said the school’s interpretation of the relevant rule is that it prohibits players from being under contract with clubs, whether through professional agreements or other contractual arrangements. However, he argued that the rules have not been consistently enforced over the years, pointing to what he described as widespread contractual arrangements involving schoolboy footballers.

He also said JC does not concede that a valid contract exists in Lyle’s case and intends to pursue that argument on appeal.

“We regard the treatment of JC as unfair,” the board chairman said. “In our view, the treatment of both the school and the player, who appears to have entered into the purported contract without independent representation, is particularly harsh when many well-known contractual arrangements have attracted no sanctions.”

He said JC had lodged complaints concerning other contractual arrangements.

A central part of the school’s position is that it was never informed by Waterhouse that Lyle had signed a professional contract or that the club was restricting him from playing for JC.

The dispute follows a disciplinary letter from Waterhouse dated October 9, in which the club said it had fined Lyle $60,000 for unauthorised participation in a Manning Cup match on October 7. Waterhouse alleged that Lyle ignored instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and General Secretary Richard McCallum not to play for JC, in breach of his professional contract and the club’s rules.

Hylton said JC was particularly concerned that a professional club would have a minor sign an agreement purporting to prevent him from continuing to play for his school.

Lyle, who turned 17 in July, has represented JC since he was 12 and was at a significant stage of his schoolboy football career, Hylton said.

The chairman added that the school had seen no indication that Lyle received independent legal representation during the process. He also said information available to JC suggested that the player did not have a parent or guardian in Jamaica supporting him through the process, including a disciplinary hearing with Waterhouse.

Hylton stressed that the school had received no written communication informing it of the purported restriction or instructing it to stop the player from participating.

He further questioned whether the restriction could be enforced against a minor, citing legal precedents concerning contracts entered into by minors, including a case involving former England footballer Wayne Rooney.

JC intends to pursue that issue as part of its appeal.

Hylton has called on Waterhouse president Donovan White to withdraw and retract a statement that the school had been informed about Lyle’s contractual status. He said the principal was adamant that he had received no telephone call or other communication from White on the matter.

Hylton also called on the Waterhouse president to identify whom he claimed to have informed, when the communication took place and how it was delivered.

According to Hylton, the school has received no response to that request.

The chairman also addressed questions from stakeholders about why the school had not sought an injunction to challenge ISSA’s ruling.

He said the disciplinary letter referred to ISSA’s rule against members taking the association to court, adding that the school had previously been warned that seeking an injunction could result in a ban from all sporting activities under ISSA’s jurisdiction.

Hylton described the restriction as constitutionally objectionable and cited the cases of Butler v KSAFA and Royale Lakes Football Club Limited v St Catherine Football Association in support of the school’s position on access to the courts.

Quoting from Chief Justice Bryan Sykes’ judgment in Butler v KSAFA, Hylton argued that membership of an association should not require individuals to surrender their fundamental right to seek judicial redress.

He said, however, that the school faces a difficult decision because court action could trigger an immediate ban while proceedings continue, potentially affecting students across all its sporting programmes.

“For now, we have decided that it is not a risk worth taking at this stage,” Hylton said in the update, while making clear that court action remains an option.

Hylton said the immediate priority is the appeal lodged within 24 hours of the October 13 hearing, with the school awaiting a decision ahead of Friday’s final.

The chairman maintained that JC had been treated unfairly and expressed regret that the controversy had overshadowed the school’s football achievements.

He thanked members of the school community for their research, assistance and support, while urging stakeholders to continue submitting questions and suggestions.

World.title: Guilty by report?
World.content:
CHUCK... questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck has questioned whether the Integrity Commission’s (IC’s) practice of publicly identifying categories of people whose matters have been referred to it could fuel perceptions of corruption, even when those matters do not result in findings of wrongdoing.

Speaking at Wednesday’s meeting of Parliament’s Integrity Commission Oversight Committee, Chuck argued that reporting such figures could create an impression of widespread corruption even when investigations might not lead to charges.

“You must say how many investigations you have started and so on, but when you start, if you see in your report that you’re investigating permanent secretaries, you have… 18 or so permanent secretaries, even if you have three where you’re investigating, all of them come under scrutiny, and so when you say you’re investigating six, nine parliamentarians, every single one of us come under scrutiny,” he expressed.

The minister questioned whether the commission’s reporting approach was helping or hurting Jamaica’s efforts to fight corruption, arguing that the public needed to see clear results from investigations, rather than repeated references to matters still being examined.

He also questioned whether the country was getting value for money from the anti-corruption body, given the resources spent on its work and the need to demonstrate progress in tackling corruption.

“Because all I’m really saying is, yes, if there is corruption, expose it, find it, but… far too many of your reports are actually saying you are investigating, and at the end of the day nothing comes of it, or you don’t hear about it, and I am concerned, because when people speak about corruption, they should at least be able to say we have investigated these, we have charged so many for failing to report,” Chuck said.

However, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the suggestion that the commission should be blamed for the effects of its reporting, arguing that public accountability required it to explain the work it was doing and the progress of its investigations.

Robinson said the commission had to report on the nature of matters referred to it, while the public should also question why so many matters were being brought to its attention.

“As far as I know, you get to an investigation, having gone through a process, and you have met a particular threshold to determine that somebody

should be investigated. Part of your accountability mandate must be to report where you are in a process, which means whether it is public officials, parliamentarians, you must indicate of the number, how many have reached so-and-so, so I don’t share the view that the issue is with the Integrity Commission. If there are a lot of people under investigation, then the issue must be why are there so many people under investigation?” Robinson questioned.

The debate prompted director of investigation at the Integrity Commission Kevon Stephenson to explain the distinction between matters referred to the commission and cases that proceed to a formal investigation.

Stephenson said not every complaint or referral led to an investigation, as each matter had to be assessed before a decision was made. He told the committee that only a small fraction of matters referred to the commission proceeded to investigation.

“I think the public could appreciate that when matters are reported to the commission as under [Section] One of the Second Schedule, there is no guarantee that those complaints will be investigated, because an assessment has to be done on each of those complaints for a decision to be made under Section 47 of the legislation as to whether an investigation will be conducted,” Stephenson said.

He added that investigations could also be discontinued if the evidence did not provide a sufficient basis to continue. In those circumstances, the director of investigation was required to issue findings to the commission, but those findings were not made public.

Stephenson said reports reached Parliament when a completed investigation found a breach of a code, policy or law. He also explained that the annual report’s description of matters referred to the commission should not be interpreted as a list of cases actively under investigation.

Stephenson suggested that if Parliament is dissatisfied with what the law required the commission to include in its annual report, any change in policy would need to be reflected in legislation.

In the meantime, committee Chairman Pearnel Charles Jr said the concerns about reputational damage had to be considered without restricting the commission’s work.

“The commission must fearlessly carry out its work. But fear perhaps can be spelled in two ways, F-E-A-R and F-A-I-R. So as you fearlessly carry it out, it must be fair to the persons who you may have thoughts of, but not established evidence about,” Charles Jr said.

Furthermore, director of information and complaints at the commission Joeth Jones also criticised the media for what she described as a failure to give sufficient attention to positive compliance findings in the commission’s reports.

Jones said parliamentarians had performed relatively well in meeting their statutory obligations, but argued that this aspect of the commission’s work was not receiving adequate coverage.

“The media does not pick up that,” Jones told the committee, referring to the group’s compliance performance.

World.title: Secret location
World.content:
CHANG... we handed them over to The International Organisation for Migration and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE location of the first batch of 22 third-country nationals (TCNs) that arrived in the island on Monday will remain concealed says National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang.

Responding to questions posed by journalists at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, Chang maintained that though he is aware of where the TCNs are being housed, it’s not his “privilege” to announce where they are.

“I cannot give you their housing. We handed them over to International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and they made arrangements for them as to where they are to stay. The officers were in Jamaica and they looked at a number of hotels; they now have the responsibility of where they are to stay. In fact, they can move them at anytime,” said Chang.

The group, which arrived under an agreement signed between the Jamaican and United States (US) governments in June this year, comprises of 15 males and seven females, representing seven nationalities.

According to the Government, under the agreement, up to 25 asylum seekers who have unresolved migration cases in the US will temporarily transit through Jamaica en route to their home countries every two weeks.

But Chang on Tuesday shared that he is unaware of when the next batch of TCNs will arrive.

“I cannot tell you when others will arrive. We have a 14-day gap. As I’ve indicated, we can get another trip after 14 days, but there’s no guarantee. It’s not like these are designated numbers as we have with the involuntary returned migrants that we receive — our own citizens. Every two weeks, we know we get a batch, a flight, anywhere from 50 to 75 individuals. The TCNs depend on the number which might penetrate the barrier getting into the United States, as well as where they are from and what the State Department will decide or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will decide where they’re sending them and to which country,” he said.

According to Chang, no limitations will be placed on the TCNs during their stay in the country.

“They are individuals from different cultures, and what they do is up to them. They are here as visitors and they are working closely with the IOM in terms of conveying relevant information. The IOM will extract the information they require to prepare them for transit to their home country. They are free to do as they wish, like any visitor to Jamaica.

“They are individuals, who just like you in this room are regular working people who have sought to migrate, but done so illegally to the United States. The ones we accept, there are no criminals in there. They’re just families looking for a better life and we are accommodating their transition back home,” Chang reiterated.

Responding to concerns about the number of people who may want to seek asylum, Chang told journalists that the issue is not one of the Government but that of the institution which deals with the applications.

“The commissioner that deals with asylum or refugee status is a public body. It’s like a court. The documents are available. And I’m not saying we’ll not say how many…It’s their right to do so. And if they do so, it will be established. The asylum committee will sit, and the public will have access to it,” he said adding that the process can be lengthy, but the Government will notify the public as the numbers are available.

“They may ask to stay without going to asylum. It’s their freedom to do so. They are here as visitors, and if they have a skill set that is in high demand, they may. Doesn’t mean we have to accept it, but they can apply for that as well as apply for refugee status. They have a number of options,” he said.

According to Chang, their options will be discussed with them by the IOM.

“The IOM will interrogate and not only make arrangements for their movement, if they seek other alternative arrangements, then the IOM will inform us and we take it from there. But that is an important part of the nature of the IOM. As indicated, the United Nations body, they do this kind of activity globally as a trusted organisation in humanitarian relief activity. And, therefore, we allow them to proceed without any interference,” he said.

World.title: Sizzla, Chronic Law among acts for Smooth Thoughts rhythm
World.content:
Chronic Law.

After two years of planning and production, eastern entertainment Promotions is gearing up for the release of its latest musical project, Smooth Thoughts rhythm, on Friday, October 16.

The project features an impressive line-up of established and emerging dancehall acts, including Sizzla, Chronic Law, Skippa, Nation Boss, Silk Boss, Shawn Storm, Karnage, Hot Turbine, Lisa Hyper, and Krish Fullforce.

According to Judah Nugent, of Eastern Entertainment Promotions, the rhythm represents another milestone for the entertainment company, which has spent the past 14 years contributing to Jamaica’s music and entertainment landscape.

“It took us approximately two years to complete the project. One of the main factors was the availability of some of the artistes, as everyone has their own schedules and professional commitments,” Nugent explained.

“Coordinating the different artistes and ensuring that everything came together took time, but we remained committed to seeing the project through. We believe good things take time, and we are excited to finally share Smooth Thoughts rhythm with the world,” he added.

Eastern Entertainment Promotions serves as executive producer of the project, overseeing its development, artiste coordination, and overall production. Nugent said the decision to assemble such a diverse line-up was deliberate, as the team wanted to capture different musical styles and perspectives while maintaining a cohesive sound.

“We wanted to bring together a diverse group of artistes, each with their own style, personality and musical identity. Every artiste brings something different to the rhythm, and that variety allows listeners to experience different perspectives and expressions within one cohesive project,” he said.

While dancehall rhythms are often associated with Chronic Law high-energy entertainment, Nugent explained that Smooth Thoughts rhythm was conceptualised to offer listeners a more reflective musical experience.

“The name Smooth Thoughts really speaks for itself. This is the type of project you can sit back with, relax, spend time with your thoughts, and genuinely resonate with each track,” he shared. “Music is not always just about dancing and having a good time; it can also be about personal experiences, reflection, and connecting with something that speaks to you.”

Adding to the excitement surrounding Friday’s release will be the world première of Chronic Law’s official music video for Streets, which will debut on the same day.

Nugent explained that the coordinated releases form part of a wider promotional strategy aimed at generating greater visibility for the project and encouraging listeners to explore the contributions of the other artistes.

“Chronic Law has a strong connection with dancehall audiences, and we believe the video première will generate excitement and help draw attention to the wider rhythm project,” he said. “Pairing the two releases gives fans more than one reason to engage with the music on the day. Our intention is to create a coordinated release moment that encourages people to watch the video, discover the rhythm, explore the other tracks, and support all the artistes involved.”

Founded in 2012, Eastern Entertainment Promotions has established a presence in Jamaica’s entertainment industry through event staging and music production. Its previous musical projects include Heaven Gates rhythm.

For Nugent, the latest release underscores the company’s commitment to creating opportunities for Jamaican entertainers while expanding its reach beyond the island.

He is particularly hopeful that Smooth Thoughts rhythm will attract international attention and enjoy longevity in an increasingly competitive music industry. “We want the project to receive strong support from fans, DJs, radio personalities, streaming audiences and the wider music industry.

We also hope it creates greater exposure for the artistes involved and opens doors to new opportunities for everyone who contributed to making it happen,” he said. “Ultimately, we want the rhythm to have longevity. We do not want it to be something people listen to only on release day. We want listeners to keep returning to it, discovering their favourite tracks and sharing the music with others.”

The project is expected to be available across major digital streaming platforms, subject to final distribution arrangements.

Meanwhile, Eastern Entertainment Promotions is also preparing for the 12th staging of its signature event, Eastern Extravaganza, scheduled for New Year’s Day, January 1, 2027.

Nugent said the event remains an important part of the company’s journey, with further announcements expected in the coming months.

World.title: Chilling confession
World.content:
Ruddock was heard on video telling detectives that he was instructed by his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, pictured here, to carry out the gruesome, human-sacrifice killing of Taneka Gardner.

A seven-member jury in the Andre Ruddock murder trial in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston on Wednesday watched video recording of the accused appearing composed as he admitted to detectives that he cut the throat of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner on October 17, 2021 at Pathways International Restoration Kingdom Ministries in Albion, St James.

Ruddock was heard in the video telling the detectives at a police station in St James, in the presence of two justices of the peace, that he was instructed by his now deceased pastor, Dr Kevin Smith, to carry out the gruesome, human-sacrifice killing of Gardner at the church.

In the video, Ruddock was seen calmly answering the 42 questions posed to him by detectives as he gave them a picture of what led up to him cutting Gardner’s throat.

Ruddock was even seen sipping what appeared to be water from a 1.5 litre bottle as he sat with his back against a wall.

The detectives did not appear to be aggressive towards him, and neither did it appear that he was forced or threatened in any way to say what he told them and the justices of the peace.

Ruddock was asked questions and he provided the responses. After the questions and answers were read out to him, Ruddock was invited to sign the document, which he stood up and completed on the table that was before him and the detectives.

One of the detectives thanked Ruddock for cooperating with them and expressed that he wished everything worked out well for him.

After the playing of the video in court, prosecutor LaToya Bernard continued her examination-in-chief of a detective corporal who was one of the two detectives present inside the room with Ruddock and the two justices of the peace. She invited him to tell the court what he did after Ruddock signed the question-and-answer document.

The detective said he packed up the video recording equipment and created two DVDs which contained all that Ruddock told them.

The prosecutor then went on to ask the witness where he was on October 21, 2021 and what activities he carried out in relation to the case.

The detective, who is now at the rank of corporal, asked to see his written statement which he gave in the matter in order to refresh his memory.

He was shown the statement and then he began to explain that he and another detective were given certain instructions by a superior.

He explained that electronic items taken from the murder scene were transported to the police’s cybercrime division where they were handed over to an analyst.

“Items included cell phones, cameras, a digital video recorder and memory cards. The analyst gave me a receipt in return and I subsequently handed over the receipt to Detective Inspector McLeod on my return to the Falmouth Police Station,” he said.

He explained that he saw the body of Taneka Gardner more than once after it was removed from the church.

“After making arrangements with the father of Taneka Gardner, I met with him at the Archer’s Funeral Home located in Spanish Town, St Catherine. We were there for the post-mortem of Taneka Gardner,” he said, explaining that a pathologist confirmed to him that Gardner’s death was as a result of a slash to the throat.

World.title: THERE’S HOPE!
World.content:
West Indies’ Captain Shai Hope plays a shot during their fourth T20 international cricket match against India at the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium in Hyderabad, India, on Wednesday. (Photo: AFP)

HYDERABAD, India (CMC) — West Indies Captain Shai Hope produced another scintillating knock while Keemo Paul came up trumps with the ball as the regional side carved out a 24-run win over host India here in the fourth T20I on Wednesday.

Shai Hope’s latest century, his fourth of the trip, helped to propel the men in maroon to 247 for three while Paul’s five-wicket haul, supported by Gudakesh Motie’s restrictive spell, sent the series into a decider in Bengaluru as India could only manage to get 223 on the newly laid Hyderabad pitch.

Put in to bat, Hope combined with Jewel Andrew to get things going quickly against an unchanged India side. The teenager immediately set the tone, crunching a clean six off Arshdeep Singh’s second ball.

A 17-run over gave West Indies momentum, and Hope quickly tapped into his red-hot form.

Mayank Yadav attempted to rattle the visitors with early pace but occasionally overdid it, including a bouncer that flew over Samson’s head. On a patchy outfield, West Indies relied on clearing the ropes, racing to 79 for one, their highest T20I Powerplay score against India.

Axar Patel’s introduction in the Powerplay gave India a breakthrough when he removed Andrew for 21, but Shimron Hetmyer wasted little time, targeting Arshdeep’s slot offerings.

Naman Dhir, who had been among the wickets, ran into a negative matchup against Hope and conceded 19 in his only over.

West Indies’ incoming batters maintained the tempo. Prince Yadav surprised Hetmyer with a crafty bouncer to get him out for 33, but Rovman Powell capitalised in a 22-run Axar over.

By the time Sherfane Rutherford arrived, Hope had raced to 75. The left-hander tore into Mayank’s final spell, taking 22 runs as West Indies moved past 200.

India’s fielding also faltered: Mayank botched a Rutherford catch, and Tilak could not sight a straight hit off the final ball as Hope completed his century.

Hope’s unbeaten 102, which included four fours and nine sixes, saw the right-hander become the first West Indies player to three T20I hundreds.

India’s reply began brightly. Samson launched a straight hit over Roston Chase’s head and almost single-handedly controlled the Powerplay as Abhishek Sharma struggled for strike.

Chase conceded 25 in his second over, and by the third over India had raced to 50 without loss.

But on a dry surface with no dew, West Indies’ seamers adapted better, mixing their pace to restrain India. Paul struck with his first ball, using a short delivery and smart field placement to hand India their first setback as Sanju Samson held out in the deep for 56.

Three balls later, Ishan Kishan fell attempting to repeat a six.

Abhishek, starved of strike, scratched his way to 29 off 24. Shreyas Iyer made 16 off 11, ball bowled by Motie, stagnating India in the middle.

Unlike West Indies, India could not capitalise on the short balls from the pacers, managing just 32 off 31 at that length.

Tilak Varma (43) and Nitish Reddy (41) adjusted well to forge a 70-run recovery in 5.2 overs, but the late surge collapsed when both departed, leaving the tail with a mountain to climb.

Paul, who claimed the last three wickets, ended with five for 41 while Motie claimed two for 13.

The result marked the first time West Indies defeated India in India while defending a total in T20Is, after six failed attempts. The series is now tied at 2-2 with the final game set for Saturday at 8:30 am Jamaica time.

World.title: Shan’s Heroes’ Weekend Spread
World.content:
Rich, flavourful, and slow-cooked to tender perfection, Shanice Gore’s curry goat brings bold Jamaican spices and authentic island flavour to the table. With Heroes’ Weekend coming up, it’s the perfect dish to gather family and friends around for a hearty, satisfying meal worth celebrating!

Serves: 6 Ingredients

3 lb goat meat, cut into pieces 1 whole onion, chopped 2 stalks scallion, chopped 4 cloves garlic, crushed 1 Scotch bonnet pepper 2 tsp all-purpose seasoning 3 tbsp curry powder, using your favourite brand 2 tbsp cooking oil Hot water, added gradually as needed 2 medium carrots, sliced 2 medium Irish potatoes, peeled and cubed 1 tsp pimento berries Additional onion, garlic and scallion, to taste, for finishing Method

1. Clean and trim the goat meat, then pat dry. Season with the onion, scallion, garlic, Scotch bonnet, allpurpose seasoning and curry powder.

2. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the seasoned goat and sauté for 5–8 minutes, stirring occasionally.

3. Cover, reduce the heat and allow the meat to simmer in its own juices. Add hot water gradually as the liquid reduces, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. Continue simmering until the goat is tender, approximately 2–3 hours, depending on the meat.

4. Once the goat is tender, add the carrots, Irish potatoes, pimento and additional onion, garlic and scallion. Taste and adjust the seasoning, adding a little more hot water if needed.

5. Simmer for another 20–30 minutes, until the vegetables are tender and the gravy reaches your preferred consistency.

6. Serve hot with rice and peas and a fresh salad.

Shan’s tip: Keep the Scotch bonnet whole for flavour with less heat, or chop it for a spicier curry. A little fresh cilantro stirred in towards the end also adds lovely flavour.

World.title: Late discord delays Franco-German deal on Made in Europe, car emissions
World.content:
Earlier this week, French President Emmanuel Macron had suggested the ball was in the German court. “There are political constraints on the other side of the Rhine, and I completely respect coalition discussions,” Macron said Monday on the sidelines of the Paris car show.

Under the terms of the proposed deal, Germany would accept stricter Made in Europe criteria for the automotive sector in the Industrial Accelerator Act, which France has pushed for, in exchange for weakening the combustion engine ban, one of Berlin’s long-term demands.

"In light of the significant technological, economic and geopolitical changes since the existing regulatory framework was established, the Automotive Package should strike a better balance between climate objectives, industrial competitiveness, technological development and the strengthening of European value creation," the two countries wrote in a draft agreement obtained by POLITICO.

"Based on the Franco-German Ministerial Councils in 2025 and 2026, Germany and France therefore propose a balanced negotiating package combining ambitious CO₂ reduction targets with additional flexibility and targeted incentives for European value creation," the agreement adds.

Currently, the EU's target is for companies to reduce combustion engine emissions by 100% from 2021 levels by 2035, with the possibility to 'earn' 10% of emissions leeway through initiatives like offsets and investments.

Under the proposed deal, France and Germany want to soften the 2035 target to 90%, and to offer a further 10% leeway in exchange for investments in alternative fuels (for a combined 80%).

World.title: Shorten EU budget to 3 or 4 years, Cyprus president tells POLITICO
World.content:
“You don’t know what’s going to be the situation in 2030, 2031,” he added. “I mean, look what happened with Covid, with the Ukrainian war … It’s not possible to declare all your priorities today.”

The EU’s seven-year, roughly €2 trillion budget has to be agreed by all 27 member countries but has two deeply entrenched camps on either side: The so-called frugals, comprised of Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and others who want a smaller budget, and the friends of cohesion, a loose grouping of 17 countries that do not want major cuts to agriculture and regional funds.

An EU official close to the budget negotiations said the idea of a shorter timeframe was weird.

EU law allows a budget of “at least five years,” though every budget has been seven years since 1993.

The odds of the budget being approved by the end of the year are increasingly slim, with an election in Spain in November, which polls indicate Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will lose to the center-right and far-right, potentially blowing out the timeline for consensus to 2027.

“Everybody used to understand that we need to finish … a political agreement by the end of the year,” Christodoulides said. “Now, with the situation in Spain, elections there,” that is less likely to happen.

World.title: ‘No logic’: Finland slams Trump for siding with Putin against Ukraine
World.content:
Trump alarmed European leaders and horrified Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week by announcing a deal to release Russian diesel onto the market, apparently in an attempt to lower fuel costs for American consumers. Ukraine’s allies fear the move will boost Russia’s revenue from fuel sales, giving it more money to spend on war.

Trump also said Ukraine should stop hitting Russian fossil fuel facilities — as part of what he said was a ceasefire on energy infrastructure — and should replace Zelenskyy.

Finland is an influential voice among Ukraine’s European allies: The country has the EU’s longest land border with Russia, at 1,300 km, and its president, Alexander Stubb — a talented sportsman — won Trump’s respect on the golf course, giving him leeway to try to influence White House policy.

Orpo said if he were in Trump’s position “I would not trust Putin.” Zelenskyy has said he fears Ukraine is losing the U.S. to Russia’s side in the war, warning the Americans and their president are on “the wrong side of history”. Orpo said he agreed: “I think he is, and they are.”

Ukraine now faces grave danger, he said. “The sky is open for Russia, there are missiles. They need more military support, air defense,” Orpo said. “Also, the situation is dangerous because of the latest deal between Trump and Putin.”

Midterms move

One possible reason Trump turned against Ukraine with that diesel deal is the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. “I think it is because of domestic reasons — elections are coming,” Orpo said. “But we need to get them back.” Nonetheless, he said the amount of Russian diesel that could be sold to the U.S. is too small to make much of a difference for American consumers.

World.title: Macron warns EU leaders they need to agree budget by end of year
World.content:
Macron "said that, starting from January, there will be no political room" for concluding an agreement, one of the diplomats said.

The EU’s 27 governments are divided over the total size of the 2028-2034 budget. Leaders gathering in Brussels are discussing the Irish plan, which envisions cuts of €159 billion in current prices to the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal.

European Council President António Costa is pushing leaders to finalize negotiations during a summit in December — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks — but some governments and EU officials have said such a timeframe is very unrealistic.

One EU diplomat dismissed Macron’s intervention as a threat to support Costa on the December deadline. “EU would be ungovernable if we were to take into account all the local elections,” they added.

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading the polls to replace Macron, pledged to halve France’s contributions to the EU budget if she comes to power.

During a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday, Le Pen accused the EU of speeding up talks to prevent France's next leader to have a say.

Several leaders are unwilling to commit to the end-of-year deadline, fearing that time pressure will undermine their leverage in the negotiations.

“We will not sign an agreement that is not beneficial to us just to meet a deadline,” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the country's parliament on Wednesday. “We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy.”

World.title: EU leaders’ summit descends into 3-hour argument over taxing car emissions
World.content:
Countries including Italy, Poland, Czechia and Hungary called for ETS2 — an already-legislated law that will put a carbon price on heating and transport from 2028 — to be delayed for two more years. Estonia suggested it could be scrapped altogether.

The push was rejected by a majority of the bloc, with several EU diplomats telling POLITICO it was, as one put it, an “unacceptable” offer. Another said the ETS2 launch date would never be changed. But the debate reflects a growing sense from right-leaning governments that the EU’s ambitious green agenda runs against their push to bring down energy costs.

While the main topic of today’s discussion was ETS2, its predecessor, the Emissions Trading System — which puts a price on carbon emissions from factories and power plants — was arguably the real target.

Put together, these two emissions trading schemes will be the EU's most powerful policy tool for bringing down planet-warming emissions.

A proposed reform of the original ETS is currently being debated in the European Parliament and in the Council of the EU. Italy and Poland have been leading a gang of 10 member-countries which have been railing against the ETS since American and Israeli bombs started falling on Iran in March.

What they want is for the European Commission’s July review of the ETS to be further weakened, even though the proposal already softens carbon restrictions over the next decade to give industry more time to invest in cleaner production methods.

World.title: Von der Leyen floats EU ‘strategic reserves’ for gas amid winter supply fears
World.content:
Ursula von der Leyen addresses members of the European Parliament during a plenary session in Strasbourg, France on Oct. 6, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wants EU leaders to look into the idea of developing bloc-wide strategic gas reserves amid concerns the continent faces a winter shortage, three diplomats and two EU officials told POLITICO.

Europe’s existing gas storage caverns — which are typically refilled over the course of the year by commercial actors — are running at record lows this year after high summer prices linked to the war in Iran undercut market incentives to restock, leaving the bloc underprepared for winter.

While it wasn't immediately clear to diplomatic officials what form the reserve idea would take, one senior EU official described it as a long-term measure to cushion the bloc against future supply risks, as countries already do with oil and refined products. The Commission president's comments came at a major summit of European leaders in Brussels on Thursday.

World.title: Le casse-tête politique du budget européen
World.content: Une rude bataille s’engage pour faire adopter le prochain budget de l’Union européenne. Non seulement les 27 pays sont divisés sur son montant et sur ses priorités mais plusieurs élections nationales compliquent l’équation politique. En amont du sommet du Conseil européen de jeudi et vendredi, Marine Le Pen s’est d’ailleurs rendue à Bruxelles pour mettre en garde contre la conclusion d’un accord avant le scrutin français. Que se joue-t-il réellement avec ces discussions ? La demande du RN de repousser l’adoption du budget est-elle justifiée ? Marine Le Pen propose-t-elle une sortie déguisée de l’UE en voulant couper dans la contribution française ? Anthony Lattier en discute avec Marion Solletty et Giorgio Leali, journalistes à POLITICO.

World.title: West Nile virus creeps north in record year for EU cases
World.content:
Workers spray to combat the spread of mosquitoes in the municipality of Kordelio in Greece after the detection of West Nile virus, on Sept. 3, 2026. | Konstantinos Tsakalidis/SOOC/AFP via Getty Images

Dozens of human cases have been recorded in the Netherlands and Belgium.

The West Nile virus is spreading across the EU at record levels and is reaching new regions of the continent, health authorities said Thursday.

In a statement, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control said 1,715 cases were reported this year, with 130 people dying from the virus, which is mainly transmitted through mosquito bites.

Greece, Italy and France are the worst affected countries, but the virus is spreading further north, authorities say.

World.title: Albania: Violent protests rock Tirana for third straight day
World.content:
Demonstrators hurled stones, firecrackers and other objects at riot police, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Fires broke out in the city centre, engulfing trees and a roadside structure as firefighters worked to contain the flames.

 

Footage shows protesters racing through smoke-filled streets, tearing down police barriers and throwing tear-gas canisters back at officers. Shops and banks were damaged, some looted, while police reported vandalism targeting ATMs, cameras, vehicles and fencing. Burnt-out vehicles, smashed windows and wrecked offices were left behind across the Albanian capital, where residents and workers began clearing debris as demonstrations continued.

What began three days ago as student protests over the cost and quality of higher education has become a broader challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama's government. Students demanding better university conditions, financial support and job prospects have joined the Flamingo movement, which opposes a luxury resort project linked to Jared Kushner and is calling for Mr Rama's resignation over corruption allegations.

World.title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal driven by ‘dubious business motives’, Latvian MEP Kols tells Euronews
World.content:
US President Donald Trump’s deal to lift restrictions on Russian diesel sends a “very bad signal” and is driven by dubious business motives, MEP Rihard Kols told Euronews’ Special Report.

 

Kols is among more than 100 MEPs calling on the EU in a signed letter to maintain its support for Ukraine and impose a full embargo on Russian oil and gas imports into the bloc. He also told Euronews that EU member states continuing to import Russian energy lack moral standing.

World.title: At least 19 injured as minibus collides with train near Channel Tunnel
World.content:
A collision between a minibus and a shuttle train at the Eurotunnel site in northern France left 19 people injured on Thursday evening, local authorities said.

 

"An accident involving a minibus transporting heavy goods vehicle drivers who were about to board a Le Shuttle shuttle occurred this evening, at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel site," the Pas-de-Calais prefecture wrote on X.

According to French broadcaster TF1, the minibus struck the departing shuttle train for reasons that remain unclear. Authorities confirmed that the vehicle did not overturn.

The minibus driver was an Eurotunnel employee, while the victims were all men of different nationalities, according to local authorities.

The sub-prefect of Calais, Agathe Cury, said a judicial investigation had been opened, adding that it was the first accident of its kind at an Eurotunnel loading platform.

Emergency services, including ambulances, helicopters and police officers, were deployed to the scene. None of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening.

Traffic through the Channel Tunnel remained operational following the collision.

World.title: Inconclusive sparring at EU summit puts budget timeline into question
World.content:
EU leaders have refused to budge on the bloc’s next long-term budget and openly cast doubt on whether a deal can be sealed by the end of the year, a slippage that would mean significant delays and a collision with a string of national elections.

 

Until now, capitals were committed to reaching a final agreement by December 2026. But at Thursday’s summit in Brussels, where talks dragged longer than expected, a growing number of governments are asking whether that is really necessary.

"We are not reaching an agreement this month. Not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year," said caretaker Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. "I think we are not in a hurry."

For months, European Council President António Costa has repeated that leaders must unanimously agree the next seven-year budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), by December at the very latest.

If talks spill into 2027, he warns, there will not be enough time to complete the complex legislative work needed to get the budget up and running by 1 January 2028.

Following the inconclusive summit, where the Irish presidency’s compromise proposal to cut the overall volume by €141 billion was largely rejected, Costa will take over the negotiations, which was largely expected.

The European Council President is due to present a new negotiating proposal in a few weeks, which is bound to follow a completely different logic from the Irish one. EU leaders have been called in for a special summit on 26 November.

In particular, Costa's proposal is due to keep the national contributions low, a new package of EU-wide taxes to finance the budget, and maintain sufficient flexibility for unforeseen expenses, a budget line the Irish proposal significantly cut down.

Already before the summit, the draft joint conclusions were watered down concerning the deadline, softening language that explicitly set out “the aim of reaching a final agreement by the end of the year.”

By contrast, the final language says that "an agreement before the end of 2026 would allow for the adoption of legislative acts in 2027, which is necessary to ensure that EU funding reaches beneficiaries without interruption in January 2028."

Speaking before the summit, several leaders made clear that they do not feel bound by an end-of-year timeline, as it would be extremely difficult to explain to their domestic audiences that they accepted a bad deal because of an artificial deadline.

"The date cannot become more important than the content," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the Senate on Wednesday.

"We will not sign an agreement that is not advantageous to us just to meet a deadline. We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy."

There is, however, no consensus on what a “good deal” looks like. Every government wants to take as much as possible from the EU budget while paying in as little as possible.

The main battle line runs between two camps: the so-called “frugals,” a German-led coalition of six net contributors pushing for steep cuts to the overall volume, and the Friends of Cohesion, a 17-strong bloc of southern and eastern countries fighting to preserve traditional funding programmes for the poorest regions.

But the camps are not monolithic. Some Friends of Cohesion, like Spain and Italy, have a vested interest in agricultural funds. Others, like the Baltic states, want to boost defence spending due to their proximity to Russia.

Among the frugals, Germany and Sweden are seen as the most radical, while Finland is keen on farming subsidies. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has yet to pick a side, trapped between its European ambitions and a runaway budget deficit.

Belgium and Luxembourg are somewhere dithering between the factions.

"In the end, we need a good Multiannual Financial Framework. So, of course, everyone wants to make speed. But it’s more important to have a good deal than a bad deal," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.

In other words, the red lines are so entrenched, and the room for compromise so slim, that a landing zone currently looks like a mirage.

In Brussels circles, deals on sensitive topics are only struck under intense time pressure, because neither side feels compelled to make concessions until the last minute. Signalling that one does not feel bound by a timeline may therefore be a negotiating tactic to stand one’s ground.

For EU officials, even more worrying than the potential delay to funding programmes are the string of elections due in 2027 in France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia and Greece. Some fear that if no deal is reached by the end of this year, it could slip to autumn 2027.

Paris is a particular concern. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is currently the favourite to win the presidential race, and she has promised to cap France’s contribution at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion.

Meanwhile, elections in Spain, where voters go to the polls on 29 November, and Sweden, which voted in September, "are likely to create some issues", said Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides.

Christodoulides reiterated the need to reach an agreement by the end of the year. He is one of the few EU leaders still saying so.

World.title: US extends sanctions waiver for Russian oil giant Lukoil until 2027
World.content:
The US Treasury Department on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver for Russian oil giant Lukoil, allowing its service stations outside Russia to continue operating until April 2027.

 

The extension allows Lukoil-branded petrol stations in countries including the United States to continue serving customers until 24 April 2027, replacing an earlier licence due to expire later this month.

However, the latest licence maintains restrictions on the "transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation".

The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, prompting the Treasury to issue a temporary licence to facilitate deliveries.

Related IEA warns diesel prices in Europe could rise as global crunch lasts into 2027

The deal, as announced by Trump on social media, envisages that Moscow will release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets immediately, with an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

The Trump-Putin diesel deal has been badly received by EU foreign ministers, who say it undermines transatlantic unity at a time when Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.

Oil prices remain elevated as the war in the Middle East enters its eighth month, following a sharp rise in energy costs since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February.

Tehran's retaliation included the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a key passage for global oil transit, sending costs up.

World.title: Zelenskyy poised to visit Budapest next week as Ukraine and Hungary move towards diplomatic reset
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to visit Budapest next week after being invited to attend events marking the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution, his deputy chief of staff, Ihor Zhovkva, confirmed to Euronews in an exclusive interview.

 

The planned visit, which has yet to be confirmed, would come amid efforts to reset relations between Kyiv and Budapest after years of diplomatic disputes that have repeatedly obstructed Ukraine's path towards EU membership.

"We have received an invitation. On 23 October, an event will be held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution," Zhovkva said when asked whether Zelenskyy had been invited to the Hungarian capital.

"The President of Ukraine has received an invitation to attend. We shall see."

The invitation comes as Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar prepare to hold their first formal bilateral meeting on Friday morning on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, following months of talks over the timing and location of their encounter.

Kyiv sees the meeting as an opportunity to turn the recent diplomatic opening into concrete progress between the two neighbouring countries.

"Our expectations are very positive," Zhovkva told Euronews, adding that Kyiv was grateful for Hungary's support in advancing Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.

The diplomatic opening follows a breakthrough earlier this week, when Ukraine adopted legislation strengthening educational rights for national minorities, addressing a longstanding source of tension with Budapest over the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Ukraine's western Transcarpathia region.

Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, the dispute became one of the main obstacles to Ukraine's EU accession process, with Budapest using its veto to block progress in negotiations.

Magyar's government has adopted a more constructive approach, although it has continued to insist that Kyiv fulfil its commitments on minority rights before further steps towards membership can proceed.

On Monday, Ukraine's parliament approved the new legislation, which Zelenskyy subsequently signed into law. The following day, the EU opened negotiations on two additional accession clusters after Hungary dropped its objections, bringing the total to four out of six.

"We have opened four clusters, with two still remaining, and we are confident that Hungary's position will continue to be as constructive as it has been so far," Zhovkva said.

He added that European integration would be a central subject of the Brussels meeting, but stressed that Kyiv wanted to broaden the relationship beyond the politically sensitive question of EU membership.

"It really is time to sit down and talk," he said.

Kyiv has also expressed openness to hosting Magyar in the Ukrainian capital, following earlier discussions about meeting in Berehove, a town in Transcarpathia with a sizeable ethnic Hungarian community.

"He has always been a very welcome guest in Kyiv, and we would certainly welcome such a meeting in the Ukrainian capital," Zhovkva said, adding that other locations in Ukraine were also possible.

Magyar, speaking in Brussels on Thursday, described Ukraine's minority education legislation as a historic breakthrough and an opportunity to place bilateral relations on a new footing. He also raised the possibility of a subsequent meeting in Berehove later this autumn.

A visit to Budapest on 23 October would carry particular historical significance, marking 70 years since the outbreak of Hungary's 1956 uprising against Soviet rule, which was ultimately crushed by Soviet forces.

Zelenskyy's presence at the commemorations could offer a symbolic opportunity for the two neighbours to demonstrate their commitment to rebuilding relations. Euronews has reached out to the Hungarian government for comments. AND WHAT DID THEY SAY?

Macron, Costa expected to take part in the commemoration

Other European leaders are also expected to join the commemoration next week. French President Emmanuel Macron has confirmed his participation, according to Magyar, while European Council President António Costa will likely attend, according to his spokesperson.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola have also been invited, but their participation has not yet been confirmed.

On 23 October 1956, Hungarian students took to the streets to protest against Soviet occupation. The demonstrations quickly grew into a popular uprising, which was later crushed by the Red Army. Zelenskyy’s visit could also draw parallels with Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The commemoration could also offer European leaders an opportunity to signal support for Magyar, who ousted Viktor Orbán and has worked to improve Hungary’s relations with the EU after years of tensions under his predecessor.

World.title: BBC asks court to compel Trump deposition in €8.6bn defamation case
World.content:
The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) has asked a judge to order US President Donald Trump to set a firm date to give sworn testimony in his $10-billion (€8.6 billion) defamation lawsuit against the network, court filings showed.

 

"Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself," the BBC's lawyers wrote.

The BBC's lawyers asked a federal court in Florida to order Trump to set a date for his deposition and to address the issue at a hearing scheduled for 22 October.

In a statement in response to the filing, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team did not address the reasons for Trump's delay, but repeated its allegations against the BBC and said the president was holding the broadcaster “accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”

What is the BBC accused of?

Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the British broadcaster of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices over a documentary titled “Trump: A Second Chance.”

The 33-page lawsuit accused the broadcaster of presenting a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump,” describing it as “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 US presidential election.

The BBC admitted to editing together parts of Trump's 6 January 2021 speech, making it appear he had encouraged violence at the US Capitol. The broadcaster apologised, and two senior executives resigned, but it denied defamation.

Trump's attacks on media outlets have seen him restrict access, badmouth journalists critical of his administration and bring lawsuits demanding huge amounts of compensation.

In April, a US federal judge dismissed a $10 billion (€8.5 billion) defamation lawsuit brought by the president against The Wall Street Journal.

World.title: Europeans ‘far more united’ on tougher China trade stance after German shift, Barkin says
World.content:
The EU is more united than it has been in years on taking a tougher line on China’s trade imbalance, following a shift towards a firmer stance by Germany, says Noah Barkin, senior adviser at Rhodium Group and author of the Watching China in Europe newsletter.

 

The EU has set an October deadline to address its growing trade deficit with China or face tougher measures. Barkin said Beijing has “retaliation dominance in the short term”, but the EU holds leverage through access to its single market and believes China also wants to avoid escalation. He was speaking on Special Report with Maria.

World.title: 'Multiple victims' at elementary school shooting in US city of Bend, Oregon. Suspected shooter is dead, officials say
World.content:
Three children, one adult dead in Oregon elementary school shooting, US media report. The suspected shooter is dead, but authorities have yet to confirm who shot the suspect.

A shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, has left multiple victims, police said Thursday, adding that the suspected shooter is dead.

Four people, including three children, were killed in the shooting, US networks reported, citing unnamed law enforcement sources.

"We don't have confirmation yet who shot the suspect. It may have been a bystander. At this time, we have multiple victims," Sheila Miller, a spokesperson for the Bend Police Department, said at a news conference.

At least two people were transported ‌to ​a hospital, but there were no details on their condition.

Bend is a ​city of some ‌100,000 people in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.

Students were evacuated from the school and the buildings were cordoned off Image: Joe Kline/AP Photo/picture alliance

Students evacuated as police respond to shooting

An updated post later said law enforcement was escorting students by bus to a separate location, where they could reunite with their families. Silver ​Rail Elementary ⁠School serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly children aged ⁠5 to ​11. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.

Miller said officers were alerted to a critical incident at 1 p.m. local time (2000 GMT) and arrived at the scene about two minutes later.

"Seconds later, we received word over the radio that the suspect in this incident was down," she said.

US grapples with recurring mass shootings

The United States, where firearms are widely available, experiences frequent gun violence, with thousands of people killed each year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among high-income countries.

The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007. South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

There have been more than 365 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter.

This is a developing story...

World.title: Bus, train collide, injuring 19 at Channel Tunnel terminal
World.content:
A minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a freight train near the Channel Tunnel entrance in France, injuring 19 people, two of them severely. Authorities launched an inquiry into what caused the accident.

A minibus collided with a stationary train near the entrance to the Channel Tunnel in northern France on Thursday, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, authorities said.

Two people, including the bus driver, were seriously injured and airlifted to a hospital in Lille, but none of the injuries were life-threatening, the local prefect said, revising down earlier reports of five people seriously injured passengers. The other injured passengers were brought to nearby hospitals for treatment.

The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities preparing to board a shuttle train through the tunnel. LeShuttle carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.

Pas-de-Calais Deputy Prefect Agathe Cury said an inquiry was launched to determine what caused the accident.

"This is the first time an incident of this type has occurred" at a Eurotunnel loading platform, she said.

Eurostar and freight service to continue

Eurostar, which runs passenger train services between mainland Europe and the UK, said the collision would not impact its services.

"An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel tonight, not involving Eurostar. This incident does not impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected," the company said in a statement.

The last two trains between Paris and London were canceled. Eurostar said this was due to engineering work, not the accident.

The 50-kilometer (31-mile) Channel Tunnel is the longest infrastructure of its kind in the world. It has linked Coquelles in northern France and Folkestone in England since 1994. Operated by Getlink, the tunnel is used by several hundred trains every day.

Eurostar operates high-speed passenger trains between the UK and mainland Europe through the Channel Tunnel [File photo] Image: Aurelien Morissard/AP/picture alliance

Eurostar, which is a separate entity, has held a monopoly on cross-Channel passenger rail services for decades, said it carried 11.8 million passengers in 2025.

World.title: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro pleads not guilty to torture charges
World.content:
Maduro and his wife were charged with leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro appeared in court on Thursday, where he rejected newly unsealed torture charges against him and his wife, Cilia Flores.

He said the indictment represented "false accusations" against him.

Maduro was combative in court as he was asked to enter a plea to the charges, condemning allegations of torture as "false accusations and false testimony."

Ultimately, Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein interjected to declare that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro."

Flores told the judge through the Spanish interpreter: "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."

The court appearance was the latest for the pair, who are currently in US custody in New York City, now eight months since they were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a nighttime raid.

The new torture charges against the couple have been added to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced.

Maduro and Flores' trial is set to begin June 14, 2027, according to a schedule approved by the judge Thursday.

What are the torture charges?

Maduro and his wife have been accused of leading a state-sponsored repression campaign that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans, during his presidency from 2013 to 2026.

They are said to have committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.

Security forces have been accused of torturing prisoners with electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Maduro stands accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims' treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner's child as a form of psychological torture.

For her part, Cilia Flores has been accused of helping develop the repressive system and ordering the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.

Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but the US indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

Maudro has been under investigation by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents, but the court has not served him with a warrant.

Torture is considered a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside of the nation where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims' nationality.

But in the US, the prosecution of foreign officials is exceedingly rare. The only recent cases include the son of Liberian President Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad's Syria.
