World.title: The Czech Republic’s Tallest Structures Have Been Torn Down
World.content:
Two 355-meter radio transmission towers in Liblice were brought down in a controlled demolition on October 15, ending nearly half a century as the country’s tallest structures.

The towers collapsed at 11:15 a.m. local time after demolition crews used approximately 4.5 kilograms of Semtex explosives to sever supporting cables, iDNES.cz reported.



Hundreds of spectators gathered to watch the demolition, some bringing binoculars and folding chairs. Several residents were visibly emotional as the towers fell.

“We’ve lost our beacon and a symbol of home,” local residents told the outlet.

The Liblice B transmitter entered service in December 1976 and was once the most powerful radio broadcasting facility in Central Europe.

Czech Radio stopped using it for medium-wave broadcasts at the end of 2021, while Country Radio continued operating there until March 2025.

Some locals had called for the towers to be preserved as part of Czechoslovakia’s engineering and broadcasting heritage. Others viewed them as obsolete structures dating from the communist era.

With the towers gone, the 347.5-meter Krašov television and radio transmitter has become the tallest structure in the Czech Republic.

Crews are expected to spend approximately 20 more days clearing the collapsed steel structures.

World.title: Brno Burger Brand Pickle Plans Up to Seven Locations in Prague
World.content:
A burger brand recently launched in Brno is preparing to expand into Prague, where it plans to open up to seven restaurants.

Pickle also has ambitions to enter other Czech and Slovak cities before expanding across Europe and eventually Asia.

The first Pickle restaurant opened in Brno in June 2026.



Co-founder Peter Szamuhel now plans to establish the brand in Prague and Bratislava before launching a franchise network. If preparations proceed as planned, the first franchise locations could open in early 2027.

The company is considering six or seven restaurants in Prague and two or three in Bratislava. Other potential locations include Ostrava, Olomouc, Hradec Králové, Liberec, Nitra and Trnava.

Pickle aims to have its franchise model ready by the end of 2026. Although prospective partners have already expressed interest, the company is not yet signing agreements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pickle Brno (@pickledoublecheese)

The same burgers at every location

Maintaining consistent quality will be a major challenge as Pickle expands. The company plans to use regular inspections, mystery shopping, regional managers and ongoing staff training to ensure that customers receive the same food and service at every restaurant.

Ingredient supplies are another priority. Meat, buns and other key products must match those used at the original Brno location.

The restaurant currently prepares approximately 1,000 to 1,300 burgers a day, according to Szamuhel. Expanding the chain will require a supply network capable of supporting substantially greater demand.

Global ambitions within ten years

Pickle aims to establish ten locations across Czechia and Slovakia within three years, followed by another ten restaurants in other European countries over the next five to six years.

Its longer-term goal is to operate hundreds of locations worldwide within a decade, with Asia among its eventual targets.

World.title: Do You Really Need 10,000 Steps a Day? A Doctor’s Guide to Walking in Prague
World.content:
Walking is part of daily life in Prague, but how much is enough to benefit your health?

A doctor at Charles University explains why 7,000 steps a day may be a more realistic target.

Living in Prague often means walking to the tram, crossing the city centre on foot or taking a stroll through one of its parks. But does this add up to enough physical activity to improve your health? And is reaching 10,000 steps a day really necessary?

According to research published in The Lancet Public Health in 2025, walking around 7,000 steps a day may be enough to deliver significant health benefits.



The study found that people taking approximately 7,000 steps daily had a 47% lower risk of premature death and a 25% lower risk of cardiovascular disease compared with those walking around 2,000 steps a day.

These figures represent associations rather than guarantees, but they suggest that the widely promoted 10,000-step target is not a requirement for better health.

Why walking matters

Regular walking can help strengthen the heart, improve circulation, regulate blood pressure and blood sugar levels, and support muscle and joint health.

Its benefits are not limited to physical fitness. Spending time outdoors and walking regularly can also help reduce stress, improve mood and support better sleep.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week. This can include brisk walking for around 30 minutes a day, five days a week, to meet the minimum recommendation.

The pace matters, too. Brisk walking should make you breathe slightly harder while still allowing you to hold a conversation comfortably.

Where to walk in Prague

Prague offers plenty of opportunities to incorporate more walking into daily life without joining a gym or travelling outside the city.

Stromovka is a good option for beginners and those looking for longer walks on relatively flat paths. The extensive park provides a break from traffic and the busy streets of the city.

For a more demanding route, Divoká Šárka offers hills and woodland trails that provide a more strenuous workout while remaining within Prague.

Vyšehrad is suitable for a shorter walk, combining gentle climbs with views of the city and the Vltava River. Its location also makes it a practical option for those who have limited time.

For a longer weekend outing, Prokopské údolí offers walking routes through valleys and green spaces away from the city centre.

How to keep walking during winter

Shorter days, cold temperatures and icy pavements can make walking less appealing during the winter months. However, the arrival of colder weather does not mean abandoning a regular routine.

Dressing in layers, wearing shoes with good grip and choosing well-lit, cleared paths can make outdoor walks safer and more comfortable.

Even a 10- to 15-minute walk during a lunch break can be worthwhile. When pavements become icy, slowing down or choosing a safer indoor alternative is advisable.

Small changes can make a difference

Building more walking into everyday life does not require a major change in routine. Getting off the tram one stop earlier, taking a walk during lunch or using the stairs when practical can all help increase daily activity.

Those who currently walk relatively little can start with 10 to 15 minutes a day and gradually increase the duration as their fitness improves.

Rather than focusing on a fixed target, people who track their steps can aim to increase their usual daily total over time.

About the author

Darren Andrew Noronha, MD, is a medical doctor and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, with a research focus on cardiovascular health and disease prevention.

World.title: Czech Republic to See Sharp Weekend Cooldown and Possible Snowfall
World.content:
The Czech Republic is set for a change in weather this weekend, with temperatures expected to fall and snow possible in mountain areas, according to the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute (CHMI).

The colder conditions will follow several relatively mild autumn days, when daytime temperatures are forecast to reach 17 to 18 degrees Celsius.



By the weekend, however, increased cloud cover and precipitation could bring the first signs of winter to higher elevations.

The transition will come after a frosty start to the week. Meteorologists expect the coldest night of the week to have already passed, meaning temperatures should remain more moderate over the coming days.

Sunshine is forecast across much of the country during the remainder of the working week, although mornings will stay chilly. Local fog and showers may develop in eastern parts of the Czech Republic.

The outlook for the weekend remains uncertain, but forecasters expect a general cooling trend, accompanied by extensive cloud cover and periods of rain.

Mountain regions are most likely to see wintry conditions. As temperatures fall, rain could turn to snow at higher elevations, particularly in the mountains. Some locations may also experience temperatures below freezing.

However, significant or lasting snowfall is not currently expected. Any snow that falls is likely to be limited to light dustings or scattered flakes, with accumulations unlikely to persist for long.

World.title: David Duchovny Brings New Album to Prague This Thursday
World.content:
David Duchovny, best known for his acting career, will perform in Prague on October 15, 2026, presenting songs from his upcoming album Prince of Pieces at Archa+.

Tickets are on sale through GoOut.

Duchovny has spent the past decade developing his career as a songwriter and recording artist, releasing music that combines melodic rock with introspective lyrics.

Prince of Pieces is his fourth album and brings together a small group of musicians and longtime collaborators.

The new record follows Hell or Highwater, Every Third Thought, released in 2017, and Gestureland, released in 2021. According to the album’s press release, the latest project is his most cohesive and collaborative work to date, reflecting the relationships he has built with fellow musicians over the years.

Duchovny’s music has received positive reviews from critics.

AllMusic described his sound as “eloquent, alt-rock-kissed country-folk in the vein of Wilco and the Wallflowers,” while The Boston Globe praised his voice for its “parched resonance and just a hint of rasp,” adding that he sings with feeling.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by David Duchovny (@davidduchovny)

The actor has said that the arrangements on his records are shaped by the mood and rhythm of each song, rather than following a single formula.

“The arrangements of the songs have always been in service of either the groove or the emotion,” Duchovny said. He added that he looks for sounds that complement the melody, including horns, bells and harmonies, while also experimenting with rhythms and beats.

World.title: Czech Doctors May Soon Prescribe Museum Visits to Prevent Depression
World.content:
Doctors in the Czech Republic could soon recommend museum visits, dance classes, singing and creative workshops to people at risk of depression, anxiety or social isolation.

The program, known as Art on Prescription, aims to connect healthcare providers with museums, galleries, libraries and other cultural institutions.

Rather than replacing medication or psychotherapy, these activities would complement existing treatment and help prevent mental health problems.



The National Institute of Mental Health (NUDZ) is preparing a National Platform for Prevention through Culture to bring together cultural organizations, healthcare providers, social services and schools. The goal is to make existing cultural activities more accessible to people who could benefit from them.

The initiative is not intended to turn cultural institutions into medical facilities. Instead, it seeks to use local resources to support mental well-being and strengthen social connections.

Research highlights benefits of cultural activities

International research suggests that participating in cultural and artistic activities can improve well-being, strengthen social ties and reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety.

According to Dominika Grygarová, a researcher at NUDZ, an analysis combining studies from more than 20 countries found significant reductions in symptoms of both depression and anxiety.

The benefits depend not only on exposure to art but also on active participation, Grygarová said. Creating something, learning a new skill, sharing experiences and interacting with others can help people focus on something beyond their difficulties and develop a sense of belonging.

However, the programs are intended primarily as a preventive and supportive measure, not a substitute for professional treatment. Researchers also want to assess their effectiveness and economic value, with preliminary analyses suggesting that some initiatives could be cost-effective.

Czech project looks to Northern Europe

NUDZ plans to build on similar programs already operating in several countries, particularly the United Kingdom and Northern Europe.

The Czech initiative intends to follow the so-called Baltic model, with researchers planning to work with Danish colleagues next year on a European project to introduce the approach more widely.

World.title: Who Is Petr Hlaváček? The Architect Set to Become Prague’s Next Mayor
World.content:
Petr Hlaváček is seeking to become the Czech capital’s next mayor after his political movement, STAN, won the municipal elections.

STAN received 23.16 percent of the vote, securing 17 seats in the Prague City Assembly and putting the movement in a strong position to negotiate the next governing coalition.



Hlaváček, currently deputy mayor for territorial and strategic development, has indicated that he wants to take the top job at City Hall.

His priorities include expanding housing construction, redeveloping former industrial sites and improving transport infrastructure.

A key role in Prague’s new zoning plan

Hlaváček’s main achievement as deputy mayor has been his involvement in preparing Prague’s new Metropolitan Plan, which replaced the previous zoning document from 1999 when it came into effect in September 2026.

The plan sets out where construction can take place and establishes rules for future development. It identifies capacity for up to 350,000 new homes, primarily through the redevelopment of brownfield sites.

One of the main projects is the transformation of Bubny-Zátory, an underused area expected to provide housing for around 20,000 people.

Hlaváček has also backed the Prague Development Company, which manages municipal land and aims to increase housing construction. According to him, the company could facilitate the development of up to 70,000 homes while helping prevent city-owned land from being sold off.

Transport and housing at the top of his agenda

If appointed mayor, Hlaváček wants to continue work on major transport projects, including Prague’s inner ring road and the Prague Ring Road. He also supports expanding public transport and reforming parking policy, arguing that parking in the city is often too cheap.

Before the elections, he said STAN would welcome continuing the existing coalition at City Hall but wanted a more prominent role, depending on its electoral support.

From architect to deputy mayor

Born in Zlín on July 31, 1961, Hlaváček graduated from the Faculty of Architecture at the Czech Technical University in Prague. He later established his own architectural studio, taught as a visiting professor at the University of Michigan and served as vice-dean at his alma mater.

His professional work includes the renovation of the Czech Embassy in Brasília, Brazil.

In 2015, he became director of the Prague Institute of Planning and Development. He was dismissed the following year amid criticism over delays to the Metropolitan Plan, a decision that prompted protests from institute employees.

Hlaváček entered Prague politics after the 2018 municipal elections and became first deputy mayor for territorial development and spatial planning in November 2021. He remained in the city leadership after the 2022 elections and took responsibility for territorial and strategic development in February 2023.

World.title: Sinatra Tribute Pairs Frank Sinatra Classics With 1930s Dining at Prague’s Mánes
World.content:
Prague’s Art Restaurant Mánes combines live performances of Frank Sinatra’s best-known songs with a three-course dinner inspired by traditional Czech cuisine of the 1930s.

The functionalist building offers views of the Vltava River and nearby Žofín Island, providing the setting for an evening dedicated to the music and style of Sinatra’s era.



The Sinatra’s Tribute musical programme features acclaimed soloists, including baritone Daniel Klánský and jazz singer Sophie Lamoš. They perform some of Sinatra’s best-known songs, including *My Way* and *Fly Me to the Moon*, accompanied by a group of musicians.

Rather than simply imitating the legendary American singer, the Sinatra Tribute offers its own interpretation of his musical legacy.

One of the programme’s highlights is a restored 1897 Steinway & Sons grand piano, an instrument once played by Czech composer and pianist Jaroslav Ježek.

The music is complemented by a three-course dinner served before the concert.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sinatra Tribute Koncert & Večeře / Sinatra Tribute Show & Dinner (@sinatratributeprague)

Created exclusively for the programme by Mánes Restaurant head chef Jaroslav Zahálka, the menu draws inspiration from Prague’s culinary traditions of the 1930s, reflecting the period associated with the evening’s musical theme.

Visitors can contact the venue for current dates, ticket prices and reservations.

World.title: Hungarian house prices fall for first time in 4 years – Is the property boom finally slowing?
World.content:
Hungarian house prices fell by 1.4% in the second quarter of 2026, marking their first quarterly decline since late 2022 and the steepest drop among European countries. Prices are still 10.2% higher than a year ago, but the slowdown in demand and more moderate rent increases suggest that the market is losing momentum.

Hungary’s housing market has taken an unexpected turn, with residential property prices falling for the first time in more than three years. According to fresh data from Eurostat, prices dropped by 1.4% between the first and second quarters of 2026, the largest quarterly decrease recorded among the European countries surveyed.

The decline marks a significant change after years of rapid price growth that placed Hungary among Europe’s strongest-performing housing markets.

France was the only other country to record a quarterly fall, with house prices slipping by 0.8%. Elsewhere, prices continued to rise, led by Lithuania, where residential property became 5% more expensive in just three months. Bulgaria and Romania also recorded substantial increases of 4.5% and 4.4%, respectively.

Despite the recent decline, Hungary’s housing market is still considerably more expensive than a year ago.

Annual house price growth slows sharply

In the second quarter of 2026, Hungarian residential property prices were still 10.2% higher than in the same period last year. This was more than double the European Union average of 4.7%. However, the annual increase represents a considerable slowdown compared with the more than 20% growth recorded towards the end of 2025.

Hungary has consequently slipped from the top tier of European housing markets to the middle of the rankings. Only eight countries recorded faster annual price increases than Hungary. The latest figures suggest that the market’s strong upward momentum is easing, although the quarterly decline alone does not establish whether a sustained fall in prices is beginning.

If you missed it: Good news for buyers: Hungarian housing market is turning, Budapest prices fall for 2nd month

Did the Home Start programme fuel the property boom?

According to Dávid Valkó, chief analyst at OTP Ingatlanpont, one of the most significant developments in Hungary’s housing market in recent years was the launch of the Home Start subsidised mortgage programme in September 2025. The scheme offers eligible buyers a fixed interest rate of 3%, helping some households finance their first home.

Valkó told Telex that the programme triggered an initial surge in demand in autumn 2025, followed by another, smaller wave at the beginning of 2026. Interest in purchasing property then declined noticeably during the spring months.

The timing suggests that the programme helped stimulate demand, although the latest Eurostat figures alone cannot establish how much of the price movement was caused by the scheme.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Rental prices are rising more slowly than house prices

Another notable development is the growing gap between the cost of buying a home and the cost of renting one. While house prices remained 10.2% higher year on year in the second quarter, rents increased by just 4.2% in real terms, after adjusting for inflation.

The Home Start programme may also be contributing to this difference. With eligible buyers able to access mortgages at a fixed 3% interest rate, some households may find purchasing a property more attractive than continuing to rent. If more people move from renting to homeownership, demand for rental properties could weaken, putting a brake on rent increases.

World.title: Cancer drug gets faster approval route in Hungary – Will patients get easier access?
World.content:
Hungary has approved a simplified procedure for using Keytruda, a widely used cancer immunotherapy, before surgery for malignant melanoma. However, the decision does not automatically mean that all eligible patients will receive state-funded treatment.

Hungary has introduced a simplified procedure for using Keytruda in the pre-operative treatment of malignant melanoma, the National Centre for Public Health and Pharmacy (NNGYK) announced on 15 October.

The decision covers two formulations of the cancer drug, whose active ingredient is pembrolizumab: a 25 mg/ml concentrate for infusion and a 395 mg solution for injection, both manufactured by Merck Sharp & Dohme BV.

The new procedure applies to neoadjuvant treatment, meaning therapy administered before a tumour is surgically removed.

However, the decision does not automatically make the treatment available with public health insurance funding to every patient who may benefit from it.

How does Keytruda work?

According to Telex, Keytruda is one of the best-known cancer immunotherapy medicines. Rather than attacking cancer cells directly in the same way as conventional chemotherapy, it helps the body’s immune system recognise and fight cancer.

Its uses include several types of cancer, among them lung cancer, breast cancer and melanoma. The latest Hungarian decision concerns its use before surgery for malignant melanoma, an aggressive form of skin cancer.

The simplified procedure represents a regulatory step towards making this particular treatment application possible in Hungary. Access to publicly funded treatment, however, remains a separate issue.

Why access to Keytruda remains a concern in Hungary

A May investigation by Direkt36 highlighted the difficulties some Hungarian cancer patients face when trying to obtain publicly funded Keytruda treatment.

According to the investigation, Hungary’s National Health Insurance Fund Management (NEAK) automatically finances the medicine only for certain cancer types and treatment indications. In other cases, patients must apply for individual funding approval.

The report featured the case of a 63-year-old woman diagnosed with severe lung cancer whose doctors recommended Keytruda. She needed special approval to receive public funding for the treatment.

“I started begging, saying that I was terminally ill and needed the treatment,” she recalled, according to the investigation. Her application was eventually approved.

Oncologists interviewed by Direkt36 said that decisions on individual funding applications could take weeks, potentially affecting treatment prospects for seriously ill patients. The NEAK said urgent, life-threatening cases were handled as a priority.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Treatment can cost millions of forints

The financial implications are substantial. Data obtained by Direkt36 indicated that a single Keytruda treatment could cost more than HUF 1.8 million (EUR 4,950).

According to the investigation, the NEAK had spent more than HUF 125 billion on the medicine since 2019. Around 1,000 individual funding applications for Keytruda are submitted each year, with close to 90% approved.

Nevertheless, incorporating additional uses of the drug into the standard public reimbursement system has historically been a lengthy process. The data obtained by Direkt36 showed that decisions on reimbursement applications took an average of 441 days.

What does the new decision mean for patients?

The simplified procedure concerns the use of Keytruda before surgery for malignant melanoma. It should not be confused with an automatic expansion of public funding for every patient who needs the medicine. For patients, access depends not only on the authorised use of a drug but also on the applicable reimbursement rules and individual eligibility.

World.title: India and Hungary strengthen ties in Budapest: Yoga, digital skills and a unique cultural fusion
World.content:
The Embassy of India in Budapest celebrated ITEC Day 2026 on 14 October 2026 at the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, Budapest, bringing together alumni of the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) Programme, distinguished guests and representatives of Hungary and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The celebration highlighted the important role of the ITEC Programme in strengthening international cooperation, sharing India’s developmental expertise and fostering enduring people-to-people ties.

Established by the Government of India in 1964, the ITEC Programme is a flagship initiative for international capacity building and technical cooperation. Through specialised training courses in diverse fields, the programme enables partner countries to benefit from India’s experience, expertise and developmental achievements while building professional networks and lasting institutional linkages. Since 2014, the ITEC Programme has provided training opportunities to 33 professionals from Hungary and 14 from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

ITEC alumni from Hungary and Bosnia and Herzegovina shared their experiences of specialised training in India. Hungarian alumni Mr. Péter Szennay and Mr. Zoltán Erdélyi highlighted their training in yoga and digital public infrastructure, respectively, while Ms. Thanh Lien Hoang The, currently attending a yoga trainers’ programme in India, shared her experience. Alumni from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Radomir Mutabdžija and Mr. Momčilo Renovica, also shared video messages on their training in data analytics and sustainable cities, respectively.

Photo: Embassy of India in Budapest Photo: Embassy of India in Budapest

The celebration also showcased India’s rich cultural heritage through musical and dance performances. A musical presentation featuring Mr. Durgesh Kanwal, tabla teacher at the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, and Mr. Mátyás Egervári on the cimbalom brought together Indian and Hungarian musical traditions. A dance presentation titled “Charishnu”, featuring Ms. Priya Garg, Kathak teacher and performer at the Centre, Ms. Zselyke Molnár, Odissi artist, and Ms. Sindhu Ravipati, Kuchipudi artist, added a vibrant cultural dimension to the occasion.

The Ambassador of India to Hungary felicitated the ITEC alumni speakers in recognition of their participation and engagement with the programme. In his remarks, he highlighted the importance of the ITEC Programme as a key part of India’s development cooperation and its commitment to sharing knowledge, skills and experience with partner countries.

He also noted the programme’s role in strengthening bilateral relations, promoting mutual understanding and building people-to-people ties. Referring to the vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the Ambassador highlighted India’s guiding principle of “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” (the world is one family), emphasising India’s belief in cooperation, shared progress and the well-being of all.

H.E. Mr. Iván Medveczky, Deputy State Secretary for Relations with the South at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Hungary, delivered the keynote address, highlighting the strong historical ties between India and Hungary and the importance of continued cooperation between the two countries. He appreciated India’s efforts to share its knowledge, skills and experience with partner countries through the ITEC Programme, noting its valuable contribution to capacity-building and strengthening bilateral relations.

The celebration highlighted the positive experiences of ITEC alumni and the Programme’s contribution to promoting knowledge exchange, professional collaboration and closer people-to-people ties between India, Hungary and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

World.title: Pakistan brings its rice, and its diplomacy, to a Budapest kitchen
World.content:
Hungarian importers, chefs and food industry professionals gathered at a cooking school in Budapest this week for a different kind of trade promotion: one conducted over a hot stove.

The Embassy of Pakistan held the first Pakistan Rice Festival in Hungary at the KuktaParty Chef Academy, an event built around a single product. Pakistani basmati, the long-grain aromatic rice is among the country’s best-known exports, and the Embassy’s aim was to put it in front of the Hungarian trade in the most persuasive form available: cooked, served and eaten.

The guest list reflected that purpose. Importers and business leaders from the food and agriculture sector made up the bulk of the room, joined by leading Hungarian master chefs, representatives of several public sector bodies and members of the diplomatic community.

Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

A grain with a legal identity

Ambassador Asif Hussain Memon opened the event, telling guests that Pakistani cuisine has considerably more range than international audiences tend to realise, and that spices and rice sit at the centre of it. Much of what is recognised abroad as Pakistani food, he suggested, represents only a fraction of what our kitchens actually produce.

He also drew attention to something that matters more to importers than to diners. Basmati is protected under Geographical Indication, a designation that ties the name to rice grown in specific regions of Pakistan and assures buyers of both its origin and its quality.

Alongside the rice, the Embassy displayed a selection of other Pakistani food products, most notably Himalayan Pink Salt, sold worldwide in both culinary and decorative forms. Guests were invited to sample its different grades, from fine ground to coarse granulated.

Among those attending were Hungarian master chefs István Asztalos and Péter Korpádi, who spoke warmly of the depth and complexity of the dishes on offer and of the quality of the rice at the centre of them.

Ambassador Asif Hussain Memon. Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

Biryani, built in layers

The centrepiece of the afternoon was a live cooking demonstration by the Embassy’s Trade & Investment Attaché, Shehryar Qaisrani, who prepared and explained the process of making biryani in front of the room.

Biryani is among the most celebrated dishes in Pakistani cooking, and also among the most demanding. The rice is parboiled rather than cooked through, then layered over spiced meat with fried onions, herbs and saffron, never stirred, and sealed under a lid to finish in its own steam. The technique, known as dum, gives the dish its characteristic separation of grains and the three-tone colour that appears when the pot is opened.

Each guest left with a sample of Pakistani basmati and a short recipe book the Embassy had prepared in Hungarian, featuring a range of rice-based dishes, so that they could try cooking them at home.

László Asztalos, owner of KuktaParty, said that hosting the event was a source of pride for the school. He described it as a welcome opportunity to contribute to the promotion of Pakistani gastronomy in Hungary while supporting the development of professional and cultural ties between the two countries.

Photo: Embassy of Pakistan in Budapest

From the kitchen to the trade floor

The food was also a route to business. The Ambassador invited participants to attend FoodAg 2026, Pakistan’s international food and agriculture exhibition, which runs at the Expo Centre in Karachi from 23 to 26 November. The exhibition brings together several hundred exporters across rice, fruit, seafood and processed foods, and offers Hungarian importers direct access to Pakistani suppliers.

The commercial ambition behind the event is not incidental. The Government of Pakistan established a dedicated Commercial Wing at its Embassy in Budapest just last year, as part of a broader effort to build trade relationships in European markets where Pakistan has not traditionally been active.

Mangoes first, then rice

It is not the first time Pakistani produce has made an impression in Hungary. When the Embassy shared Pakistani mangoes earlier this summer, the response was unusually warm, and Prime Minister Péter Magyar posted his appreciation publicly.

Speaking about the wider relationship between the two countries, Ambassador Memon said that food has proved one of the most natural bridges between them.

“Relations between Pakistan and Hungary have traditionally been friendly, built on mutual respect and trust,” he said. “I believe this relationship holds considerable untapped potential, and my aim as Ambassador is to turn our political trust into real economic results and lasting friendships between our people.”

He added that the Rice Festival was an illustration of what that means in practice.

“It allowed us to introduce Pakistani basmati to Hungarian chefs, importers and food professionals in the most direct way possible: by cooking it and sharing it. Diplomacy is often conducted across a table. On this occasion it happened around one.”

World.title: Budapest Christmas market crowned Europe’s most beautiful for 2026! Here’s when it opens
World.content:
Budapest’s Advent Basilica Christmas market has won Europe’s top Christmas market title for 2026, adding another international accolade to its collection. The popular festive attraction opens on 13 November, bringing Christmas cheer back to the Hungarian capital.

Budapest’s Advent Basilica Christmas market has been named Europe’s most beautiful Christmas market for 2026 by European Best Destinations (EBD), beating competitors from across the continent. The award ceremony took place in Monaco on 9 October, with 40 Christmas markets reaching the final.

The latest recognition is particularly prestigious, as Advent Basilica won in the organisation’s ‘All Stars’ category, which brings together previous award winners. The Budapest attraction has already earned the title of Europe’s Best Christmas Market four times, further cementing its reputation as one of the continent’s leading festive destinations.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Why does Budapest’s Advent Basilica stand out?

Set in front of St Stephen’s Basilica, one of Budapest’s most recognisable landmarks, the market combines traditional crafts, festive food and drink, and spectacular lighting to create a distinctive Christmas atmosphere.

According to EBD, the balance between culture, gastronomy and the setting is a key reason for its continued popularity among international visitors. The combination of the historic basilica, carefully designed decorations and culinary offerings makes the market an attraction that draws tourists back year after year.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Maximilien Lejeune, EBD’s managing director, said the event had repeatedly succeeded in delivering the beauty, magical atmosphere and originality that visitors expect from a Christmas market.

He also highlighted how closely the market’s promise matches the experience visitors encounter in person, with Budapest providing the ideal backdrop for the festive event.

The market’s growing international reputation has also attracted attention across the travel media. Forbes included Budapest in its coverage of Europe’s most beautiful Christmas markets for 2026, placing the Hungarian capital firmly on the festive travel map.

Photo: Advent Basilica

Advent Basilica celebrates its 15th anniversary

The 2026 edition marks the 15th anniversary of Advent Basilica. Over the years, it has collected several major international awards, including the title of Europe’s Best Christmas Market in 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024.

In 2024, it also received the distinction of being named the best European Christmas market of all time.

Budapest has enjoyed further success with its other major festive attraction, the Vörösmarty Classic Xmas market. In 2025, it was named Europe’s most popular Christmas market in an analysis by travel experts at Tollwayr, reportedly beating established destinations such as Strasbourg, Vienna and Prague.

The Hungarian capital also secured second place in Travel and Tour World’s ranking of the world’s best Christmas destinations in 2025, behind only New York. Budapest was the highest-ranked European destination, ahead of cities including London, Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Vienna.

Photo: Advent Basilica

When does the Budapest Christmas market open in 2026?

This year’s Advent Basilica Christmas market opens on 13 November 2026, welcoming visitors to the square in front of St Stephen’s Basilica.

The festive attractions will also extend to Vörösmarty Square, where the Vörösmarty Classic Xmas market offers another popular destination for Christmas shopping, traditional Hungarian food and seasonal treats.

For tourists planning a winter city break, the two markets provide an opportunity to experience Budapest’s festive atmosphere while exploring some of its best-known central locations.

Photo: Advent Basilica

What is European Best Destinations?

European Best Destinations has organised tourism competitions involving travellers from around the world since 2009. The organisation works with more than 500 European destinations, including Marbella, Monaco and Madrid, and aims to increase their international visibility and appeal.

Its media partners include Forbes, Condé Nast Traveler and National Geographic. This year’s award ceremony was held in Monaco on 9 October, with Princess Stéphanie of Monaco and Eva Longoria among those attending.

World.title: Drunk driver with no licence accused of fatal hit-and-run in Hungary
World.content:
A 36-year-old woman has been charged over a fatal hit-and-run near Szigetszentmiklós, Hungary, after allegedly drunk driving without a driving licence, killing an electric tricycle rider and leaving the victim without assistance.

Drunk woman with no driving licence caused fatal accident

The Budakörnyék District Prosecutor’s Office has requested an eight-year prison sentence, an eight-year ban from public affairs and a permanent driving ban for the accused. The case will be heard by the Szigetszentmiklós District Court.

According to prosecutors, the woman was working at a car wash near Szigetszentmiklós when the incident happened in February 2025. She allegedly took two customers’ cars without their permission on separate occasions to buy alcohol.

Took customers’ cars to buy alcohol

The woman first drove a car left at the car wash for cleaning to a nearby alcohol shop without the owner’s knowledge. After purchasing and consuming the alcohol, she allegedly took another vehicle – while already drunk – entrusted to the business for cleaning and set off for the shop again.

As she approached the shop’s car park, the woman reportedly turned at speed without noticing an electric tricycle approaching from the opposite direction. The tricycle rider had the right of way. The front left side of the car struck the tricycle, causing it to overturn and throwing its rider to the ground. The victim, reported by local media to have been 41 years old, suffered fatal injuries.

Driver examined victim before fleeing

After the collision, the drunk woman reportedly got out of the car and approached the unconscious woman lying on the ground. When she was unable to lift the victim, she returned to the vehicle and drove away without calling emergency services or providing further assistance.

People who came out of the nearby shop and an adjacent property called an ambulance. However, the victim’s injuries were so severe that she died at the scene. The prosecutor’s office has charged the woman with causing death through drink-driving, two counts of unauthorised use of a vehicle and an aggravated offence of failing to provide assistance.

Join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel.

Prosecutors seek eight-year prison sentence

The prosecution has asked the court to impose an eight-year custodial sentence and bar the defendant from public affairs for the same period. It has also requested that she be permanently disqualified from driving. The accused is currently under criminal supervision, according to the prosecution’s announcement. Local media have also reported that she did not give a statement during the investigation.

The case will now proceed before the Szigetszentmiklós District Court, which will decide whether the defendant is guilty and determine any sentence. The charges and requested penalties represent the prosecution’s position; the court has yet to deliver its verdict.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW OUT NOW: Kosovo’s foreign minister warns of Serbian threats
World.content:
Kosovo’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Glauk Konjufca, has warned that the risk of renewed armed confrontation with Serbia must be taken seriously. In an exclusive interview with Hungary Insider, he accused Belgrade of pursuing territorial ambitions and called for stronger international measures to prevent further instability in the Western Balkans. The minister also addressed NATO’s role in maintaining regional security and the continuing dispute over the deadly 2023 Banjska attack.

Tensions between Kosovo and Serbia remain a significant security concern in the Western Balkans, nearly two decades after Kosovo declared independence in 2008.

The Republic of Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and is recognised as an independent and sovereign state by Hungary and 120 other countries. Serbia continues to reject its independence and maintain territorial claims over the country. The dispute has repeatedly triggered political crises and security incidents, particularly in northern Kosovo, where a substantial ethnic Serb population maintains close ties with Belgrade.

Speaking exclusively to Hungary Insider, Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca argued that recent statements by Serbian officials should be viewed in the context of previous armed incidents and military deployments.

“The threat to the Republic of Kosovo is real, and the international community must recognise the gravity of this pattern,” he said.

Kosovo warns that Serbian rhetoric could signal a wider security threat

Konjufca condemned Serbian Deputy Prime Minister Ivica Dacic’s explicit declaration that the Serbian flag would “sooner or later fly over Prizren”, a city in southern Kosovo, describing it as evidence of Belgrade’s continuing territorial ambitions against the Republic of Kosovo.

According to the minister, such statements cannot be separated from developments on the ground.

He also highlighted the public appearance of Milan Radoicic, former vice-president of the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista and the admitted organiser of the armed group responsible for the September 2023 Banjska terrorist attack, alongside Danilo Vucic, son of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, at a ruling-party campaign rally.

Konjufca described these developments as evidence of a persistent pattern of Serbian territorial revisionism and the political protection afforded to individuals responsible for armed aggression against the Republic of Kosovo, particularly Milan Radoicic, who publicly acknowledged organising the armed group responsible for the Banjska terrorist attack.

The Government of the Republic of Kosovo has consistently maintained that the Banjska terrorist attack was supported by Serbian state structures. The Special Prosecution’s indictment details an organised operation aimed at annexing north of Kosovo to Serbia, including allegations that military infrastructure in Serbia was provided for the group’s training.

Konjufca also pointed to Radoicic’s longstanding political relationship with Aleksandar Vucic, who publicly praised him on several occasions and later acknowledged him as a close political ally. Serbia denies state involvement, while Radoicic maintains that he acted independently.

The Banjska attack continues to fuel tensions

The September 2023 attack in Banjska, northern Kosovo, remains one of the most serious security incidents in relations between Belgrade and Pristina in recent years.

A heavily armed group carried out a terrorist attack against Kosovo Police in Banjska, killing Police Sergeant Afrim Bunjaku. Three members of the attacking group were subsequently killed during the ensuing armed confrontation.

In the days following the Banjska terrorist attack, Serbia amassed tanks, artillery and mechanized infantry along its border with the Republic of Kosovo. The unprecedented scale of this military deployment prompted an extraordinary public warning from the White House, which demanded the withdrawal of Serbian forces. NATO subsequently reinforced its KFOR peacekeeping presence in Kosovo.

In the exclusive interview, Konjufca criticised the lack of accountability for those responsible for the attack, particularly the fact that Radoičić remains in Serbia.

Minister Konjufca called on the European Union to exert decisive pressure on Belgrade to surrender Milan Radoicic and the other indicted perpetrators to the judicial authorities of the Republic of Kosovo. He also recalled the European Parliament’s 2023 call for targeted restrictive measures against Radoicic, emphasising that these demands must now be translated into concrete action.

“Justice for Banjska is essential to preventing further aggression and establishing lasting security in our region,” he said.

How serious is the risk of another Serbia–Kosovo conflict?

Asked whether a renewed armed confrontation was a realistic possibility, Konjufca made clear that his government takes the danger seriously.

Minister Konjufca. Source: Facebook

“We take the risk of renewed confrontation seriously, knowing the devastating consequences of war,” he told Hungary Insider.

He identified a renewed concentration of Serbian combat forces near Kosovo’s borders or another armed attack against Kosovo’s territory and critical infrastructure as developments that would constitute a grave escalation.

Nevertheless, the minister stressed that Kosovo remains committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful relations with neighbouring countries.

According to Konjufca, preventing further violence requires credible deterrence, a strong NATO presence through KFOR, and close coordination with the United States and European partners.

Why Kosovo’s security matters to Hungary

For Hungary, developments in Kosovo have direct regional security implications.

Hungary has long contributed troops to NATO’s Kosovo Force, which is tasked with maintaining a safe and secure environment and freedom of movement in the territory.

The proximity of the Western Balkans also makes regional stability an important consideration for Hungarian foreign and security policy.

Hungary recognised Kosovo’s independence in March 2008 and has maintained diplomatic relations with Pristina since then.

Konjufca acknowledged Hungary’s longstanding contribution to Kosovo’s security in his interview, while also discussing how political developments in Budapest could influence future bilateral relations.

The minister emphasised that Kosovo’s longer-term ambitions remain focused on European integration, international cooperation and membership of NATO.

What else did Kosovo’s foreign minister reveal in the exclusive interview?

Beyond the security tensions with Serbia, Glauk Konjufca addressed several important political and diplomatic questions in his extensive interview with Hungary Insider.

He discussed how Kosovo views Hungary’s political transition under Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whether Budapest could play a greater role in the Western Balkans, and what opportunities exist for closer Hungarian–Kosovar cooperation.

The minister also examined the political connections surrounding the Banjska attack, the measures he expects from the European Union, and Kosovo’s efforts to secure EU candidate status.

He further addressed Kosovo’s ambitions to join NATO, its campaign for wider international recognition, and the message he wants to send to European governments, particularly those in Central Europe.

What does Glauk Konjufca expect from Péter Magyar’s government? How could Hungary influence Kosovo’s European future? And what further action does he want the EU to take towards Serbia?
