World.title: ‘Deadly consequences’: How lack of proper prison in Abkhazia leads to further crimes
World.content:
The recent murder of a Russian tourist has exposed problems with prison sentences in Abkhazia. Edgar Abukhba, who stands accused of murdering Amina Bikbova, received a nine-year sentence for a previous serious crime. In practice, however, he served only half that time. This proved fatal for his next victim.

Amina’s murder prompted Abkhazian society to take a closer look at how courts enforce their rulings. It emerged that in Abkhazia, a sentence tells you very little about how long someone will actually spend in prison. The republic has no proper prison, and a complicated system of “penitentiary arithmetic” determines how much time a person spends behind bars. Even those who apply the rules struggle to make sense of them.

One last coffee

Amina Bikbova’s family had a rule: call her mother every evening. The 26-year-old followed it without fail when she travelled to Abkhazia with her friend Adila for a holiday in September 2026. But one evening, she did not call and failed to answer her phone either. The next day, her phone remained silent. Her family then realised that something serious had happened.

Amina Bikbova

The circumstances surrounding Amina’s final day are known from accounts given by her family and witness testimony reported by Abkhazian and Russian media. Amina and Adila met Edgar Abukhba, a 25-year-old fruit seller. A couple of days later, he invited Amina for coffee. Adila says she tried to talk her friend out of going, but failed. Amina went to meet Edgar and never returned.

During his initial questioning, he denied any wrongdoing. He claimed that he and Amina had simply had coffee, after which she got into someone’s car and drove away. Investigators quickly disproved this account, and Edgar admitted that they had argued, that he had strangled Amina and left her body in bushes beside the road.

A familiar name

Edgar Abukhba

For Abkhazians who follow local crime reports, the surname Abukhba sounded familiar. In July 2019, a 24-year-old Russian tourist suffered a brutal attack in central Sukhum. Her assailants beat, raped and robbed her. Everyone familiar with the case said they had rarely encountered such brutality. Authorities arrested Edgar Abukhba on suspicion of the crime. The case took more than two years to reach court, and in 2021 a judge sentenced him to nine years in prison.

If the nine-year sentence is counted from 2019, when Abukhba entered pre-trial detention, he should not have been released before 2028. Yet by the summer of 2026, he was already selling fruit in Gagra.

Sentences without a prison

Court rulings specify the regime under which a convicted person must serve their sentence, and this affects the time they spend in prison. But Abkhazia has no prison colony with different security regimes, which creates confusion. Officials recalculate sentences differently depending on how much time a prisoner has spent under various conditions. The final figure depends on the coefficient they apply and can differ significantly from the court’s verdict.

Got that? No, of course not. For anyone unfamiliar with the system, it is almost impossible to understand. Even staff at the relevant institutions struggle to explain on the spot how they calculate a particular sentence, how long a specific prisoner will serve and when they will be released.

Perhaps this explains why a man who, on paper, received a nine-year prison sentence attacked another woman long before that term had expired.

Leniency vs prudence

There is another legal complication in Edgar Abukhba’s case. He was still a minor when he committed his first crime, and under Abkhazian law, courts must not take juvenile convictions into account in the future.

There are two opposing views on this rule.

The logic of juvenile justice holds that a teenager’s actions should not determine the rest of their life. But this approach conflicts with public safety concerns, which suggest that authorities cannot simply ignore a proven threat posed by an individual.

Many countries face this dilemma, but they also assess risks before releasing offenders and supervise them afterwards. They may also restrict where former prisoners can work or live and impose other measures. Abkhazia, however, has no such safeguards in place.

A tarnished reputation

Cynical as it may sound, Abkhazia’s tourism sector — and, consequently, its budget — can also be counted among the “victims” of this tragedy.

Abkhazia effectively lives off Russian tourists, who provide the republic’s main source of income. Its reputation as a safe holiday destination is vital to its survival. Now, Amina Bikbova’s murder has left a major black mark on that reputation. This is particularly troubling because it is not the first attack on tourists.

Tourists may forgive reckless taxi drivers or poor service. But they are unlikely to accept the idea that killers who have not served their full sentences can freely walk the streets in search of new victims.

Many Abkhazian lawyers believe the authorities should publish a breakdown of Edgar Abukhba’s first sentence, including the coefficients they applied and his release date. In other words, they should at least explain why he regained his freedom so quickly. Perhaps the authorities should also review the system for calculating prison sentences. Better still, they should finally build a proper prison colony so that no one has to perform these calculations in the first place.

The public, meanwhile, wants an open trial in this case. People are waiting for an explanation of how this mysterious coefficient can allow rapists and murderers to walk free earlier than petty thieves.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

What the lack of a proper prison in Abkhazia leads to

World.title: ‘Whether we should ‘marry’ the EU is question for future’, Armenia’s foreign minister says about EU membership
World.content:
Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

The Armenian parliament approved a law launching the country’s EU accession process in spring 2025. However, only now has Armenian society begun to hold “serious, in-depth” discussions about membership. Foreign Minister and Minister of International Trade Ararat Mirzoyan made the remarks on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.

During a panel discussion entitled “Half-Readiness or a Gradual Approach: Rethinking EU Enlargement”, Mirzoyan was asked where the train taking Armenia towards Europe would ultimately stop. The minister replied that nobody knew — neither Armenia, nor the EU, nor its member states.

He said the good news was that both Armenia and the European Union were enjoying their current process of engagement.

“So let us enjoy these warm relations, discover new opportunities and explore new dimensions of cooperation. At some point in the future, we can sit down together and discuss whether we should ‘get married’,” Mirzoyan said.

During the panel discussion, the minister also addressed the reopening of the Armenian-Turkish border and the peace process with Azerbaijan.

He stressed that Armenia’s efforts to improve relations with its neighbours do not stem from its desire to integrate with European institutions.

Moreover, he assured the audience that this process would continue regardless of other factors.

“On the other hand, we should acknowledge that if our goal is to become a full member of the European Union, problems or conflicts with our neighbours are likely to become an obstacle along the way,” Ararat Mirzoyan noted.

Armenia and the EU are pursuing more than just political dialogue

“Our relations with the European Union have reached an unprecedented depth, covering a wide range of areas and forms of cooperation. We are holding a dialogue on visa liberalisation. The EU has established a monitoring mission in Armenia, which continues to operate and monitor the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. We recently welcomed a second mission. Although temporary, it operates on a permanent basis and helps us counter hybrid threats.

Although we are not an EU candidate country, the Union has granted us preferential trade access with its member states.

This is the latest development. The EU has approved autonomous trade measures to help Armenia diversify its export markets. We have also signed an agreement with the Union that will allow us to take part in various EU missions around the world.

Moreover, although we are not a candidate country, we have received a Resilience and Growth Plan and assistance from the EU, including support through the European Peace Facility.

Our cooperation therefore extends beyond support for political dialogue, the economy and trade. It also covers security, foreign policy and other areas.

Together with the European Union, we continue to explore new opportunities as we seek to strengthen our ties even further.”

On unblocking transport links, the interests of major powers align

“In my country, and probably across the entire South Caucasus region, the interests of the US and the EU do not conflict. On the contrary, they work together very well.

The United States is actively involved in the South Caucasus. In particular, it is taking part in efforts to open and unblock transport links between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

This will provide a vital transport connection, for example between Portugal and China, linking the West and the East.

I believe the EU and its member states will also benefit from this process.

Thus, many countries and major powers around the world share an interest in unblocking the South Caucasus.”

Opening the Armenian-Turkish border is entirely possible

“We are normalising relations with Turkey. The border remains closed, but I believe the process has already reached a significant level of maturity.

It is entirely possible that tomorrow morning we will wake up and see this headline in the news: ‘Armenia-Turkey border opens’.”

Peace with Azerbaijan and the situation in neighbouring countries

“In our case, Armenia’s neighbours are a critically important factor. Let us look at them.

Azerbaijan. We recently established peace and began bilateral trade. We are opening our territories to transport and transit, and unblocking regional communications. However, several sensitive issues still need to be resolved.

To the west lies Turkey, with which we are engaged in intensive dialogue. We are normalising relations, but the border remains closed.

To the south lies Iran, with its complex regional situation, specific conditions and challenges.

To the north lie Georgia and Russia […].

**As for Georgia, imagine how much easier the situation would be if it continued on its path towards EU integration. That would bring about significant changes.”

Moscow’s reaction must be managed carefully

“As for Russia, you can imagine how it might react to Armenia joining the EU, given the specific nature of our relationship with that country.

Historically, we have had very close ties, and we continue to maintain close relations to this day. However, we must manage any potential reaction carefully.

Nobody wants to make new enemies. Nor are we interested in harming any third party.”

Armenia’s foreign minister at the Warsaw Security Forum

World.title: Azerbaijani government websites hit by cyberattack allegedly originating in Turkey
World.content:
Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

More than 100 government domains in Azerbaijan were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted access to several government agencies’ websites. According to the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security, the attacks began at around 22:00 Baku time on 13 October. The agency said a foreign hacking group was behind them.

The agency said technical measures had helped limit the impact of the cyberattack and keep the websites running reliably. However, it has not disclosed detailed information about how the attack was carried out, who organised it or what motivated it.

As Meydan TV reports, one theory under discussion is that the cyberattack may have links to Turkey.

The incident has prompted debate about the resilience of the country’s digital government infrastructure and the possible political motives behind the attack. Available information confirms that the websites experienced disruptions, but it is not yet possible to assess the full scale of the cyberattack or its consequences.

Clarify the agency’s responseTighten the final paragraphUse more cautious attribution

Which websites were targeted?

According to initial reports in local media, users experienced access problems with the websites of the Cabinet of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Health and the State Examination Centre. An official statement confirming a cyberattack followed simultaneous disruptions affecting several government websites.

According to official figures, the attack targeted more than 100 domains. However, this does not mean that the attackers managed to disrupt all these websites or gain unauthorised access to their systems. The number of resources targeted must be distinguished from the number of systems that actually suffered damage.

The official statement does not specify which websites became unavailable or how long the disruptions lasted. It is also unclear whether the outages affected only information pages or disrupted electronic services as well. The State Service for Special Communications and Information Security says it is continuing its cybersecurity measures.

The nature of the cyberattack remains unclear

Disrupting a website and gaining unauthorised access to its database are two different types of cybersecurity incident. In the first case, users lose access to the resource. In the second, the confidentiality and integrity of data may be at risk.

One common method of disrupting websites is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. This involves sending a large volume of requests to a server simultaneously from different sources. The resulting traffic overloads the servers or network infrastructure, leaving legitimate users’ requests unanswered. Such an attack can disrupt a website without anyone gaining unauthorised access to its database.

There is no official confirmation that the latest cyberattack in Azerbaijan used this particular method. Authorities have also published no findings from checks for possible data leaks. The available information therefore does not establish either that personal data belonging to citizens were stolen or that the authorities have fully resolved all the consequences of the attack.

The restoration of websites indicates that users have regained access to them. However, determining whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to the systems or whether any data leaked requires a separate technical investigation.

Possible motives and speculation about links to Turkey

Cyberattacks on government websites may aim not only to disrupt online services but also to express political views, attract public attention or undermine trust in state institutions. In its report on denial-of-service attacks, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) lists political and ideological objectives, as well as financial interests, among the possible motives behind such attacks.

The specific motives behind the latest cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites remain unknown. The fact that the incident occurred amid political tensions has prompted speculation about a possible link between the events. However, further evidence is needed to substantiate such claims.

According to Meydan TV, social media users are discussing a possible link between the cyberattack and Turkey. The outlet examines this speculation against the backdrop of protests by members of some religiously conservative groups in Turkey against restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools, as well as Baku’s relations with Israel. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani embassy in Ankara and the country’s consulate general in Istanbul.

However, no evidence has established a link between the cyberattack and these protests or any groups in Turkey. The Azerbaijani authorities have also refrained from naming specific countries or organisations in their official statement.

The phrase “foreign hacking group” used in the official statement does not, in itself, indicate that any foreign state was involved. Identifying those who organised and carried out the attack, establishing their motives and determining whether they have links to state institutions will require a separate investigation.

Warning about cyber threats issued five days before the attack

On 8 October, five days before the cyberattack, Azerbaijan’s Electronic Security Service published a warning about active cyber threats targeting several information systems. The statement noted that some attacks involved outdated database management software and default login credentials that administrators had failed to change.

The warning also said that attackers who gained access to inadequately protected systems could use them to launch attacks against other resources. The service advised administrators to update their software, change default passwords, restrict access to systems and monitor suspicious activity.

The service did not report any possible connection between this warning and the cyberattack that began on 13 October. There is currently no evidence to suggest that the two incidents formed part of the same operation. Nevertheless, the warning highlights that cybersecurity depends not only on responding to attacks but also on regularly updating software and controlling access to systems.

Questions left unanswered after services were restored

One of the key criteria for assessing the impact of a cyberattack is the extent to which it disrupts government electronic services. The temporary unavailability of an informational website can have very different consequences for users from disruptions to systems for submitting documents, registering applications and processing requests.

No specific data has yet been published on whether the latest cyberattack interrupted users’ transactions, caused people to miss deadlines for submitting documents or applications, or resulted in data loss. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the actual damage caused by the incident based solely on the number of domains targeted.

Future official statements will be particularly important in clarifying which services were affected, whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to internal systems, and what the security checks found regarding personal data.

The restoration of the websites demonstrates that the authorities have taken steps to respond to the cyberattack. However, a fuller assessment of how resilient the country’s digital government infrastructure proved to be against such threats will only be possible once more detailed information becomes available.

Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites

World.title: Škoda plant to open in Baku: Project progress so far
World.content:
Škoda Group plans rail vehicle production plant in Baku

Czech company Škoda Group plans to establish a rail vehicle production and maintenance facility in Baku.

The project could boost local industry, create jobs and facilitate technology transfer. However, investment figures, production capacity and a timeline have yet to be announced.

Czech transport equipment manufacturer Škoda Group has announced plans to establish a production facility and maintenance centre in Azerbaijan. The company aims to eventually use the facility to serve customers not only in Azerbaijan but also across the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

The plans emerged on 12 October during a meeting between Czech Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik and representatives of Azerbaijan Transport and Communication Holding (AZCON). The meeting was attended by AZCON head Shahin Babayev, Baku Metro chairman Vusal Aslanov and Azerbaijan Railways chairman Rovshan Rustamov.

Škoda Group vice-chairman Tomáš Ignačák said the company intended to establish a joint venture with a local partner in Azerbaijan and gradually expand production.

The proposal covers not only the supply of finished rolling stock but also maintenance services, training for local specialists, the involvement of Azerbaijani companies in component supply chains and the transfer of European manufacturing technologies.

However, the project remains at the proposal stage, with no investment agreement signed so far.

What is Škoda Group planning in Azerbaijan?

Škoda Group is one of Europe’s rail transport manufacturers. The company produces metro trains, trams, suburban electric trains, trolleybuses, as well as vehicle control and drive systems.

Škoda Group should not be confused with carmaker Škoda Auto. The latter is owned by Volkswagen Group, while Škoda Group, which specialises in rail transport, is part of Czech investment group PPF.

According to the company, it has production facilities in the Czech Republic, Finland and Turkey. In 2025, the group’s revenue, including figures from Turkish manufacturer TEMSA, reached €1.45bn.

Škoda Group’s proposal to Azerbaijan focuses primarily on modernising the metro and suburban rail networks. The planned joint venture would gradually develop local production and maintenance capabilities, using local resources and facilities.

One potential benefit would be reduced dependence on foreign manufacturers for maintenance, spare parts and repairs throughout the service life of rail vehicles.

Training local engineers and technicians could also become an important part of long-term industrial cooperation. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on which production and maintenance operations are carried out at the new facility.

Baku Metro expansion creates new opportunities

Škoda Group’s interest in the Azerbaijani market coincides with the country’s plans to expand its public transport infrastructure. Under a state programme approved in January 2025, Baku plans to build 10 new metro stations, modernise existing lines and purchase 299 new carriages by 2030.

In addition to new stations, the programme includes expanding train depots, upgrading power supply systems and increasing the metro network’s capacity. According to AZCON, around $2.5bn is earmarked for the expansion.

In June 2026, Baku Metro and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signed loan agreements worth a total of $180m to finance the first phase of the expansion. The funds will primarily support ongoing work at the Darnagul and Khojasan train depots, as well as upgrades to existing metro stations.

Azerbaijan has therefore already approved a metro modernisation programme and secured funding for several projects. The Czech company’s proposal aims to meet potential demand for equipment, maintenance services and industrial cooperation arising from these plans.

How much production will take place locally?

One of the key factors determining the project’s economic significance will be the scale of production established in Azerbaijan.

Rail vehicle manufacturing involves various levels of localisation. Some facilities specialise in assembling components imported from abroad and testing finished vehicles. Others also manufacture metal structures and electrical equipment, and carry out engineering and design work. Each model requires different levels of investment, technical infrastructure and skilled personnel.

Azerbaijan already has experience assembling metro carriages at local facilities. In 2024, Baku Metro began assembling new-generation carriages using existing infrastructure. According to official figures, under a contract to supply 65 carriages between 2024 and 2026, specialists from the manufacturer also took part in assembling, commissioning and testing rolling stock in Azerbaijan.

This experience demonstrates that existing infrastructure can be used for final assembly and technical testing. However, it remains unclear how Škoda Group’s proposed model would differ from current practices.

The company has yet to disclose which stages of production would take place in Azerbaijan, what proportion of components would be locally manufactured, the terms of technology transfer or the facility’s annual production capacity. These indicators will help assess how much added value the project could generate for local industry.

Even if the facility initially focuses only on assembly and maintenance, the project could help train skilled workers and expand rolling stock repair capabilities. However, manufacturing more complex components in Azerbaijan would require additional investment and a steady flow of orders.

Škoda Group is not the only contender

Azerbaijan’s talks on purchasing new metro carriages and introducing modern technologies are not limited to the Czech company. In January 2026, Baku Metro officials met representatives of Swiss company Stadler Rail Group. They discussed the possible purchase of up to 300 new carriages, reducing operating costs and introducing modern signalling systems.

In February, a Škoda Group delegation led by CEO Petr Novotný also held talks with Baku Metro officials. Discussions focused on purchasing new carriages and prospects for long-term technological cooperation. Potential cooperation between AZCON and Škoda Group had also been discussed in May 2025.

These meetings indicate that Azerbaijan is exploring opportunities to involve international suppliers in modernising Baku Metro. However, Škoda Group’s proposal to establish a facility in Baku does not mean the company has secured orders for the carriages envisaged under the state programme.

Key criteria for selecting suppliers will include compliance with technical requirements, purchase price, energy consumption, maintenance costs and long-term operating conditions.

Localising production in Azerbaijan could bring additional economic benefits. However, its impact on procurement costs and competition will depend on the specific commercial proposals.

What does Uzbekistan’s experience show?

Škoda Group already has experience of a similar cooperation model in Central Asia. In April 2026, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the supply of 10 electric trains to Uzbekistan and their maintenance.

The project, worth more than €120m, also includes establishing a joint venture, localising maintenance services and training specialists. The company also plans to launch a Škoda Academy educational programme in Uzbekistan.

This example shows that Škoda Group’s cooperation model goes beyond supplying rolling stock to include developing local maintenance infrastructure and transferring technology. However, its projects in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are at different stages.

In Uzbekistan, the number of trains and project cost have already been agreed, and a strategic cooperation agreement has been signed. In Azerbaijan, the company has so far only announced plans to establish a production and maintenance facility.

The proposed Baku facility’s potential to serve regional markets will also depend on commercial prospects. This would require orders from neighbouring countries, compliance with technical standards and competitive production costs.

World.title: Progress or disaster? Armenia begins operations at Amulsar mine
World.content:
Operations begin at Amulsar mine

The Amulsar gold mine has begun operations in Armenia. Guests attending the official opening ceremony were shown the mining process and the production of the first gold bar. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also attended the ceremony.

The Armenian government expects the project to generate $130m annually in tax revenue and other income for the state budget.

Environmental campaigners, who have warned about the risks associated with the project for years, condemned the government’s decision. More than 60 organisations issued a statement warning that mining at Amulsar would lead to an “irreversible environmental catastrophe”.

However, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan maintains that concerns about environmental risks have been comprehensively addressed. He insists that all questions raised by environmentalists have received thorough and conclusive answers, dispelling their fears.

“There were alarming statements and concerns, including about the possible poisoning of Lake Sevan and so on. And we are here today because we are convinced that none of these risks actually exist,” Pashinyan said.

Economist Suren Parsyan expects the development of the Amulsar deposit to bring significant economic and social benefits.

He also believes that the launch of the mine will demonstrate to investors that Armenia continues to operate in accordance with international standards and is ready to implement new projects.



$750m already invested in the project

The Amulsar mining project is being implemented as part of a strategic partnership between Lydian Armenia and the Armenian government.

According to the government, Lydian Armenia has:

introduced international best practices and standards at Amulsar;

adopted the principles of modern, responsible mining;

promoted a new culture of occupational safety, environmental management, social responsibility and the use of modern technologies.

The company has already invested around $750m in the project.

The Amulsar mine is expected to produce approximately 210,000 ounces (around 6.5 tonnes) of gold annually.

“According to expert estimates, the annual taxes and other contributions paid by Lydian Armenia to the state budget as a result of the mine’s operation will amount to approximately $130m, contributing an estimated 1.5–2% to Armenia’s GDP,” the government said in a statement.

The project is also expected to create more than 4,000 direct and indirect jobs.

Under an agreement between the government and Lydian Armenia, the company will allocate 7m–9m annually to socio-economic development programmes in nearby communities throughout the mine’s operational lifespan.

Pashinyan: ‘Country is entering a new stage of development’

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described the launch of operations at the Amulsar mine not only as a successful investment project but also as a new stage in the country’s development and an important milestone in the history of Armenia’s mining industry and economic development.

“In the context of Armenia’s history, this is a major step forward. But I hope and firmly believe that in the near future, such steps will become routine and part of our everyday practice. And what we consider a major step in the future will involve projects on an even larger scale.”

According to Pashinyan, the project will provide Armenia with greater opportunities to invest in the security and well-being of its citizens.

He stressed that the country’s mineral resources belong to the Armenian people and that the government’s key responsibility is to ensure that this wealth “serves the development and prosperity” of every citizen.

Nikol Pashinyan inspected the facilities and infrastructure developed for the operation of the mine.

The prime minister said that Lydian Armenia had imported modern equipment to develop the deposit. In his view, Armenia can now boast a high-quality mining industry:

“For any developed country, mining of this calibre, carried out in compliance with environmental and social standards, is a key driver of national development.“

‘Ignoring the risks is unacceptable’: Environmental NGOs’ statement

According to civil society representatives, they have still not received information about realistic and well-founded measures to address the environmental and socio-economic risks associated with the project.

They described the ceremonial opening of the mine just days before the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), due to take place in Yerevan, as “a very bold and irresponsible step”.

“By hosting COP17, Armenia is seeking to demonstrate its commitment to the green agenda to the international community, while an environmental catastrophe is unfolding within the country. Armenia’s natural environment, water resources and the future of local communities cannot be put at risk without proper public accountability and evidence that the project is safe. We consider it unacceptable to ignore these risks,” the statement said.

Expert commentary

According to economist Suren Parsyan, Amulsar is the largest investment project in Armenia’s modern history.

In an interview with Armenpress, he said the Amulsar deposit had sufficient reserves to sustain mining operations for at least 20–25 years. He therefore believes that the mine will have a significant economic impact not only on nearby communities but also on the country as a whole.

Parsyan said the company’s turnover or exports would amount to around $930m, meaning that Armenia would gain a new “industrial giant” comparable to the Zangezur Copper and Molybdenum Combine.

“We now have the second-largest mining company, which will have a direct impact of around 2% on the economy. Its indirect impact could amount to another 1.5–2%.”

He stressed that the company would become a customer for more than 200 small and medium-sized enterprises, serving as a “driving force for regional businesses”.

The economist also believes that the mine’s operation will bring significant social benefits. Around 1,000 direct jobs are expected to be created, alongside 4,000–6,000 indirect jobs.

“Salaries here are quite high, averaging 900,000 drams ($2,356) or more. This is a fairly high figure, even exceeding the average salary at other mining companies in Armenia,” he explained.

Suren Parsyan pointed out that Vayots Dzor is one of Armenia’s poorest regions, with a poverty rate of around 25%, above the national average.

He also noted that, in addition to creating jobs, the project includes a social component aimed at supporting nearby communities.

“The poverty rate could fall significantly, by around two to three times. In Vayots Dzor, where the population is small and employment opportunities are limited, this could provide a long-term solution to the problem,” he concluded.

World.title: Venice Commission issues critical opinion on Georgia’s law on grants
World.content:
Venice Commission on Georgia’s Law on Grants

The Venice Commission has published a critical opinion on Georgia’s Law on Grants. In its final opinion, the Commission firmly maintains that the legislation does not serve its stated aims of protecting and strengthening Georgia’s sovereignty or shielding political parties from foreign influence and interference.

The Venice Commission, officially known as the European Commission for Democracy through Law, is an independent advisory body of the Council of Europe that deals with constitutional and legal matters. For more than two years, the Georgian authorities have sharply criticised the Commission. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze called it one of the least serious European institutions, while parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili said it had effectively become an ordinary political commentator.

According to the opinion, the law imposes disproportionate and unjustified restrictions on the fundamental rights and political freedoms of Georgian citizens, particularly freedom of association and freedom of expression. It also obstructs the formation and continued existence of political opposition.

The 25-page opinion was adopted at the Commission’s plenary session on 9–10 October 2027 and published on 13 October. The Commission prepared its assessment at the request of Elvira Kovács, chair of the Monitoring Committee of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

The document examines a package of legislative amendments that the parliamentary majority of the ruling Georgian Dream party adopted on 4 March 2026. The amendments affect the Law on Grants, the Organic Law on Political Associations of Citizens, the Criminal Code and related legislation.

What does the opinion say?

The Venice Commission has called on the Georgian authorities to revise legislation governing foreign grants, political activity and the associated criminal liability. In the Commission’s assessment, broad and vague wording in these laws gives the executive excessive powers and could lead to restrictions on political pluralism.

The Commission strongly urges the authorities to pay particular attention to reviewing criminal penalties and ambiguous provisions that give the executive wide scope to interpret the law.

One of the Venice Commission’s main concerns is the broad definition of a “grant”. Under the current legislation, grants can include not only financial assistance but also technical support, expert advice, various services, training and other forms of cooperation.

In addition, organisations must obtain prior approval from the state authorities to receive certain types of foreign funding.

In the Commission’s view, the combination of a broad definition of a grant and the requirement for prior approval leaves organisations in a state of legal uncertainty and gives the authorities wide scope to restrict their activities.

The opinion notes that vague legislative wording fails to meet the principle of legal certainty. This principle requires laws to be sufficiently clear and predictable to allow individuals and organisations to determine their rights and obligations.

The Venice Commission believes that the restrictions could obstruct the formation and continued existence of opposition political forces and, consequently, undermine political pluralism.

The Commission stresses that protecting national sovereignty and preventing foreign interference do not, in themselves, justify disproportionate restrictions on fundamental rights.

Authorities refused to cooperate with the Commission

In its opinion, the Venice Commission notes that the Georgian government, the parliamentary majority, the State Grants Management Agency and the State Audit Office all declined to meet its representatives.

The State Grants Management Agency is the very body that is due to be dissolved.

“The Venice Commission regrets that the Georgian authorities were unwilling to engage with the Commission while it prepared this opinion, although the Commission itself remains open to dialogue,” the document concludes.

Commentaries

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Centre:

Among other things, the Commission stated the following:

The legal framework underpinning the law lacks legal certainty and predictability. Key concepts — such as “grant”, activities “related to political issues”, “an organisation representing the interests of a foreign state”, “a person with a declared party-political objective”, “creating an impression of illegitimacy” and “harming state interests” — rely on excessively broad and imprecise wording. The mechanisms for repression, sanctions and inspections provided for by the law raise serious concerns under international human rights standards.

The Commission strongly recommends reconsidering the use of criminal penalties for breaches of the procedures and obligations established by the Law on Grants. Such breaches should be dealt with exclusively through administrative measures, provided that adequate and robust procedural safeguards are in place.

The chilling effect across the sector and public sphere will lead to their paralysis. Faced with the authorities’ powers of prior control and extensive monitoring, as well as the threat of investigations, criminal prosecution and imprisonment, individuals and organisations may reasonably decide to refrain from lawful activities protected by the European Convention on Human Rights. As a result, the exercise of freedom of association and freedom of expression, as well as the right to participate in political processes, is likely to be restricted — not so much through direct prohibitions, but, more significantly, by creating a legal environment in which the risks associated with civic engagement become so high that taking them may seem unjustifiably dangerous.

I am convinced that the European Court will reach the same conclusion very soon in the cases we have brought before it. Georgian Dream claims to be committed to the rule of law and to complying with court rulings. Let us see how it honours that commitment.

Tamar Oniani, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association:

The amendments introduced in March 2026 to the Law on Grants and related legislation, including the Criminal Code, have had destructive consequences. They greatly broadened the definition of a “grant” while deliberately leaving the wording ambiguous, thereby criminalising the receipt of so-called “unauthorised” grants. The aim was to create another powerful tool of control in the hands of the authorities.

Let us now consider the Venice Commission’s findings on these amendments.

They can be summarised in two main points (see also paragraph 83 of the original opinion):

The amendments have no legitimate aim.

The Venice Commission concludes that the legislation does not serve the stated purpose of protecting or strengthening Georgia’s sovereignty or shielding its political parties from foreign influence and interference.

In reality, the amendments aim to use the law as a tool to advance a political agenda, namely to tighten control over civil society and opposition political groups. In the Venice Commission’s view, the amendments impose disproportionate and excessive restrictions on the fundamental rights and political freedoms of Georgian citizens, particularly freedom of association and freedom of expression.

The legislation obstructs the formation and continued existence of political opposition.

This is particularly relevant when considering the cumulative and systemic impact of the legislative framework as a whole, as it stood on 4 March 2026.

The legislation under review contradicts international standards on pluralism and democracy.

Rather than protecting Georgia’s sovereignty, constitutional order and political parties from foreign influence and interference, the legislation creates a risk of undermining them.

What does the so-called Law on Grants provide for?

A package of legislative acts adopted on 4 March 2026 significantly broadened the definition of a “grant” to include both financial and non-financial support, provided that such support could be used to influence domestic or foreign policy, including activities related to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of the provision and receipt of grants. Foreign legal entities that provide funding to branches operating in Georgia without government approval face penalties, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violations of grant legislation can also result in criminal liability. The penalties include fines, community service or imprisonment for up to six years.

The amendments also affect the political process. People who work primarily for organisations funded from foreign sources cannot join political parties for eight years. Moreover, restrictions on political parties also apply to entities that are not formally parties but engage in political activity in practice.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies that take part in public political activities.

One of the most controversial aspects of the amendments is a set of new provisions in the Criminal Code that broaden the definition of “extremism”. Under a new article, public calls for actions against the constitutional order — including calls to disobey the authorities or establish alternative structures — may constitute criminal offences.

In addition, crimes motivated by a refusal to recognise constitutional authorities qualify as offences committed under aggravating circumstances, increasing the sentence by at least one year.

Experts argue that such wording allows for broad interpretation and increases the risk that the law could be used against dissent and critical activity.

Venice Commission on Georgia’s Law on Grants

World.title: EU to consider reviewing its policy towards Georgia: what will change in January?
World.content:
The EU and Georgia: what will change?

The European Union acknowledges that its current policy towards Georgia is failing to deliver results. It has neither changed the course of the Georgian Dream government nor fully protected the EU’s own strategic interests in the region. Following a meeting of foreign ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October 2027, Kaja Kallas said the EU would revisit the issue of Georgia in January.

Brussels faces a difficult dilemma: how to increase pressure on the government without losing Georgia as a key partner in the Black Sea region.

Tbilisi has responded with even sharper confrontation. Georgian Dream leaders accuse EU representatives of trying to drag Georgia into a war, undermine its sovereignty and impose values that are alien to the country. At the same time, they insist that Georgia’s European choice remains unchanged and say they are ready for dialogue with Brussels.

Against this backdrop, Georgia’s European integration process has effectively stalled. However, statements by EU officials suggest that Brussels has no intention of severing all ties with Georgia.

Why the EU’s current policy is no longer working

Following a meeting on 12 October 2027, Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, described the current approach to Georgia as inadequate.

“Our current approach is not creating enough pressure to bring about change, nor is it allowing us to fully pursue Europe’s strategic interests. We will return to this issue in January,” Kallas said.

In her assessment, democratic backsliding in Georgia is worsening. Opposition parties face the threat of being banned, while legislation on foreign influence restricts the work of civil society. “The people of Georgia want a European future, but Georgian Dream is systematically depriving them of this opportunity,” Kallas noted.

The significance of her statement lies not only in the sharpness of the criticism. The EU’s High Representative has publicly acknowledged that Brussels’ policy is failing to achieve two important objectives.

The first is to put pressure on the Georgian government to change its approach to democratic institutions and human rights. The second is to maintain cooperation with Georgia in areas vital to the EU’s security and economic interests.

Postponing further discussions until January does not mean the EU has decided to impose new sanctions or take other specific measures. However, Kallas’s statement shows that the need to review the current approach is already on the agenda.

‘A candidate in name only’: what the European Commission is telling the Georgian government

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, has outlined the conditions for restoring active cooperation with the Georgian government.

She said Georgia’s EU candidate status currently exists only on paper. The European Commission has made renewed cooperation conditional on ending democratic backsliding and taking concrete steps towards European values.

“As long as they are not moving forward — and are actually moving backwards because of the laws they have adopted — and until there is progress and steps towards European values, we will not cooperate with them,” Kos said.

At the same time, the commissioner drew a distinction between relations with the government and support for the Georgian people.

“Although we are not cooperating with the government, we are engaging with civil society and supporting the people. There are many areas in which we provide assistance, and we will continue to do so in the future,” she said.

This approach is already being put into practice. Speaking at an event marking Europe Day in Telavi, the EU ambassador to Georgia, Paweł Herczyński, said the European Union was implementing new projects worth €38 million in Georgia in 2026.

The projects cover areas including education, employment, rural development, support for women and vulnerable groups, environmental protection and food quality.

Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže also stressed that, although the Georgian people aspire to a European future, the government had failed to take the necessary steps towards it. She confirmed, however, that diplomatic dialogue with Georgia was continuing and that the country had not been excluded from international processes.

Why the European Union needs Georgia

The meeting in Luxembourg highlighted another important point: regardless of the state of democracy in Georgia, the country has strategic importance for the European Union.

This is particularly true of security in the Black Sea region, energy and transport links.

Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova said Georgia was part of the Black Sea region and that its participation in security dialogue was essential.

“It is very important to involve them in the dialogue on how we ensure security in the Black Sea region,” she said.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana-Silvia Țoiu also addressed energy and infrastructure projects involving Georgia. She noted that Romania was working to strengthen connectivity with countries in the region and stressed the importance of continuing this process.

These statements do not mean that EU member states endorse the Georgian government’s policies. Rather, they show that despite the political crisis, there are areas of cooperation where cutting ties would harm the European Union’s own interests.

Who is refusing to engage in dialogue?

One of Georgian Dream’s main arguments is that the European Commission’s leadership is avoiding dialogue with Georgia.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the government is ready to discuss any issue, but the European Commission’s leadership is preventing relations from being restored.

Parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili also argues that, while EU member states want dialogue with Georgia, the institutions in Brussels are pursuing a policy of boycott.

“Unfortunately, Brussels is currently acting as a barrier to relations between Georgia and the European Union, as well as its member states,” Papuashvili said.

Irakli Kirtskhalia, leader of the parliamentary majority, takes a similar view. He argues that EU representatives make critical statements but do not engage in substantive discussions with the Georgian government.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana-Silvia Țoiu, however, disagreed with this assessment.

“I do not entirely agree with your view that the European Union is the one boycotting dialogue,” she said.

She explained that the EU was ready to cooperate with governments committed to democracy and willing to give the opposition an opportunity to compete in elections.

How a debate about democracy turned into a campaign to ‘defend identity’

In response to criticism from the European Union, Georgian Dream leaders increasingly talk not about the specific problems raised by European officials, but about the need to protect Christian values, national identity and sovereignty.

Irakli Kobakhidze claims that the EU is demanding that Georgia grant same-sex couples the right to adopt children and allow people to legally change their gender.

“Europe is Georgia’s historic choice. The European Union was established several decades ago. Our choice is Europe,” Kobakhidze said.

In the same statement, he spoke of a crisis of ethnic, religious and personal identity in Europe, presenting the avoidance of similar developments as a necessity for Georgia. Shalva Papuashvili interpreted Marta Kos’s call for Georgia to return to European values as a potential attempt to undermine Christian values.

“Georgia is founded on Christian values. If Commissioner Kos has objections to Christian values, let her tell us exactly what she objects to,” he said.

However, in her statement on 12 October, Kos spoke about laws adopted by the government, democratic backsliding and the need to uphold European values. She did not criticise Christian values.

Moreover, the available material contains no official EU demand that Georgia grant same-sex couples the right to adopt children.

EU ambassador comes under attack from the government

The hostility towards the European Union was particularly evident in Telavi following an event marking Europe Day.

At the event, EU ambassador Paweł Herczyński addressed the audience in Georgian. He compared the European Union to Georgian polyphonic singing, noting that Georgia did not have to choose between its own culture and a European future.

Herczyński also spoke about the deterioration of democracy in Georgia and the growing anti-European rhetoric.

However, government representatives focused mainly on their political assessment of the event and criticised the musicians who took part.

Irakli Kobakhidze criticised the EU delegation for inviting a musical group that, in his view, insults supporters of the ruling party.

Shalva Papuashvili called the event a political rally and said the ambassador had turned Europe Day into “days of hatred towards Europe”.

Papuashvili also accused Herczyński of violating the Vienna Convention.

Other ruling party representatives went further. Irakli Zarkua accused the ambassador of supporting revolutionary scenarios, while Guram Macharashvili questioned his possible financial motives without providing any evidence.

Meanwhile, Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze, commenting on the meeting of EU foreign ministers, said:

“If you gave Kaja Kallas a map, she wouldn’t be able to point out where Georgia is.”

Kaladze also accused EU representatives of trying to bring a government to power in Georgia that would serve their own interests.

A ‘European choice’ without EU institutions

Another aspect of the crisis in relations with the European Union is the ruling party’s attempt to distinguish European integration from the EU’s current institutions.

Irakli Kobakhidze describes Georgia’s European choice as a historic decision. At the same time, he blames the European Commission’s leadership for the deterioration in relations.

Shalva Papuashvili goes further. Commenting on a European Parliament draft resolution calling for sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili and other government representatives, he said:

“With a European Parliament like this, we certainly should not expect to join the EU. We have no intention of sitting at the same table as people who treat the Georgian people with contempt.”

Papuashvili also claims that the EU’s current institutions resemble Soviet bureaucracy. In his view, Brussels treats Georgia as a second-class country.

The Russian market and the economic cost of the ‘balancing policy’

The deterioration in relations with the European Union also has economic implications.

The Georgian Dream government often describes its foreign policy as pragmatic and balanced. The authorities cite this pragmatism to justify Georgia’s decision not to join sanctions against Russia and to maintain economic ties with the country.

Irakli Kobakhidze also pointed to the US decision to ease some restrictions on Russian diesel fuel to justify the Georgian government’s position.

Against this backdrop, new restrictions imposed by Russia on Georgian products have once again raised doubts about the reliability of the Russian market for Georgian exporters.

Gigi Tsereteli, chairman of the European Georgia party, acknowledges that a balancing policy makes sense for a small country. However, he argues that the Georgian government has failed both to maintain relations with the West and to create a reliable economic environment in its dealings with Russia.

“Balancing does not mean destroying relations with anyone, but maintaining them,” Tsereteli said. In his view, dependence on the Russian market is particularly dangerous because political decisions can change the nature of trade relations at any moment.

“Betting on the Russian market will one day lead to disaster,” the opposition politician believes.

Economic success as a response to criticism from pro-democracy forces

Shalva Papuashvili responds to criticism from the EU by pointing to economic indicators.

He says Georgia is outpacing EU member states and candidate countries in economic growth. The parliamentary speaker argues that the country’s economic success stems precisely from a policy independent of Brussels’ recommendations.

“Those who listen to Brussels suffer economic damage, while those who do not see economic growth,” Papuashvili said.

The EU and Georgia: what will change?

The meeting of EU foreign ministers on 12 October did not result in the announcement of new sanctions against Georgia. The official outcome was an expression of concern over democratic backsliding and a decision to discuss the issue in greater detail in January.

Opposition circles are also discussing the possibility of a tougher EU stance.

Grigol Gegelia, a representative of the opposition Lelo party, believes the government has already received repeated opportunities to change course, so the EU’s response is likely to become tougher.

At the same time, Gigi Tsereteli notes that Brussels has so far refrained from severing ties with Georgia altogether.

“We are not only losing enormous potential, but also forfeiting tangible, concrete benefits, while facing the prospect of further deterioration. If things continue this way, the path to EU membership could be completely blocked — although, for now, they are reluctant to take that final step,” he said.

The main issue for discussion in January will be how the EU should revise a policy that it itself considers inadequate.

It remains unclear which specific measures EU member states are considering. However, the 12 October meeting showed that Brussels no longer considers the current approach to Georgia sufficient.

The EU and Georgia: what will change?

World.title: ‘Nostalgic exploitation’: South Ossetia’s new president sends schoolchildren to collect rosehips
World.content:
An initiative by Marat Kambolov, the new president of South Ossetia, to get schoolchildren to collect rosehips has drawn public criticism.

Photos and videos shared on the president’s official Telegram channel and in the media show children picking berries from thorny branches with their bare hands. In some images, they are even wearing school uniforms with white shirts. One girl is wearing a lace apron.

Kambolov came up with the idea in a fit of nostalgia for his own schooldays.

“When I saw how many rosehips we had this year, I immediately remembered Khaznidon, a village in North Ossetia. As children, we often ran up the mountain to collect them. It was a normal thing for us: climb higher, gather rosehips and bring them home.

“Of course, back then we didn’t think about vitamins or their health benefits. We simply grew up close to nature and made use of what it gave us. That is why I suggested organising this activity for our schoolchildren,” the president explained.

According to Kambolov, after he issued the relevant order, around 1,500 pupils in Years 8–11 across South Ossetia went out to collect rosehips. They gathered around 250kg in total, which the authorities will “distribute to medical facilities, educational institutions and social care homes”.

“Rosehips are a useful product, rich in vitamin C. People here have always collected them, dried them and brewed them into tea. But for me, this is about something else, too. I want our children to know their land, to see what it has to offer, to go into the mountains and understand that even something as simple as spending a few hours collecting rosehips can be worthwhile.

“We used to run into the mountains to collect them when we were boys ourselves. Years have passed, but rosehips still grow on our hillsides. And it is good to see the next generations collecting them now,” Kambolov said.

However, local bloggers did not share his enthusiasm for passing traditions down through the generations. They criticised the president’s idea as an example of exploiting schoolchildren in the Soviet style.

Blogger Sidamon, for example, wrote that he was curious to know “what genius came up with the idea of sending children to collect rosehips in brand-new school uniforms, when just a couple of months ago Kambolov ordered 10,000 roubles [around $119] to be allocated for their purchase?”

The fact that the children wore school uniforms also led the blogger to suspect that they collected the berries during school hours — or, more precisely, instead of attending lessons.

The author of another Telegram channel recalled taking part in “voluntary-compulsory activities” as a child. However, he said, at least “they organised them more competently back then”:

“At the appointed time, we would arrive at school in work clothes. They would put us on a bus and take us to the apple orchards, where we would be given all the equipment we needed.

“They could at least have given the schoolchildren in the photos some gloves. Anyone who has ever picked rosehips knows exactly why they have ‘thorn’ in their name.”

A teacher at a school in Tskhinval said the school administration had informed pupils in advance that they would collect rosehips on Saturday. She insisted that pupils from her school wore sportswear and gloves.

“That girl in the lace apron apparently didn’t know about it. I don’t know how she ended up there in her school uniform either. She isn’t from our school,” the teacher added.

She suspects the education ministry passed the president’s order on to schools, which then carried it out as they saw fit. In any case, she believes such mishaps are hardly surprising given the chaos surrounding the change of power.

“There is such confusion at our ministry. The government has resigned, and everyone is worried about keeping their jobs. No one knows who is responsible for what.”

The mother of one schoolchild, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said she disapproved of the practice of using children as an unpaid workforce. She was unhappy that the school had sent children to collect rosehips without consulting their parents, but said she “didn’t pursue the matter”.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Türkiye's AI adoption gap by firm size triples to 24 points by 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. The gap in artificial intelligence adoption between Türkiye's largest and smallest enterprises has roughly tripled to 24 points since 2021.

According to Trend's calculations based on data released by TÜİK on October 2, smaller firms posted the fastest relative growth in AI uptake.

TÜİK reported that the share of enterprises using at least one AI technology rose from 2.7% in 2021 to 14% in 2026 overall. By size, adoption among enterprises with 10-49 employees rose from 2.3% to 12.8%, among those with 50-249 employees from 3.6% to 17%, and among those with 250 or more employees from 9.6% to 37.1%.

According to Trend's calculations, the gap between the largest and smallest size categories widened from 7.3%age points in 2021 to 24.3%age points in 2026 - roughly 3.3 times wider. Yet Trend's calculations also show smaller enterprises grew fastest in relative terms: adoption among 10-49-employee firms increased approximately 5.57-fold over the period, compared with a 4.72-fold increase among mid-sized firms and a 3.86-fold increase among the largest firms, meaning large enterprises' head start has translated into a widening absolute gap even as smaller firms catch up proportionally faster.

TÜİK also reported that 8.3% of enterprises not using AI said they were considering adopting it, with this share rising by firm size - from 7.4% among 10-49-employee firms to 14.9% among those with 250 or more employees.

World.title: EBRD reports inflation developments in Kyrgyzstan
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Inflationary pressures in Kyrgyzstan intensified in 2026 amid higher energy and food prices as well as expansionary fiscal policy, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said in its September Regional Economic Prospects report.

"Inflationary pressures intensified amid higher energy and food prices as well as expansionary fiscal policy," the statement said.

In response, the authorities introduced temporary fuel subsidies estimated at approximately 1 billion Kyrgyz soms, retail fuel price caps, excise tax deferrals and a one-year moratorium on tariff and fee increases.

The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic has kept its policy rate at 12% since February, while inflation accelerated to 11.5% year on year in July 2026, compared with 8.8% a year earlier.

The EBRD projects real GDP growth of 8.7% in 2026 and 7% in 2027.

Trend estimates suggest that inflation in Kyrgyzstan could gradually moderate as energy and food price pressures ease and the impact of temporary government measures becomes more pronounced.

Moreover, Trend’s calculations indicate that under a scenario of improving supply conditions and continued monetary restraint, annual inflation could decline toward 8–9 percent in 2027 and 6–8 percent in 2028.

If inflationary pressures continue to ease, the National Bank could gradually gain more room to adjust monetary conditions while maintaining price stability. Lower inflation would also support household purchasing power and create more predictable conditions for businesses and investment.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 16, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist," on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 20th day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by the Haber TV channel.

- "Azerbaijan’s glorious Army has liberated Khirmanjig, Aghbulag and Akhullu villages of Khojavend district. Long live Azerbaijan’s Army! Karabakh is Azerbaijan!" President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev made a post on his official Twitter account.

- The artillery battery belonging to the Armenian armed forces was destroyed, and the deputy commander of the forces regiment was injured. A list of the equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces destroyed at night was disclosed.

- The Azerbaijani Prosecutor General's Office reported that 47 civilians were killed and 222 injured as a result of shelling of Azerbaijani settlements by the Armenian armed forces.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared footage from villages of the Khojavend district of Azerbaijan, which were liberated from the Armenian occupation.

- The Armenian armed forces, grossly violating the humanitarian ceasefire, continued shelling the territories of Goranboy, Tartar, Aghdam, Aghjabadi, and Fuzuli districts of Azerbaijan.

- The Armenian armed forces launched a missile strike on the territory of the Ordubad district of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of Azerbaijan.

- The Armenian side bombarded a cemetery in Ahmadaghalilar village, Aghdam district.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared new footage from the liberated Hadrut settlement.

- The state flag of Azerbaijan was raised above the border outposts liberated from Armenian occupation.
