World.title: Chickens allowed free range again in Victoria as bird flu lockdown ends
World.content:
A lockdown order to protect Victorian poultry farms from H5N1 bird flu is being lifted today, despite the continuing spread of the deadly disease among wildlife.

Flocks of 50 or more birds in metropolitan Melbourne and southern parts of the state have been forced to stay indoors, or be confined, since the order was first announced in early August.

H5N1 is spreading among wildlife in Australia but has not been detected in poultry or livestock.

The control order applied in Melbourne and across southern parts of Victoria. (Supplied: Agriculture Victoria)

Agriculture Victoria said it took into consideration "animal welfare" and "hotter than average" forecast summer temperatures when deciding to lift the housing order.

Chief veterinary officer Graeme Cooke said farmers were supportive of the protection measures so far.

He said producers needed to continue to protect their flocks from wildlife as much as possible.

"Reducing contact between poultry and wild birds remains one of the most effective ways to lower the risk of disease," he said.

" We strongly encourage poultry owners to continue taking practical steps to separate birds wherever possible. "

Graeme Cooke says poultry flocks should be protected from wild birds. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

Biosecurity 'best defence'

The lifting of the order brings 10 weeks of lockdown to an end for poultry farmers in Victoria's south.

"It's been a huge joint effort to keep bird flu out of our commercial poultry industry," Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate said.

Ryan Milgate says farmers need to remain vigilant for any signs of bird flu. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

"Strong biosecurity practices remain our best defence to reducing the risk of disease outbreaks, such as H5."

Mr Milgate urged producers to stay on the lookout for sick or diseased birds.

"We must not rest on our laurels and become complacent," he said.

There have been 234 confirmed events of H5N1 in wildlife in Victoria so far.

And while the lockdown ends today, Dr Cooke says the risk of disease spread remains.

"We will continue monitoring the risk closely and retain the ability to introduce additional controls if circumstances change."

Victorians have been told to avoid contact with unwell or dead wildlife.

Reports can be made to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888 or on the Agriculture Victoria website.

World.title: Breaking: Children among dead in shooting at an elementary school in Oregon
World.content:
Three children and one adult have been killed in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, CNN and CBS News reported.

Sheila Miller, communications manager for the Bend Police Department, told reporters she had no information about the shooter, who was shot and killed. She also was unaware of who it was that responded.

"We don't have confirmation yet of who shot the suspect; it may have been a bystander," Ms Miller said.

The shooter opened fire on Thursday, local time, at an elementary school but was promptly shot dead.

Police received reports of a shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School who fired at a vehicle, Ms Miller said.

Police were on campus within minutes, at which time the shooter went down almost immediately, Ms Miller said.

Bend is a city of some 100,000 people in central Oregon, about 280 kilometres south-east of Portland.

Silver Rail Elementary School serves grades kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11.

It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Ms Miller said.

Reuters

World.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
World.content:
Supercars will return to Phillip Island from next year, helping plug an economic gap left by the loss of the MotoGP to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on tourism from the events.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

World.title: Mums get back to nature for mental and physical reboot
World.content:
On the banks of Lake Weyba, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a group of intrepid toddlers have assembled with their mothers in tow.

Their little feet set the pace for this weekday walk, which means there are plenty of stops along the way as they scramble up rocks or bend down to grab sticks or leaves.

"That has been a big change from maybe struggling to walk because they're very young toddlers to being very confident outside and climbing, and they all know each other now, which is so special," Sabina Kath said.

The mothers say their toddlers have grown in confidence with each walk. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Ms Kath, who previously worked as an outdoor educator, started Mums Who Hike about 18 months ago.

"I've always loved hiking but I didn't have any friends who were into the same thing as me, so I just decided to find those people myself," she said.

Loading...

Since then, the group's free walks have been attended by about 700 mothers.

"Whether somebody has to stop to do a quick feed or they need to do a nappy change on the trail, everyone helps each other out," Ms Kath said.

"Sometimes people forget nappies or sunscreen or wipes, and everyone's got something in their bag or their car, and we're always, just as a collective, sharing our stuff."

The mums help each other get through the hikes. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

A shared journey

Emma Burgess said the group had made a huge difference to her wellbeing.

"Motherhood is very lonely and it kind of catches you by surprise, even if you are a social person, and so this was the first group that I joined that actually got me out of the house," Ms Burgess said.

"I think it's just given a lot of confidence for me to make new friends. It's hard to make friends when you're over 30, so that's been really good too."

Ms Burgess said the group has helped her feel more confident getting outside with her child. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Jess Calligan said her toddler was just as excited as she was to join the hikes.

"He bangs on the door at seven o'clock to get outside now," Ms Calligan said.

"We try really hard not to show our son too many screens, and getting outside is a great excuse and distraction and a good reset for all of us."

The mums say their children are developing a love for the outdoors. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Ms Kath said watching the group members connect had been incredibly rewarding.

"I find mums who have never met each other before, [then] 10 minutes into the walk, they're yapping away having quite a deep and meaningful chat often," Ms Kath said.

" Walking opens you up to talking about things that you might be a bit more intimidated to talk about if you're looking someone directly in the eye. "

Group members pictured at Baxter Falls in Mapleton, in the Sunshine Coast hinterland. (Supplied: Mums Who Hike)

Tourism ambassadors

Ms Kath shares the group's adventures on social media, and her images are often reposted by tourism pages.

She was recently named a finalist in the volunteer category of the 2026 Outdoors Queensland Awards. Winners will be announced on October 30.

"I'm really passionate about how beautiful the Sunshine Coast is," Ms Kath said.

"We've got lakes, beaches, the Glass House Mountains, rainforests, waterfalls to swim in — there is so much within half an hour's drive of wherever you live."

The group has climbed to the top of Mount Ngungun, in the Glass House Mountains. (Supplied: Mums Who Hike)

She said the mothers also felt more secure bushwalking as a group.

"I have had situations hiking by myself where I have felt a little bit fearful," Ms Kath said.

" If you're hiking then with a child you can feel more vulnerable, so when you've got a pack of mums and you're all together you've got each other's back. "

World.title: Royal Children's Hospital handed $66m after fear new beds would sit empty
World.content:
The Victorian government has committed an extra $66 million to staff 20 new beds at Victoria's leading children's hospital after a funding stand-off threatened to leave them sitting empty.

The new beds were promised under a $55 million upgrade to the Royal Children's Hospital in 2018 and were set to open in November this year.

Last month, hospital sources told the ABC the beds would not be used because there was no funding for staff.

Staff told the ABC they were devastated, with signs posted around the emergency department as part of protected industrial actions amid ongoing pay negotiations.

A letter from an emergency department manager sent to staff at the time said the state government had rejected a funding request for staff to operate the new beds, and lamented that the hospital had battled under-resourcing for years.

Premier Ben Carroll has pledged funding for 85 extra full-time equivalent nursing positions. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

When approached for comment on the issue at the time, the government did not answer specific questions about the funding issue, saying it was working with the hospital.

After the issue became public, the state government denied it had rejected the funding request.

The government has now pledged an additional $66 million to fund 85 extra full-time equivalent nursing positions, including up to 25 graduate nurses.

The government has promised that the new beds will be staffed with nurses and ready to treat kids from when they open, now in December.

Premier Ben Carroll said the new beds would mean an extra 13,000 children could receive the emergency care they needed from "the best team in the world".

"Working people need a strong, free health system — and our kids deserve the best care," he said.

Do you know more? Contact Antonia O'Flaherty at Oflaherty.Antonia@abc.net.au or on antoniaoflaherty@protonmail.com

Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said every additional bed would open from day one.

The new treatment area will include new cubicles, short-stay beds and fast-track bays, the government said, along with a new procedure room where minor procedures can be performed without admission to a ward.

The emergency department already treats about 90,000 patients a year but has fewer staff than equivalent facilities, according to Australian College of Emergency Medicine figures.

A poster displayed in the ED last month apologised to patients for the "long wait", explaining that an average ED of the same size has 50 per cent more doctors, 40 per cent more nurses and 60 per cent more beds.

World.title: Complex surgery successfully separates Fijian conjoined twins
World.content:
Doctors in Saudi Arabia say a complex operation to separate 13-month-old Fijian conjoined twins has been successful.

In what was described as an "exceptionally rare" case, the sisters, Dicecea and Jesepeli Kikau, were born joined at the lower abdomen and pelvis.

It is a condition known as omphalo-ischiopagus tetrapus.

The girls had their own hearts and lungs and required an almost 13-hour operation to separate their liver, bowel, urinary tract and anal canal.

Loading...

As the procedure reached a critical stage on Thursday night, local time, doctors announced they had successfully separated the pair and were starting on their reconstruction.

Mother Akeneta Vulimaiigiladi said she was nervous when the girls were wheeled into the operating theatre, but became less so as she watched on via a video link.

"We just kissed them goodbye and we wished our babies well," she said.

Before the twins went into theatre, Ms Vulimaiigiladi and her husband, Watisoni, chose to give them new Arabic names: Noorah for Jesepeli and Sarah for Dicecea.

Dicecea and Jesepeli Kikau's mother, Akeneta Vulimaiigiladi, farewelled them before their surgery. ( )

Dicecea and Jesepeli Kikau were assessed by doctors in Saudi Arabia for months ahead of the surgery. ( )

The twins were joined at the chest, abdomen and pelvis. ( )

Abdullah Al Rabeeah, surgical lead at the King Abdullah Specialist Children's Hospital, told the ABC the surgery consisted of nine phases, starting with separating the liver and bowel and ending with reconstruction.

Three hours into the operation, he said it was "going well".

"Better than our expectation, and the two girls are doing well so far in spite of the complexity of surgery," Dr Al Rabeeah said.

He said separating the liver and the bowel was undertaken "with good success and stability and no major bleeding".

Abdullah Al Rabeeah (centre) led the surgery. ( )

Dicecea and Jesepeli Kikau underwent surgery in Saudi Arabia. ( )

The operation was carried out for free under the hospital's Saudi Conjoined Twins Program.

According to the hospital, the twins were its 74th set of conjoined twins to be separated from 29 countries.

The Fijian government said the family sent the twins to Saudi Arabia after hospitals in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Mexico wanted large up-front payments.

Akeneta and Watisoni Vulimaiigiladi arrived in Riyadh with their twins in late July. ( )

It said the offer of free treatment through the Saudi Conjoined Twins Program was a lifeline for the family.

The twins, born eight weeks premature, also have a triplet sister, Hossana, who was not conjoined.

The girls are the second recorded case of conjoined twins in Fiji in 50 years, according to the government.

World.title: Town's only unleaded service station cuts fuel supply over rising costs
World.content:
The north-west Victorian town of Birchip has been without unleaded petrol for almost a month, after the community's only pumps were left to run dry.

The Birchip Motel and Caravan Park is the sole supplier of unleaded fuel to the farming town of about 700 residents, 100 kilometres north-east of Horsham.

The Birchip Motel and Caravan Park is the only place selling unleaded fuel in the town. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

For more than three weeks, its owner has declined to order unleaded fuel, forcing residents to drive 30 to 40 kilometres to neighbouring towns to fill up.

The motel has also discontinued its diesel offering.

Elsewhere in town, there are two self-serve diesel pumps, but only one of those stations has a regular nozzle required for filling medium and small cars.

'We had no choice'

After questions from the ABC, owner Sarathi Muthukrishnan committed to delivering at least one more shipment of unleaded petrol (ULP).

"We have placed an order for ULP to be delivered … so that we can continue servicing the community in the immediate term," Mr Muthukrishnan said.

" However, I am honestly not sure whether we will be able to continue doing this on an ongoing basis if the current cost pressures remain. "

Mr Muthukrishnan bought the business a year ago and said the decision to cut unleaded fuel was due to increasing costs.

Residents are having to drive to nearby towns like Wycheproof for fuel. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"Earlier this year, when we had no choice but to increase our retail fuel prices in Birchip to reflect the higher wholesale costs, a number of customers chose to stop purchasing fuel from us," Mr Muthukrishnan said.

"We completely understand that everyone is feeling the pressure of rising costs; however, this had a significant impact on our sales.

"As a small business, we have been struggling to cover the increasing cost of fuel together with the day-to-day expenses of operating the site."

'Its very cruel'

Pensioner Maureen Donnellon, 79, said the lack of fuel was restricting her ability to leave her home and get to appointments.

"It feels like COVID-19 all over again, that horrible restriction of movement," Ms Donnellon said.

"It's very cruel, really.

Maureen Donnellon is rationing her tank of unleaded petrol. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Ms Donnellan said the town's Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) also relied on unleaded fuel.

"We don't have an ambulance," Ms Donnellon said.

"Our CERT car runs on petrol and our community car, which takes people to appointments, is also on petrol.

"With fire season coming, [some] mowers and whipper snippers rely on petrol. The fire danger is going to be huge."

Ambulance Victoria said it was investigating options to minimise any impact of fuel availability on the community emergency response for Birchip and surrounds.

'It's definitely not safe'

Resident Gillian Flett said the lack of unleaded fuel created a safety risk.

Gillian Flett is worried about anyone who may need to drive out of town in an emergency. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"It's definitely not safe because the nearest fuel is 30 kilometres away," Ms Flett said.

" If you haven't got enough to leave town, then it's a real problem. "

Retail assistant Emily Hotker said she exclusively bought diesel from the motel for her sedan and would now have to find an alternative option.

"For [unleaded drivers] who live out of town or on a farm, a lot of people wouldn't be able to get to work," Ms Hotker said.

Emily Hotker drives a diesel sedan. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

'We will have to help our locals'

Buloke Council Shire Mayor Graeme Milne said he was disappointed in the prolonged outage.

He said the council was exploring alternative options.

Graeme Milne says the council is exploring alternative options. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"To buy into a business in town and then cut off the only fuel supply available for unleaded fuel is, to me, very disappointing," Mr Milne said.

"If they can't guarantee that they're going to play the game and supply fuel on a regular basis, then we will have to help our locals find another alternative."

World.title: Interests of homebuyers and sellers collide in fight for transparency
World.content:
New laws will let prospective homebuyers know the price a seller is willing to say "yes" to.

The Victorian laws that took effect at the start of the month are being watched closely nationwide and bring radical transparency before and after sales.

They will force agents to:

Make the reserve price public at least a week before an auction.

Publish the sale price for at least 18 months after the sale.

Agents use underquoting to artificially increase turnout to auctions by attracting bidders unlikely to be able to afford the property. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Council)

The laws aim to reduce underquoting, when agents market a property for a price for well below what it is expected to sell for to artificially generate interest in a property.

"Victorians are sick of wasting their weekends chasing homes they were never going to get," said state Minister for Consumer Affairs Paul Edbrooke.

Paul Edbrooke says Victorians are sick of wasting their time chasing homes they can not afford. (ABC News)

But Real Estate Institute of Victoria (REIV) chief executive Toby Balazs, who represents agents, opposes the details of the new laws.

"If you look at the problem that was trying to be solved, egregious underquoting, and the results — people wasting their time and money on getting things like building reports — that's a good thing," he said.

" We just don't think this is the way to do it. "

The institute thinks potential buyers should have guidance on the likely range a property will sell, but not the precise figure.

Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds.

Because most sales campaigns run for a month and the reserve price must be published 7 days before the auction, Mr Balazs argues there is little time to get feedback from potential buyers.

"What you're probably going to get is overquoting … because if I [quote] over, it's easier to come down."

He argues the seller (otherwise known as the vendor) "has a right to manage what is the sale of, most likely, their biggest asset".

Laws with good intent but poor design, expert argues

Independent property economist Cameron Kusher is all for crushing the scourge of underquoting, which is generally illegal in Australia.

But he does not think these laws will do it.

Cameron Kusher says real estate agents do not have a clear picture of the auction a week out, and it will be harder to set an accurate reserve price. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

"Declaring [the reserve] on the morning of, or before the auction commences, is a much better solution than having to declare a week out," he said, because agents and the seller were still understanding who the bidders were likely to be and what they were willing to pay.

Cate Bakos, a buyer's advocate in Victoria, agreed and added that, while underquoting was a big problem, the new laws could make things more difficult for both vendors and buyers.

"It's been a problem for a long time. I've been in the industry for 23 years and it's been a problem for every single year," she said.

"Seven days is a long runway for vendors; I don't think it's enough, and it will make it really stressful for them."

She said that, ultimately, real estate agents would still find a way around the rules.

Confusion over new rules

Ray White Group managing director Dan White said the new laws were inconsistent and confusing for buyers, vendors and agents.

He said the government gave the company conflicting advice on whether the reserve could be changed after it was set. The government did not respond to ABC requests for clarification.

"The minister said you can change it, and the cabinet said you can't," Mr White said.

Dan White, Cate Bakos and Cameron Kusher all say that a lot can change in the week ahead of an auction from when a reserve price is published. (ABC News: Michael Coggan)

But, he said, the reserve was only one piece of information and buyers should do their own research.

While the new laws mean the property price statement now includes a swathe of facts about the property, Ms Bakos says this could make buyers feel more informed than they really are.

" I'm concerned that buyers will have a false sense of security. "

It will now include new information such as the internal floor area and number of car spaces, but she says it misses key facts about the zoning and land quality.

Cate Bakos says the new laws are well-intentioned but could lure buyers into thinking they have a full set of facts on a property. (Supplied: Cate Bakos)

"What's the point of counting bedrooms and car spots if it's in a flood zone?"

But a typical consumer might not understand these implications, which could significantly affect the property's value, she said.

Unclear if other states will follow

New South Wales has been cracking down on underquoting, but it is not using the same laws as Victoria.

In February, NSW Fair Trading introduced a Name and Shame register that publicly lists fines and breaches from real estate agents and strata managers, including underquoting.

The government conducted 131 inspections across July to September and 31 penalty notices were issued, totalling more than $68,000.

While underquoting is generally illegal across Australia, no other state has said it plans to introduce similar laws to Victoria.

Will this lower prices?

Victoria's property prices have been falling, or rising more slowly than other jurisdictions, in recent years.

Expanded supply and a swathe of new rules and taxes that have made property investment less attractive have seen the median property price fall to the lowest of all the capital cities bar Hobart and Darwin in recent data.

These changes are unlikely to alter that picture.

Property Council of Australia Victorian deputy executive director Andrew Lowcock said greater transparency alone will not solve housing affordability.

"The biggest drivers of prices remain supply and demand," he said.

" If Victoria wants more affordable housing, it needs to focus on getting more homes built. "

Real Estate Institute of Victoria's Toby Balazs agrees.

"It won't affect prices at all," he said.

Ms Bakos said it was unlikely to affect prices over the longer term, but that adding the laws during a downward market was "terrible" timing.

"If you're in a hot market, you can set the reserve price as whatever you want."

World.content:
Greens leader David Shoebridge has refused to say whether the results of an inquiry into allegations against Greens senator Jordon Steele-John should be made public, as he argues he should not have a hand in determining the process of the investigation.

“This is a process that will be commissioned by the WA Greens, and the parameters that we are very clear about is it will be fair, and it will be independent, and it will be timely. But it is not my role to put parameters around what we have said must be and will be an independent process,” Shoebridge told journalists at Parliament House in Canberra this morning.

Pressed on whether the Greens had ignored allegations made against the senator in the past, Shoebridge said: “I’ve been leader now for two weeks, and when I received these complaints, I took the most timely action that I believe you could take, and I’d ask people to judge me and on the response that’s been taken, the timely response that’s been taken”.

“Everybody in this deserves a process that is fair, a process that is timely, and I think timely is critical, and a process that is independent. And we are committed to undertaking that process, and committed to doing justice to the matters that have been raised, and justice to any party that has been involved in the matter, and I think that should be actually a bedrock. That should actually be a bedrock of politics.”

World.content:

Sports presenter Danika Mason has joined the exodus from the Today show, announcing her departure from the program on Friday morning. “Bit of news from me ... I’m going on maternity leave,” Mason said on the show. “I’ve had to make the decision as to whether what I do when I come back next year … obviously juggling all my NRL commitments, [the] Today show, and then a new baby as well. Loading “Something had to give, so I’ve made a pretty tough decision ... when I return next year, I won’t be coming back to the show.” Mason’s announcement marks the fourth high-profile departure of Today presenters since June, when the network terminated media personality Karl Stefanovic’s multimedia contract after an interview with far-right British activist Tommy Robinson.



Last month, Stefanovic’s former co-host, Sarah Abo, confirmed while she was on maternity leave that she was leaving the program, while weather presenter Tim Davies announced in August he would leave the show. Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort were in September announced as the new hosts of Today. Mason is one of Nine’s NRL and sports presenters and joined Today in May 2025, after beginning at Nine (also the owner of this masthead) in 2012. Today sport presenter Danika Mason has announced she is leaving the show. Instagram In July, Mason, who is married to former NRL prop Liam Knight, announced she was pregnant. The decision to leave the program was not easy, Mason said on air. “I’ve absolutely loved my time with everyone. We have the best audience, we have the best team, and it has been an absolute, just such a fun two years, and everyone who is in here in the morning, all our floor crew, you guys are just amazing, and I’ve had the best time,” she said.



In February, Mason made international headlines and had to apologise for drinking before an awkward live cross from the Winter Olympics in Italy, during which she stumbled over her words. Related Article Australian TV ‘Like chess pieces in motion’: Inside the big Today show shake-up Mason’s departure comes at a dire time for Nine’s flagship breakfast program, which continues to lag Seven’s Sunrise in the hard-fought timeslot. On Wednesday, Sunrise boasted a 421,000 total national average audience rating, while Today was well behind at 273,000. The appointments of Jeffreys and Steinfort followed an era of the show marked by a rotating roster of fill-in hosts. Jeffreys recently revealed she is pregnant with her third child and is likely to be on maternity leave for at least a few months early next year, which suggests the hosting shuffling will continue to some extent. World.title: Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America
World.content:
TechnologyAI Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America Emmy Martin October 16, 2026 — 6:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The OpenAI engineer who was charged this week with planting a secret recording device at the artificial intelligence company recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, and was listed as a partner at a venture capital firm alongside a member of the Saudi royal family. In an Arabic podcast interview last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organisations, including the kingdom’s social insurance agency. Separately, RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, lists Alfozan as a venture partner on its website, along with Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud. Abdulrahman Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. Instagram Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. He was an engineer at Meta before joining a startup that went through Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley startup accelerator. He gained permanent residency status in the United States in 2020, according to court documents, and was hired by OpenAI in July 2025. Details about Alfozan are emerging after OpenAI disclosed earlier this week that it had discovered a hidden recording device in a conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings. The company said it had traced the device to Alfozan, who was arrested by the FBI and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device.



The incident has fuelled concerns about the security of leading AI labs like OpenAI that create advanced AI models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the US technology industry. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that what had happened at OpenAI underscored how winning the AI race “is a national security prerogative.” An image released by the US Department of Justice appears to show Abdulrahman Alfozan behind the TV where a bug was hidden. US Department of Justice OpenAI said Alfozan did not appear to have inappropriately obtained or extracted sensitive information about its technology or customers. But the cloak-and-dagger details of the case have gained attention in Silicon Valley and in law enforcement and national security circles. “Silicon Valley is ground zero for espionage from a variety of countries around the world,” said Amy Zegart, a professor at Stanford University who specialises in national security and intelligence. She added that she was “troubled” by the OpenAI incident and expected more cases “because these companies are so important.” An OpenAI spokesperson said the company had “a rigorous insider risk program to protect our employees, our intellectual property and customer data” and declined to discuss its monitoring process.



Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment. His lawyer, William Pernik, said in an email that his client “poses no flight risk whatsoever,” cited his “long-standing ties to the community” and said that he would contest the allegations and detention at a hearing on Monday. “I am aware of the narrative that is being painted,” Pernik said, “and we will fight it wholeheartedly.” In a court filing, prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. US Department of Justice RAED and the Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment. In a filing in US District Court for the Northern District of California, which was unsealed prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. Only executives and their assistants could reserve the room, which was used for leadership meetings and briefings with government officials, the complaint said.



OpenAI employees then placed a camera in the conference room, prosecutors said, and it recorded Alfozan checking behind the TV on October 5. That day, security staff found a second device in a bag that Alfozan had left in a printer room, the complaint said. Related Article Exclusive

AI Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt Last month, an AI chatbot account linked to Alfozan’s wife was used to ask how to build a continuous audio recorder, add Wi-Fi connectivity, encrypt its memory card and hide its activity, according to the complaint. Alfozan asked an AI tool to list meeting rooms in OpenAI’s offices and asked about locations for “leadership and exec,” prosecutors said. Alfozan, his wife and another relative had booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for this past Monday, prosecutors said in another court filing. Born in Saudi Arabia’s central region of Qassim and raised in Dammam, Alfozan got into Mawhiba, the kingdom’s national program for gifted students, he said in the interview with “Identity Capital,” an Arabic podcast about professionals and careers. He later received a scholarship through a gifted-student program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.



On the podcast, Alfozan described meeting Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then the deputy crown prince, during the prince’s 2016 visit to Silicon Valley. He said the prince had advised young Saudis in Silicon Valley to build their skills at the world’s leading companies and then bring that expertise home. Warning: Graphic content London: A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand has told a court the actor underwent a sudden change in manner as they talked in her hotel room, demanding she take photographs of him before pushing her onto a bed. The woman told jurors that Brand became suddenly “monster-like” after they had talked for hours on the night they met in September 1999, leaving her in pain after he forced himself on top of her and raped her. The 1999 photographs of Russell Brand that were tendered as evidence in court at his rape trial on Thursday (UK time). Metropolitan Police “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe,” she told the court, saying she was pinned down by the actor’s weight. “I know I said ‘No’.”



Brand, 51, is facing trial in London on three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has insisted he never engaged in non-consensual sex. The woman, described as the first complainant among six women alleging sexual assault and rape, said she thought Brand was gay because of his “effeminate” manner when they met at a cabaret where he was appearing on the sidelines of a Labour conference in Bournemouth. Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court on Thursday (UK time). Jordan Pettitt/PA via AP They spoke about her ideas for a play, she told the court, and went to her hotel room to continue the conversation because she was not drinking and did not want to go to a pub because it would be hard to hear. She said that after she suggested Brand make a coffee while she went to the bathroom, she returned to find him “prancing” around the room “like an ostrich” without his shirt, and that he then demanded she take photographs of him with her camera.



In key evidence produced in court, jurors were shown two photographs of the actor, who was 24 at the time, staring at the camera with a mirror and small wash basin behind him. In one image he appears to gesture to the camera. Related Article Graphic content

Courts Russell Brand a ‘ruthless sexual predator’, prosecutor alleges as rape trial opens The woman, who was in her late 20s at the time, said that Brand became aroused while she was taking photographs and that she saw this clearly at one stage because he was in his underpants, which she referred to as “budgie smugglers”. In a video interview with police that was shown to the court, the woman said Brand forced her onto the bed and pulled her trousers and underwear down. He kissed her in a “lizard-like” way and put his fingers in her mouth, making it hard for her to breathe. “He knew I didn’t want it. He put himself straight in. It was hurting. He was having sex, pushing, pushing.” She said she had her eyes shut and could not do anything because of his weight.



Her statements in the police interview were challenged by Brand’s counsel when the woman appeared in court to give direct evidence, after the video was shown. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial The defence counsel, Ian Winter, KC, said the photographs were at odds with the woman’s statement to police because they showed Brand was wearing white pants rather than being in his underwear as she had said. The woman rejected those doubts by saying she had kept taking photographs even if some did not turn out, and she was adamant that he had been in his “budgie smugglers” at one stage – and that she had become scared. When Winter asked the woman in cross-examination why she did not leave the hotel room when Brand took off his clothes, she replied that she had nowhere to go and there were no staff at the hotel late in the night.

Brand married singer Katy Perry in 2010, but they divorced two years later. In 2017, he married author Laura Gallacher, who has supported him against the allegations and appeared alongside him on the first day of the trial.

World.title: ‘As if the sky had fallen’: School roof collapse kills at least 34 children and a teacher
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy ‘As if the sky had fallen’: School roof collapse kills at least 34 children and a teacher Riaz Khan and Hritam Mukherjee Updated October 16, 2026 — 6:29am ,first published 6:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Peshawar: The roof of a private school collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, killing at least 34 children and a teacher and injuring more than 50 other people in the deadliest building collapse ever in the country, authorities and a hospital official said. Most of the children killed or injured at Al-Khair school on Thursday were between six and 12 years old, while the oldest was 14, Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said. Some of the injured were in critical condition, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded. Hours after the collapse in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, emergency services spokesperson Bilal Faizi said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews had cleared debris.



He said the roofs of two classrooms collapsed when second- and third-grade children were in them with their teachers. Faizi said ambulances and disaster management personnel arrived from a nearby facility within five minutes of being alerted. Nearly 100 rescuers eventually joined the operation, he said. Panicked, grieving parents were trying to help when crews arrived, Faizi said. Mourners attend funeral prayers for children killed when the roof of a school, in Peshawar collapsed. AP He credited the rapid evacuation with saving at least 40 lives. More than a dozen children suffered minor injuries, he said. Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs.



One teacher said it felt as though the sky had fallen Hundreds of mourners later gathered at Rehman Baba cemetery for mass funeral prayers as grief gripped the neighbourhood and announcements echoed from mosque loudspeakers, urging residents to join in prayers for those killed. Residents said most of the children killed lived in the Dir Colony neighbourhood, where the school is located, leaving them unsure which bereaved family to visit first to offer condolences. A rescue worker gestures toward roof as he searches through the rubble. AP Ambulances were seen leaving the hospital to bring the children’s bodies home as mourners wept and wailed.



Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said the school had about 1200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She said she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children. According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighbourhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene. A man shows a picture of his young relative who was killed in the roof collapse. AP Resident Samiullah Khan said he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom for a drink of water.



Another resident, Mohammad Khan, said that rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived. Officials offer condolences and promise investigations Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school’s owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak. However, following his arrest, the owner, Mohammad Khan, blamed recent rains for weakening one of the roofs, according to police, who said the investigation was still underway. The provincial government said a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse of the three-storey building.



Provincial government spokeswoman Samar Haroon Bilour praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety. In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements. “The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow,” Zardari said. He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies. Greens leader David Shoebridge has refused to say whether the results of an inquiry into allegations against Greens senator Jordon Steele-John should be made public, as he argues he should not have a hand in determining the process of the investigation.

“This is a process that will be commissioned by the WA Greens, and the parameters that we are very clear about is it will be fair, and it will be independent, and it will be timely. But it is not my role to put parameters around what we have said must be and will be an independent process,” Shoebridge told journalists at Parliament House in Canberra this morning.

Pressed on whether the Greens had ignored allegations made against the senator in the past, Shoebridge said: “I’ve been leader now for two weeks, and when I received these complaints, I took the most timely action that I believe you could take, and I’d ask people to judge me and on the response that’s been taken, the timely response that’s been taken”.

“Everybody in this deserves a process that is fair, a process that is timely, and I think timely is critical, and a process that is independent. And we are committed to undertaking that process, and committed to doing justice to the matters that have been raised, and justice to any party that has been involved in the matter, and I think that should be actually a bedrock. That should actually be a bedrock of politics.”

World.content:
CultureTV & radioNews & current affairs Sport presenter Danika Mason joins Today exodus Kayla Olaya October 16, 2026 — 7:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Sports presenter Danika Mason has joined the exodus from the Today show, announcing her departure from the program on Friday morning. “Bit of news from me ... I’m going on maternity leave,” Mason said on the show. “I’ve had to make the decision as to whether what I do when I come back next year … obviously juggling all my NRL commitments, [the] Today show, and then a new baby as well. Loading “Something had to give, so I’ve made a pretty tough decision ... when I return next year, I won’t be coming back to the show.” Mason’s announcement marks the fourth high-profile departure of Today presenters since June, when the network terminated media personality Karl Stefanovic’s multimedia contract after an interview with far-right British activist Tommy Robinson.



Last month, Stefanovic’s former co-host, Sarah Abo, confirmed while she was on maternity leave that she was leaving the program, while weather presenter Tim Davies announced in August he would leave the show. Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort were in September announced as the new hosts of Today. Mason is one of Nine’s NRL and sports presenters and joined Today in May 2025, after beginning at Nine (also the owner of this masthead) in 2012. Today sport presenter Danika Mason has announced she is leaving the show. Instagram In July, Mason, who is married to former NRL prop Liam Knight, announced she was pregnant. The decision to leave the program was not easy, Mason said on air. “I’ve absolutely loved my time with everyone. We have the best audience, we have the best team, and it has been an absolute, just such a fun two years, and everyone who is in here in the morning, all our floor crew, you guys are just amazing, and I’ve had the best time,” she said.



In February, Mason made international headlines and had to apologise for drinking before an awkward live cross from the Winter Olympics in Italy, during which she stumbled over her words. Related Article Australian TV ‘Like chess pieces in motion’: Inside the big Today show shake-up Mason’s departure comes at a dire time for Nine’s flagship breakfast program, which continues to lag Seven’s Sunrise in the hard-fought timeslot. On Wednesday, Sunrise boasted a 421,000 total national average audience rating, while Today was well behind at 273,000. The appointments of Jeffreys and Steinfort followed an era of the show marked by a rotating roster of fill-in hosts. Jeffreys recently revealed she is pregnant with her third child and is likely to be on maternity leave for at least a few months early next year, which suggests the hosting shuffling will continue to some extent. A man was shot dead in Melbourne’s outer north on Thursday evening in what police suspect was a targeted attack. Emergency services were called to Gypsum Drive in Wollert and found the man deceased about 5.30pm. Police officers in Wollert on Friday after a man was shot dead on Thursday afternoon. Wayne Taylor “The 42-year-old Wollert man sustained injuries consistent with a shooting,” police said in a statement. Footage posted to social media shows two black-clad figures running around the corner of Gypsum Drive into Lowline Way, moments before multiple loud bangs are heard.



Another two bangs ring out as the pair fumble at the door of a weathered red sedan. One man then climbs into the driver’s seat, while the other runs around to the passenger side. A crime scene has been established on Gypsum Drive. Wayne Taylor As the driver floors the accelerator and the sedan speeds away, a third figure can be seen between the tree leaves at the other end of the corner block. Police believe the shooting was a targeted attack. Nine Another video obtained by Nine News also shows ambulance paramedics comforting a woman who was reportedly screaming at the crime scene on Thursday.



Homicide detectives remained at the scene on Friday morning. “No arrests have been made and at this early stage of the investigation, police are treating the incident as targeted,” police said. No arrests have been made. Wayne Taylor In the same suburb last year, Melbourne underworld figure Athan Boursinos was shot in a laneway behind his family home. The 21-year-old, who was part of a street gang controlled by tobacco kingpin Kazem “Kaz” Hamad and his cousin, was ambushed in broad daylight on July 31, 2025 by hitmen hired by a NSW crime syndicate.



The site of Boursinos’ death in Wollert is a five-minute drive from the scene of Thursday’s homicide. World.title: Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America
World.content:
TechnologyAI Toilet paper, recording devices and one-way tickets: Inside the OpenAI spying case that has rattled America Emmy Martin October 16, 2026 — 6:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The OpenAI engineer who was charged this week with planting a secret recording device at the artificial intelligence company recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, and was listed as a partner at a venture capital firm alongside a member of the Saudi royal family. In an Arabic podcast interview last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organisations, including the kingdom’s social insurance agency. Separately, RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, lists Alfozan as a venture partner on its website, along with Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud. Abdulrahman Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. Instagram Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. He was an engineer at Meta before joining a startup that went through Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley startup accelerator. He gained permanent residency status in the United States in 2020, according to court documents, and was hired by OpenAI in July 2025. Details about Alfozan are emerging after OpenAI disclosed earlier this week that it had discovered a hidden recording device in a conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings. The company said it had traced the device to Alfozan, who was arrested by the FBI and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device.



The incident has fuelled concerns about the security of leading AI labs like OpenAI that create advanced AI models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the US technology industry. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that what had happened at OpenAI underscored how winning the AI race “is a national security prerogative.” An image released by the US Department of Justice appears to show Abdulrahman Alfozan behind the TV where a bug was hidden. US Department of Justice OpenAI said Alfozan did not appear to have inappropriately obtained or extracted sensitive information about its technology or customers. But the cloak-and-dagger details of the case have gained attention in Silicon Valley and in law enforcement and national security circles. “Silicon Valley is ground zero for espionage from a variety of countries around the world,” said Amy Zegart, a professor at Stanford University who specialises in national security and intelligence. She added that she was “troubled” by the OpenAI incident and expected more cases “because these companies are so important.” An OpenAI spokesperson said the company had “a rigorous insider risk program to protect our employees, our intellectual property and customer data” and declined to discuss its monitoring process.



Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment. His lawyer, William Pernik, said in an email that his client “poses no flight risk whatsoever,” cited his “long-standing ties to the community” and said that he would contest the allegations and detention at a hearing on Monday. “I am aware of the narrative that is being painted,” Pernik said, “and we will fight it wholeheartedly.” In a court filing, prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. US Department of Justice RAED and the Saudi Embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment. In a filing in US District Court for the Northern District of California, which was unsealed prosecutors detailed how OpenAI’s security team had found a thumb-size recording device on September 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into the back of a television in an executive conference room. Only executives and their assistants could reserve the room, which was used for leadership meetings and briefings with government officials, the complaint said.



OpenAI employees then placed a camera in the conference room, prosecutors said, and it recorded Alfozan checking behind the TV on October 5. That day, security staff found a second device in a bag that Alfozan had left in a printer room, the complaint said. Related Article Exclusive

AI Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt Last month, an AI chatbot account linked to Alfozan’s wife was used to ask how to build a continuous audio recorder, add Wi-Fi connectivity, encrypt its memory card and hide its activity, according to the complaint. Alfozan asked an AI tool to list meeting rooms in OpenAI’s offices and asked about locations for “leadership and exec,” prosecutors said. Alfozan, his wife and another relative had booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for this past Monday, prosecutors said in another court filing. Born in Saudi Arabia’s central region of Qassim and raised in Dammam, Alfozan got into Mawhiba, the kingdom’s national program for gifted students, he said in the interview with “Identity Capital,” an Arabic podcast about professionals and careers. He later received a scholarship through a gifted-student program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and studied computer science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.



On the podcast, Alfozan described meeting Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then the deputy crown prince, during the prince’s 2016 visit to Silicon Valley. He said the prince had advised young Saudis in Silicon Valley to build their skills at the world’s leading companies and then bring that expertise home. AP Resident Samiullah Khan said he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom for a drink of water.



Another resident, Mohammad Khan, said that rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived. Officials offer condolences and promise investigations Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school’s owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak. However, following his arrest, the owner, Mohammad Khan, blamed recent rains for weakening one of the roofs, according to police, who said the investigation was still underway. The provincial government said a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse of the three-storey building.



Provincial government spokeswoman Samar Haroon Bilour praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety. In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements. “The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow,” Zardari said. He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies. World.title: Tropical Storm Champi: Another typhoon threatens Marianas
World.content:
Another potentially powerful typhoon is threatening the Commonwealth of the Mariana Islands, with Tropical Storm Champi forecast to strengthen into a category 2 typhoon before passing over or near Guam on Sunday.

The Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) upgraded the system to a tropical storm early Friday, with sustained winds of 40 miles per hour.

Champi was about 825 miles east of Guam, moving west at 12 miles per hour, with a typhoon watch in effect for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan.

Forecasters warn that even a slight change in the storm's track could significantly affect wind and rainfall conditions across the islands.

The latest threat comes as the region continues to recover from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which caused widespread damage earlier this year, and Tropical Storm Choi-wan earlier this month.

No time to recover

American Red Cross coordinating officer Charles Blake said repeated storms have stretched disaster response capabilities.

"When you get hit with multiple storms, one right after the other, and you don't get time to fully recover from those storms, there's going to be some gaps," he said.

The Red Cross is deploying approximately 85 additional personnel from Guam, Hawaii and the US mainland to assist with evacuation shelters and disaster response operations.

Shelters are being prepared across Saipan, Tinian and Rota, while residents have been urged to stock up on food, water, fuel and medications for at least 48 hours.

Blake warned that power, water, and fuel shortages could complicate recovery efforts.

"We won't be able to do everything for everybody, but we're going to do the best we can to meet people's needs and meet them where they're at," he said.

World.title: Greens promise universal payment for trainee teachers, nurses, vets and dentists
World.content:
The Green Party says it will give students a universal payment while they complete their training to be teachers, nurses, and other essential health and social support workers such as midwives, vets, and dentists.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said students should not have to "go broke" while they train for the jobs New Zealand needs.

"Our paid placements policy will make sure they can afford the essentials while training."

The party has costed the policy at around $311 million over four years.

The party said it would also support students who need to relocate for their placement, making training more accessible for students in the regions.

"We will prioritise sectors where unpaid placements mean that some students have no choice but to drop out.

"Unpaid placements push students out of sectors where the workforce is struggling to keep up with demand, like health and education."

The paid placements policy would:

Support students to afford the basics while training by providing them with a universal weekly payment of $380, available on top of any pre-existing student loan or student allowance, for the duration of their compulsory placements.

Make it easier for students who need to relocate for their placement by covering some of their costs with a relocation payment of $1500.

Improve student retention and widen access so students from all backgrounds and financial situations can train for the crucial roles New Zealand needs more of.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said people training to be nurses, teachers and social workers were currently forced to do hundreds or thousands of hours for free in order to get into a profession that no one was doing for the money or the glory in the first place.

"Imagine being required to spend 30 hours a week working and not being paid for it.

"That's messed up. It doesn't have to be that way. The Greens will fix it."

World.title: Suspected copper thieves cause major internet outage in Bay of Islands
World.content:
A second major internet outage in a week caused by suspected copper thieves is another blow to Bay of Islands businesses trying to recover from a slow winter.

The outage has affected 750 homes and businesses in the wider Russell area, leaving shops, hotels and the town's crucial ferries unable to take electronic payments.

Chorus' outage website shows the incident occurred at 1.27am on Friday.

The company said technicians were preparing the damaged cables for splicing and would start work once access was available.

There was no estimate as yet for the restoration time.

Anton Haagh, co-owner of the Duke of Marlborough Hotel, said only about 5 percent of customers paid with cash - so losing the internet was a huge disruption.

He said copper thieves had also caused a major outage on Monday.

"So it's the second time this week. We're about to go into cruise ship season. We've got wedding season coming up. We had a 15 percent drop-off in domestic trade this winter. It's been a tough winter and this is the last thing everyone needs."

Haagh said staff had rushed home this morning to bring in their own Starlink units to get the hotel's Eftpos back up and running.

However, for businesses with no access to satellite internet, it could mean losing a day's income.

The Duke of Marlborough Hotel in Russell is one of the businesses affected by the internet disruption.

For the hotel it meant a lot of extra time and hassle.

It would also make it harder for people to get to Russell because the ferries relied on electronic payments.

"They'll struggle to get people to pay the fares. It just cascades through the economy, particularly the tourism economy."

If the thefts and outages continued the hotel would have to switch to Starlink, Haagh said.

"It's just another added cost that no one really needs."

Chorus' outage map shows the affected area covers the entire Russell peninsula, including Russell township and Ōkiato, as well as Rāwhiti, Waikare, Karetu, and State Highway 11 between Ōpua and Kawakawa.

A Chorus spokeswoman told RNZ the outage affected 550 fibre broadband and 200 copper services customers between Kawakawa and Russell.

Technicians were on site and working towards restoring services.

"Early signs point towards vandalism of our cables, and we've reported it to the police. Our priority right now is to restore connectivity as quickly as possible," she said.

The company apologised for the disruption and thanked customers for their patience while the damage was repaired.

The latest internet outage has prompted Northland MP Grant McCallum to call for action against copper thieves - and any dodgy scrap dealers buying stolen metal.

"This is beyond frustrating. People targeting copper are damaging fibre cables and cutting off essential services to entire communities," he said.

"It's not just an inconvenience. Businesses rely on internet connections to process Eftpos payments, take bookings and serve customers. Families need reliable connections to work, access services and stay in touch. When the network goes down, the impact is enormous."

McCallum said Chorus had told him that copper and fibre cables were often located together, meaning people targeting copper could also damage the fibre network, causing widespread disruption.

"With the cruise ship season upon us and tourism businesses gearing up for a busy summer, the last thing Russell and Bay of Islands operators need is repeated internet outages," he said.

"And let's be clear, this is not Chorus's fault. Their teams are left repairing damage caused by vandals, while residents and businesses are left dealing with the consequences."

He said attention also had to turn to where stolen copper was ending up.

"We need to look at who is purchasing stolen copper and make sure those knowingly dealing in stolen material are held accountable. Scrap metal dealers have an important role to play. If someone turns up with suspicious quantities of copper cable or piping, questions need to be asked about where it has come from," he said.

World.title: Former dairy manager sentenced over $320,000 kickbacks from overseas customer
World.content:
A former dairy processing company manager has been sentenced to a year of home detention after admitting to taking $320,000 in kickbacks from an overseas customer.

Simon Stewart appeared at the Manukau District Court on Thursday. He was also ordered to pay $250,000 in reparations to his former employer - Open Country Dairy.

Stewart earlier admitted to providing commercially sensitive price information to an Indonesian company and customer of Open Country.

The Serious Fraud Office said there were 27 bank transfers made to Stewart's account.

SFO director Karen Chang said corruption and fraud threaten New Zealand's key trade industries including dairy.

"It is essential that those who engage in corrupt practices are held to account, particularly when their actions risk impacting the integrity and reputation of a key sector," Chang said.

"This case is also a good reminder that corruption is not limited to the public sector. It can occur in any sector and any industry. The SFO plays a crucial role in detecting, investigating and prosecuting serious fraud and corruption, including corporate offending that threatens New Zealand's key trade-related industries."

World.title: Haze over Papua from forest fires causes mass disruptions, health issues
World.content:
Haze and smoke from large wildfires in Indonesia, including West Papua, have resulted in flight disruptions and respiratory problems in the region and are also affecting neighbouring Papua New Guinea.

The fires are concentrated around parts of Indonesia where there has been large scale land and forest clearance, often for oil palm plantations, including Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua.

Prolonged dry conditions due to an intensifying El Niño phase in the wider region have exacerbated the conditions for such fires.

The Jakarta Globe reported reported widespread flight disruptions as as smoke reduced visibility at several airports, causing delays, cancellations, and diversions.

Papua's Jubi News reports that thick smoke haze has blanketed Mimika Regency in Central Papua, with smoke from forest and land fires in Merauke Regency, South Papua, carried by the wind into the region.

Residents have reported health problems amid the worsening haze, while early childhood education centres and primary school have been temporarily closed, with students switching to remote learning from this week

High school students are still attending classes but required to wear masks. As early as last month, Al Jazeera reported that the haze was causing a surge in respiratory illnesses, with millions exposed to smoke.

In neighbouring PNG, haze from the fires has reached as far east as the capital Port Moresby, with authorities urging caution from residents.

According to The National, the assistant director of the National Weather Service, Kasis Inape, has warned the smoke can contain harmful pollutants which can affect the health of people.

He has urged the public to reduce prolonged outdoor activities, to protect children and the elderly, and to use masks when exposure to heavy smoke cannot be avoided.

Meanwhile, Indonesia's media outlet Tempo reports that emergency responses by the National Disaster Mitigation Agency (BNPB) have swung into action.

It says BNPB is conducting "weather modification operations" in West Papua to address haze and assist in the management of forest and land fires.

World.title: 'Four-headed beast': ACT leader David Seymour hints at potential for coalition with Opportunity
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour says he could be open to a "four-headed beast" coalition with Opportunity to stop a left-wing coalition taking power.

Speaking to a crowd of supporters in Wānaka, he admitted that if Opportunity crossed the 5 percent threshold, a coalition with them to keep the Greens and Te Pāti Māori from running the country "would be a good outcome".

However, Seymour said he felt Opportunity may not be the kingmaker, "despite the best efforts of the media".

National has ruled out working with the Opportunity on multiple occasions.
