Winding up Winston, the rule of ruling things out, Peter Dunne's heir, and the boring work of saving democracy Caucus Download MP3 52m

Leader Christopher Luxon initially stated he would not do business with a party that wants to raise taxes at the end of July.

Following the TVNZ leaders' debate last week, Luxon reiterated he would not work with Opportunity.

"I have been crystal clear with who we could or couldn't work with. I've laid that out from the very beginning of the year. I've been clear about Opportunity," he said at the time.

Last week, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong dismissed the comments.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong is continuing to keep the door open to coalition negotiations with National. RNZ / Blessen Tom

"I don't believe him. Because he would rather be in government than in opposition, I assume," she said at the time.

"There are many things we could work with National on, I think the five bottom lines are realistic for them to commit to."

At the end of September, Opportunity set out its five minimum requirements a potential coalition partner would have to agree to.

The party's bottom lines are giving the Commerce Commission more teeth, regulating lobbying and capping political donations to "clean up politics", developing a 10-year plan to "fix the health system" alongside health professionals, phasing out bottom trawling, and recommitting to Paris Agreement emissions reduction obligations and protecting the Climate Change Commission's independence.

Multiple polls have shown Opportunity poised to decide who will lead the next government.

The latest 1News Verian Poll, released earlier this week, showed Opportunity winning a potential 10 seats in the election.

If that poll's results were replicated at the election, National would get 34 MPs and New Zealand First and ACT would each get 12 - a coalition bloc of 58.

On the left, Labour would get 34 MPs, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori four - depending on how the Māori seats were calculated - and Te Tai Tokerau Party one seat - for a total of 57.

World.title: Labour supporters told to harness 'hope and rage'; National voters fear 'handout society'
World.content:
Audio player for " Winding up Winston, the rule of ruling things out, Peter Dunne's heir, and the boring work of saving democracy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1940271%2Flabour-supporters-told-to-harness-hope-and-rage-national-voters-fear-handout-society

Winding up Winston, the rule of ruling things out, Peter Dunne's heir, and the boring work of saving democracy Caucus Download MP3 52m

Labour supporters have been told to harness their "hope and rage" this election while National voters say fear the worst should the left bloc take power.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins joined a number of Labour candidates, including his deputy Carmel Sepuloni, Phil Twyford and newcomer and foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters in the working-class suburb of Kelston in West Auckland, in the auditorium of the local girls' high school, attracting a few hundred locals and party volunteers.

In her speech, Walters said Labour supporters had a mixture of "outrage and hope" to the campaign.

"Some of you, like me, will remember going on a march not long after the last election when they cancelled the smoke-free generation for our children - if they win, there will be marches for three years.

"I ask you one thing: bring all that energy, all of that hope and rage that you would put into those three years ahead, bring it now," she said.

Hipkins took the stage donning a lei presented to him on stage by Sepuloni, who has been the MP for Kelston for over a decade.

Labour supporters cheering on leader Chris Hipkins and local candidates. RNZ / Tuwhenuaroa Natanahira

He used his speech to lay into Christopher Luxon - rolling out his party's new attack line claiming Luxon had left people $6000 worse off - and laid out his party's plan to make life cheaper.

Jobs, in particular, got the crowd riled up.

"Those on the other side who currently sit on the treasury benches say it's not the government's job to create jobs, well, they've certainly demonstrated that they don't think it's their job to create jobs.

"Under our government, we achieved record low unemployment despite some of the most challenging economic conditions any government in New Zealand has faced ... we saved people's jobs [and] we've now got a government that celebrates losing them," he said.

Down south, the National party had their own rally on the West Coast.

Leader Christopher Luxon proved a popular figure among the estimated hundred supporters in Greymouth, many clad in royal blue.

After speaking for about 20 minutes, he then mingled with patrons and posed for a number of photos.

About 100 people gathered in Greymouth on Thursday for the National party's West Coast rally. RNZ / Adam Burns

Luxon also heard staunch views from the locals as pre-election tension ramped up.

Property developer Geoff Ball endorsed Luxon but admitted he was "seriously concerned" heading into the election.

"We've got a country that's in trouble," he said.

"I'm not 100 percent confident that National and the current coalition is going to get in. I think it's a big, big problem."

Ball's concerns stemmed from the belief that three years was not long enough for the coalition to boost the economy.

"I think they made a bloody good start, but I personally think they've got a long way to go," he said.

"To me, the country's got to be run like a business. It's not a handout society.

"We used to be a country where we had a reputation of number eight wire, and we get sh*t done. Now we're a country of red tape, bureaucrats, and b*llshit."

National leader Christopher Luxon is flanked by Brett Cummings (L) and Geoff Ball. RNZ / Adam Burns

Local man Brett Cummings had a post-speech one-on-one with Luxon, where he said they discussed "a few things that needed to be tidied up" on the West Coast, particularly around the repeal of regional councils and the overhaul of the Resource Management Act.

"There's a whole lot of changes they've been promising, but it's taking a long time to implement.

"All that land use and stuff, it's a long time ago. Not that long ago in my lifetime, you used to have permitted activities to be gold mining.

"Now you've got to get three consents plus a bond and all the rest of it."

RNZ asked both men to rate the past three years under the coalition government.

World.title: World Cup opener a reminder of Test rugby league's glory days
World.content:
The Sydney Football Stadium is as modern a football temple as you'll find, but Australia's opening match in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup was like a trip back in time.

The game against New Zealand was played in the shadow of the Sydney Cricket Ground, where the Kangaroos have played ever since rugby league arrived in Australia in 1908.

It remains the site of so many sepia-toned memories of furious, blood-and-thunder battles because Test matches were the biggest, best and most brutal spectacles the game had to offer.

They would give these matches names like the Rorke's Drift Test or the Swinton Massacre, making them sound like wars.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

Those days are past, swallowed by the twin beasts of State of Origin and the ever-expanding club competition, but last night's 24-22 win for Australia is proof they can live again, even if only for a night.

The crowd of 41,225 was the biggest attendance for any Test match in Sydney since 1974, and this was a game that reminded everyone of how it used to be as the two teams put on an utter classic.

The journey to the green and gold's victory was studded with indelible moments like Casey McLean's acrobatic opening effort and the twin length-of-the-field intercept efforts from Jack Bostock and Tom Trbojevic.

Tom Trbojevic scored one of Australia's two length-of-the-field intercepts. (Getty Images: Matt King)

But none were better than Kalyn Ponga's three battles with Reece Walsh, which were the kind of one-on-one duels that exist in the brief moments when a team game becomes an individual sport.

If they were gunslingers, this would have been high noon.

Walsh won their first meeting, bundling Ponga over the sideline in a try-saving tackle after the Kiwi debutant made a break in the first half.

But Ponga's revenge was beautiful. In the second half, after slicing through again, he left Walsh chasing ghosts with a left-foot step they should write songs about en route to scoring his second try of the night.

It was a glorious moment, but few bathe in glory like Walsh.

His reply was a length-of-the-field effort in which he stepped Ponga and Jahrome Hughes so comprehensively they ran into each other.

It was a gut-busting effort from Walsh, literally. He went for the technicolour yawn afterwards, so much so that Latrell Mitchell had to take the sideline conversion.

In the end, it was Bostock's third try, the Dolphin flyer's debut for good measure, sealing the deal for Australia as the World Cup began with one of the best matches — NRL, Origin or otherwise — of recent times.

It was a spectacle a long time coming. This was the Kangaroos' first game at the new SFS, which has been open for four years.

It was their first game against New Zealand in Sydney since 2014, and they'd only played there twice in the past decade before last night.

That absence began as a symptom of the decline in fan interest in the national side — the punters just stopped showing up — until it became a cause.

Jack Bostock was magnificent in his Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Taking the show on the road is important, and in recent years Australia has played all across its own land and beyond. They are a team for the nation, not just for the cities with the big, fancy stadiums.

But to stay in people's hearts and minds, to feel large in the life of a sport, to remind them how big this can be and how important it's supposed to feel, sometimes you need to play the old songs, the ones everyone used to know, in the big house.

Australia has so many wins it's hard for them to stand out, but this one will. Apart from Bostock's two aerial efforts, every try they scored originated inside their own quarter as they ran to victory from the back of beyond.

New Zealand will be filthy with itself for losing a game where its vaunted forward pack did everything it was expected to do as it trampled all over Australia.

Australia and New Zealand are expected to meet again in the final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The Kiwis finished with five line breaks to one, and more than 300 extra run metres. They scored 22 points but left more on the board with some sub-par execution in the attacking 20.

A poor end to a set from Hughes, who had plenty of time on the last inside the red zone but came up with a kick that led to a seven-tackle set before Bostock's leap to heaven, will loom large in their minds.

Against Australia, even if they lose a key player like Mitchell Moses to injury, even if their forwards get bashed, and even if they're the better team for great swathes of the game, you cannot ever give them an inch.

They can and will get better. After talk about the Kiwis and the Pasifika nations dominated the lead-up, Australia reminded us all that it is still its tournament to lose.

Tom Bostock was man of the match in a famous Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Kind )

A rematch between these two in the final seems likely, but it's a long road to get there. Ponga's late departure with a suspected broken arm might put paid to the Kiwis' chances of claiming a second World Cup.

But before we look to the future, let us sit in the present a little longer as we bask in this glorious reminder of the past.

This was the good stuff. This is what it's all about. This is how it used to be and perhaps can be again.

One great match does not make a World Cup, and the international game cannot be taken back to its most legendary nights in just 80 minutes, no matter how good they might be.

Rugby league needs more of this: the best teams in the world, filled with the best players dancing on the edge of the blade, in the biggest and best stadiums when the stakes are highest.

It's a simple recipe, but the appetite for it is mighty. The crowd alone is proof of that, and there should be more of it to come.

Samoa and Tonga are almost certain to provide it when they play the latest round of a rivalry older than time in their sold-out pool match in a fortnight.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The semifinals, which will almost definitely pit Australia and New Zealand against one of the two island nations or England, have the potential to be like the tournament opener.

In rebuilding the prestige of international football — its oldest treasure — the sport can strike gold again.

Rugby league gave up that prize once when it took Test matches for granted for years.

What happened last night gives it an electrifying shot in the arm and a taste of what it gave up, a sin this epic Australian victory proves would be madness to repeat.

World.title: Wallaroos believe 'possibilities are endless' ahead of 2029 World Cup
World.content:
Like every Test rugby player, Wallaroos lock Kaitlan Leaney knows a team cannot be defined by anything less than an 80-minute performance.

But on the recent WXV Global Series tour of Great Britain and France, Leaney feels the Wallaroos gave glimpses of the team they can be ahead of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.

The Wallaroos' 48-15 loss to England in Salford last month is a case in point.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

The final scoreline suggests a thrashing, but it does not tell the story of the first half when the Wallaroos held the upper hand over the world champions.

England did not hit the front on the scoreboard until the 46th minute after the Wallaroos led 10-5 at half-time.

"That first half just showed the potential that we have as a squad," Leaney told ABC Sport.

"I don't think it came down to England being rusty, or us having a few more games under our belt before we played them.

"I think it came down to us having that pure intent. We knew the way we wanted to play.

"We were physical on both sides of the ball. We spoke about winning the collision, and I think that we definitely did that."

The Wallaroos' Allana Sikimeti (right) takes on England's defence last month. (Getty images: Lewis Storey)

It was not just the Wallaroos' brute force that gave them the advantage, but also their intelligent strategy.

Faliki Pohiva's 31st-minute try came after the Wallaroos identified weaknesses in England's defensive formation and line-out.

"England is the best in the world and we took it to them for 45 minutes," said Leaney, who has been among the Wallaroos' most consistent players in 2026.

"We're definitely not happy with just that. We want to be able to come away with wins, but I think it just shows the growth and the capabilities we have."

Kaitlan Leaney has been one of the Wallaroos' best players this year. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A 29-26 defeat to world number four France in Aix-en-Provence the following week also provided encouraging signs, although the match was there for the taking.

The seventh-ranked Wallaroos failed to land the decisive blow, having squandered a 19-0 lead against a French side reduced to 11 players at one stage during the first half.

They rebounded seven days later to defeat Scotland 30-10 in Edinburgh; however, Leaney and her teammates were dissatisfied with their display after trailing 10-5 at half-time.

"In the first half, I think we let ourselves down in terms of discipline and missing some key opportunities that we created," Leaney said.

'Possibilities are endless'

The establishment of a full-time Wallaroos program is in progress, and will be a game-changer for women's rugby in Australia.

England invested wisely when it first offered full-time contracts in 2019, and it is little surprise the Red Roses have not lost a match in four years.

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A veteran of 43 Tests, Leaney knows the Wallaroos will improve immensely once they are no longer semi-professional.

"I think once we have that and we're together full-time, you'll see the results come from that," she said.

"I think the possibilities are endless in that space."

Wallaroos lose star for Scotland Test The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos' immediate focus is tomorrow's WXV Global Series Test against Scotland in Sydney.

It is the first of two Tests against the Scots on Australian soil, with the second match to be played in Canberra on October 23.

Winning is the obvious goal, but Leaney is also determined that the Wallaroos produce a complete performance across both halves.

"That's something we're working on for this weekend and making sure we're firing from the get-go and sticking to our game plan," she said.

"Because when we do, it works. We just need to do it from the start.

"We just haven't reached that 80-minute performance yet."

World.title: De Minaur falls to world number one Zverev in Shanghai
World.content:
Top-ranked Alexander Zverev said he felt good on court after beating Alex de Minaur 6-4, 6-4 at the Shanghai Masters.

Behind his impregnable serve, Zverev, who is guaranteed to end the year as the top-ranked men's player after a season-ending injury to Jannik Sinner, enjoyed his most clinical match of the tournament after struggling with foot problems in earlier contests.

Zverev made 80 per cent of his first serves and saved all five of the break points he faced as he set up a semifinal meeting with Alejandro Davidovich Fokina.

"I felt both of us were playing really, really well. I was a lot of times out-hitting Alex, which is difficult to do from the baseline because he is so fast and he loves this kind of court speed here," Zverev said.

"I felt good, and I'm happy with the step up from the last couple of matches."

World number nine de Minaur, one of the best returners in the game, managed to eke out five break points over two key games, one in each set, but was then thwarted by Zverev's delivery.

After being broken for 3-2 in the opening stanza when the German unleashed a series of monster forehands, de Minaur immediately hit back in the next game by carving out three break points, only for Zverev to pound down five unreturnable serves in a row.

Having wrapped up that set in 37 minutes, Zverev then found himself under pressure from the Sydneysider in the second stanza as de Minaur earned two break points, sniffing an opportunity to move into a 4-2 lead.

Again, though, Zverev rescued the situation with fine serving and immediately broke a deflated "Demon'' in the next game to effectively seal the deal, earning his ninth win over the Australian, this time with 10 aces and 14 searing winners.

It continued de Minaur's depressing record against the German, having beaten Zverev only four times in team competition but never in an individual tournament.

The consolation for de Minaur, though, is that he ends another promising tournament by improving his chances of reaching the end-of-season, eight-man ATP Finals for the third straight year as he has moved up to seventh in the live Race to Turin standings.

That leaves him sixth overall, with Sinner's season already over because of his knee injury.

AP/AAP

World.title: Builder revealed, but cost of new stadium still 'being worked through'
World.content:
The head of the government body tasked with delivering a new stadium in Hobart has acknowledged that "cost pressures" could impact the final price tag of the project.

The construction of a 23,000-seat, roofed stadium is a key requirement for the entry of the Tasmania Devils into the AFL and AFLW competitions in 2028.

The project is currently budgeted at $1.13 billion, but that estimate is now more than a year old.

Builder chosen for Hobart's stadium The company that built a 30,000-seat arena in Christchurch, New Zealand, has been selected to construct Hobart's new roofed stadium.

Since then, construction costs have increased significantly because of the war in the Middle East.

Macquarie Point Development Corporation chief executive Anne Beach said further work would now be done to finalise the cost before the contract is signed by the end of the year.

"Through this next stage an important part of that is moving from the target construction sum to actually locking down the lump sum that will go into the contract," Ms Beach said.

"The stage two process will end in around mid-November.

" We'll then go through an assessment, and that's when we'll be coming back to government to discuss that cost. "

Loading...

On Thursday, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder of the stadium.

Ms Beach said "cost pressures" would play a part in the outcome.

"We'll need to consider, as we go through this process, cost pressures that are in the market and the cost to build as at today.

"We'll be continuing to analyse that, and we'll provide an update once we can after stage two."

At a press conference, Jeremy Rockliff did not take up the chance to promise Tasmania's input to the stadium would be limited to $875 million. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the final cost would be publicly revealed shortly before the contract is signed.

But when asked whether he could promise the state's input would be limited to $875 million, as previously flagged, he repeatedly skirted the question.

"We're working through a very rigorous process," Mr Rockliff said.

"We're at stage one, and we're working through and continuing that to get to stage two and, of course, signing the contract.

" And I'm not going to detail costs — they are being, they continue to be, worked through. "

Work is being done at the Macquarie Point site in preparation for the stadium construction. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Cost will be 'quite north' of $1.13b, MLC says

The state government's $875 million funding cap was part of its agreement with independent MLC Bec Thomas, who voted in favour of the development in December last year.

As part of that agreement, any further funds required to build the stadium would either be clawed back via "value management", a reduction in scope, or be sought from either the federal government, AFL or Cricket Australia.

The Greens remain sceptical the stadium can be built within the current funding envelope.

"We don't trust the premier and his commitment to stick to $875 million," Greens MP Vica Bayley said.

"That's why it's incumbent upon him to be transparent about where the additional money is going to come from and how parliament is going to be involved."

Vica Bayley says the state government needs to be transparent about where extra funds could come from. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Independent MLC Meg Webb said it would be "naïve" to think the cost of building the stadium won't be more than envisaged last year.

"I think all of us can look at the world's events since then, can look at other costs that have clearly gone up and imagine that now we're looking at a full cost for this stadium that's somewhere quite north of $1.13 billion."

She urged the government to disclose the cost to parliament before the contract is signed.

"We know that Tasmanians would like there to be transparency around that cost and now that a builder has been announced, there's no reason for the state government not to come clean and be really open and transparent and give us the expected full cost of the stadium."

Meg Webb says it's clear the full cost of the stadium will be far more than the current $1.13 billion figure. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Expert says Middle East conflict likely 'having impacts'

Kiri Parr is a construction industry advocate and senior fellow at the University of Melbourne Law School who lectures in the delivery of major projects.

She said it was common for large-scale construction projects to go over budget because of external factors and long timeframes that can significantly affect costs.

"An external war that drives up prices that's happened since you did your budget won't have been factored into that original budget," Ms Parr said.

"So, it's exactly the kind of external factor that major projects are exposed to and it likely is having impacts on the budget.

" The exact nature of how it all plays out over the next three or four years is unknown. "

BESIX Watpac built Christchurch's new 30,000-seat stadium at a cost of just over $530 million. (Supplied: One New Zealand)

Ms Parr said the key was to limit the scale of any potential cost overruns through good management.

"It's the importance of working very, very hard on your projects to resolve problems as early as possible and not allowing them to escalate," she said.

"The importance of experts, people who have experience on major projects."

The stadium is due for completion by the end of 2030.

World.title: How the joy of Pride is 'a form of resistance' against queer discrimination
World.content:
GWS player Tilly Lucas-Rodd says AFLW Pride Round is important to continue celebrating and championing while harmful attitudes towards queer people persist.

Lucas-Rodd, who is non-binary, said the joy and pride of the moment are an important counter to the discrimination queer people can still face in sport.

"I feel like we were getting to a place of more acceptance and now we're going backwards, and there's more discrimination, and more homophobia, and transphobia," Lucas-Rodd told ABC Sport.

First current AFLW player undergoes gender affirming top surgery Over the AFLW off-season, Hawthorn's Tilly Lucas-Rodd underwent top surgery, a gender-affirming procedure that involves the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

They said this is particularly evident in online comment sections containing discriminatory rhetoric towards queer people, including, at times, AFLW posts on social media.

"People are coming out of the woodwork, and they're proud and happy to have these opinions, and they think it's okay, which is why I think it's so important that we still have Pride round, and show up and represent the community and challenge these dangerous beliefs with joy," they said.

"There's a time and place to be reflective on the harm and the negative parts in terms of, like, the discrimination we face and truly reflect on that and sit in that and be like 'this is not okay'.

"But there's also a time to use joy and pride and celebration as a form of resistance."

They have seen the impact representation can have on people's lives.

Last year, Lucas-Rodd went public with having had gender affirming chest surgery in an exclusive with the ABC Sport.

The top surgery was a procedure that involved the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd in the Pride guernsey that GWS will wear for the club's home game during Pride round. (Supplied: GWS Giants)

They received many messages from people after the story came out, with people sharing it had opened up conversations with family members and given them a better understanding of the gender diverse and trans experience.

"A parent at my school that I taught at was like, 'You being so visible shows that for young trans (and) gender-diverse kids you can be successful, because they're often so hard on themselves and they don't see a future that's bright,'" they said.

"They see hardship, they see discrimination, they see transphobia as their future, but then they see someone being successful, being championed, being celebrated publicly, and they can see a way forward for themselves.

This year, what makes Pride Round even more special for Lucas-Rodd is it coincides with their 100th game.

Over the past 11 seasons, Lucas-Rodd has played for four different clubs, including Carlton (2017-2020), St Kilda (2020-2022), Hawthorn (2022-2025) and now GWS.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd was an inaugural player for Carlton. (Getty: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

"It is so funny," Lucas-Rodd laughed, noting in particular the years at Carlton when they had shaved sides and bun. "There's been so many eras.

"I've changed completely as a person, and it was guided by AFLW. All I've ever known (as an adult) is AFLW, and all I've ever really been overly passionate about in my 20s is AFLW," they said.

The environments of the league helped shape them, which, they say, is why Pride Round is so important: the welcoming rooms they've been in aren't the same for everyone in sport.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd moved from Hawthorn to GWS ahead of the 2026 season. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

They did a video with men's GWS player Tom Green earlier this week for the club's channel for Pride Round, during which he asked Lucas-Rodd if they ever struggle with using their platform.

It made them reflect on how they use their social media accounts — quite often championing trans and gender-diverse people playing sport and playing footy — and how it has created a two-way dialogue with more people in the community.

"When I speak to people or hear from people's actual lived experience in community sports, it's not safe," they said.

"And I was like, that's something I've only ever learned through more conversations around Pride Round."

AFLW Pride Round The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch wants to see the power of the AFLW's dedicated Pride Round harnessed and extended across the whole code.

Lucas-Rodd sometimes thinks, "Oh, this is probably getting old; people are probably bored of it", when they speak about their LGBTQ+ experience.

"But then I have someone message me being like, 'Oh, my parents read this, they heard this, they watched your video, and that made the conversation easy for me.'

"And it takes you back to why it's so important that we still have Pride Round.

"That's why it's so important that we have visibility and representation and keep talking about it over and over again because it helps make other people's lives easier out there in community."

World.title: Quick hits: Walsh vomits after try, Ponga shines then suffers in epic duel
World.content:
Australia and New Zealand have set a high standard for the 17th edition of the Rugby League World Cup, opening the 2026 tournament with an all-time classic.

Young Kiwi Casey McLean defied gravity and debutant Aussie Jack Bostock won the match for the Kangaroos.

Meanwhile, a vomiting Reece Walsh and a broken-armed Kalyn Ponga produced one of the great fullback duels.

Here are the quick hits from the opening match.

1. McLean defies gravity in all-time finish

Casey McLean is Kiwi superman.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

After a towering bomb from Jahrome Hughes was batted back by Ronaldo Mulitalo, Isaiah Papali'i threw what could best be described as a one-handed chuck, collected by McLean on the blind side.

With no space to work in, and Kangaroos halfback Mitchell Moses smothering him while directing him towards touch, McLean went airborne.

Somehow, seemingly in slow motion, as his body hovered horizontally over the sideline, McLean grounded the ball in the corner.

ABC Sport expert commentator Luke Lewis described it as "one of the best finishes you will see in this game".

And just four minutes into this World Cup, a contender for try of the tournament was born.

2. Long-range intercepts put Kangaroos on top

The Kiwis dominated the first half at the Sydney Football Stadium.

The New Zealanders had 59 per cent of the ball, made 300 more metres running, and had 66 fewer tackles.

But they went into the break level after the Kangaroos scored two 90-metre intercept tries.

The first Kangaroos score came from debutant Jack Bostock, who rushed out of the defensive line to grab a looping pass by Kiwi halfback Jahrome Hughes.

If that ball got over his head, it would have been a try for the Kiwis. But the Australian winger took the ball cleanly, broke the grasp of a Kiwi, and ran for the goal line.

Incredibly, an almost identical play happened for Australia's other winger, Tom Trbojevic, on the other side of the field.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean gave a pass meant for his unmarked winger, but Trbojevic stuck his arm in the way and caught the footy.

Trbojevic then showed the speed he was known for at the start of his career, beating the cover tackle attempt of Kodi Nikorima and streaking away.

3. After first-half denial, Ponga breathes fire

The duel of the opposing fullbacks was one of the most hyped heading into this game, featuring two of the most electric talents in the game.

Kalyn Ponga was a standout for the Kiwis, before leaving the game with a suspected broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

And it produced everything fans could hope for.

Kiwi custodian Kalyn Ponga came into the tournament off the back of a breathtaking season for the Knights, while Kangaroos number one Reece Walsh was considered a somewhat controversial selection, preferred over the Roosters' Clive Churchill medallist, James Tedesco.

After being kept relatively quiet for most of the first half, Ponga burst to life on the left, dancing, darting and taunting the Kangaroos.

He slipped past Staggs and tried to sidestep Walsh, who produced a scintillating try-saver, bundling Ponga into touch.

It was one for the purists, in shades of Scott Sattler's tackle on Toddy Byrne in the 2003 NRL grand final.

Ponga shook it off after the break, and the Kiwis' debutant was on the end of some slick passing from the Kiwis for a straightforward finish for his first try.

His second was better, a 40-metre vintage Ponga effort.

With his shorts pulled halfway down his legs, he still managed to power past Walsh with a classic step, sending the sizeable Kiwi contingent in Sydney into delirium.

4. Walsh plunders then chunders, Ponga goes off

The Kangaroos were staring down a rare defeat to their arch-rivals in this arena, when Walsh responded to his opposite number's heroics and left the Kiwis in his dust.

Reece Walsh struggled to regain his composure after scoring his try. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Deep in their own half and trailing by six, Bostock slipped a clever flick pass behind his back, and the Broncos superstar swooped.

He swerved past defenders, running 60 metres to go over in the corner.

But he gave everything in the effort, and as he prepared to take the conversion, he was interrupted by his exhaustion.

He threw up and was unable to take the kick, with Lattrell Mitchell stepping up instead.

Walsh continued to dry retch and looked completely spent. But he managed to keep it together (and inside) to stay on the field and see out the game.

But it was a horrible end to the game for Ponga; his night ended early with a suspected broken arm — a huge blow for the Kiwis' title hopes.

Ponga had nursed his left arm after a tackle on Cam Munster early in the second half.

He stayed out there, but appeared to hit his arm again in a collision with teammate Hughes in an attempt to tackle Walsh.

5. Bostock hat trick

Jack Bostock had already made his mark on international rugby league with his 90-metre intercept try in the first half.

But he was not done scoring and it proved a match-winning performance.

His second try came in the 57th minute, with the Aussies trailing by six points.

Kangaroos five-eighth Cam Munster put up a pinpoint kick for Bostock to chase.

The Australian went up against his Dolphins teammate Jamayne Isaako, beat him in the air, and scored a fantastic try to help level the scores.

But Bostock had an even better effort to win the game.

Down by two with less than four minutes to play, it was Munster again who put up a high kick for Bostock to chase.

Isaako was in a much better position this time, and appeared to have caught the footy.

But Bostock ripped the ball out of the Kiwi's arms, in turn, ripping the game away from New Zealand.

World.title: A-League star in fiery exchange with reporter over suspension loophole
World.content:
Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.

Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.

Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.

That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.

The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.

In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".

Loading Instagram content

"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.

"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"

Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.

"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.

"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.

"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."

Auckland FC are the reigning A-League Men champions. (Getty Images: New Zealand Herald/Alyse Wright)

The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.

"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.

An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.

"You know what football's like in this country, mate? We f***ing work hard to get it good. You bring it down with shit like that," Cosgrove said, prompting a chuckle from the reporter.

"What are you laughing for? We'll just f*** you off. You won't get back here again."

In a podcast episode posted on Tuesday, Cosgrove said he was relieved when news of the rule's workaround became public so he could "finally stop lying about it".

"It was a poor challenge in oppressive heat and late in the game, but the two-game suspension was a little bit harsh," he told The Unused Subs podcast.

"We were trying to get that reduced, and the power of lawyers and legal teams these days, they managed to find a way to sign me up with the Auckland reserves."

The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday, before an away trip to face Western Sydney Wanderers on October 24.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Aussies win all-time World Cup classic, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm
World.content:
Jack Bostock has saved Australia from an embarrassing World Cup opening, with the winger scoring a hat-trick on debut to edge the Kangaroos past New Zealand 24-22.

New Zealand was left sweating over the fitness of Kalyn Ponga after he failed to finish an electrifying debut on Thursday in front of 41,255 at Sydney Football Stadium with a suspected broken arm.

With Ponga off the field late, Bostock leapt high to score the winning try in the 75th minute by climbing over Dolphins' teammate Jamayne Isaako for his third of the night.

Bostock's brilliance ensured Australia narrowly avoided their first home defeat in 11 years, with the Kangaroos all but certain to finish top of group A ahead of games with Fiji and the Cook Islands over the next fortnight.

There were question marks over many of Kevin Walters' selections, but Bostock, who mainly plays as a centre for Redcliffe, vindicated his coach's faith in his ability to play on the wing.

"I don't think I've seen a better debut game from a winger or from any Australian player," Walters said of the 23-year-old's display.

"He was just in everything good about the attack, the defence, his athleticism. He should be really proud of his performance."

Other Walters decisions paid off, including the call to give Brisbane superstar Reece Walsh first shot at the fullback jersey.

Walsh showed few signs of rust in his first game in two months, and there will be significant intrigue through Australia's campaign as to whether Walters settles on the Brisbane No.1 or James Tedesco as his first-choice option.

But Walters is likely to face a headache in the halves after Mitchell Moses limped off soon after halftime with a calf injury.

"He's not too good, we'll get some scans for him," Walters said.

The shortcomings of the Kangaroos' forward selections were also highlighted against a monstrous Kiwi pack.

In front of the biggest crowd for a Sydney Test since the 1970s, the Kangaroos were manhandled and dominated by the Kiwis, who ran for close to 300 more metres.

But New Zealand lacked polish and it will be their inability to ice such games that will invite more questions about their credentials as genuine challengers to Australia's World Cup stranglehold.

A big part of New Zealand's chances will hinge on 28-year-old fullback Ponga, who scored twice in the second half on his Kiwis debut, the best of which was when he sidestepped Walsh and left him for dead.

"It's a possible fracture of the arm but he's going to go for scans and we're not going to make any call on him right now," said Kiwis coach Stacey Jones.

"There's lots of stuff to be proud of and lots of stuff to like but there's a lot more to go in this tournament."

Even before Ponga trudged off, the Kiwis had the opportunity to put Australia to the sword but failed.

Casey McLean scored the opener after three minutes, before Tom Trbojevic and Bostock scored intercept tries for the home side.

Mitchell Moses couldn't stop Casey McLean from scoring the first try of this year's World Cup. (Supplied/AAP PHOTOS)

With Kotoni Staggs sin-binned for a professional foul and Moses limping off after halftime with the scores at 10-10, Ponga put New Zealand back in front when he pinballed his way through the Australian line.

And despite Ponga weaving past Walsh for a breathtaking try, the Brisbane man had the last laugh.

Between Bostock's second and his match-winner, Walsh weaved around Ponga with a brilliant solo effort.

AAP

Tech.title: The tech backlash is now in theaters
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.

Especially when you compare them to classics like The Social Network, the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but The Social Reckoning builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by whistleblower Frances Haugen, the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful executive who wields autocratic control over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.

What The Social Reckoning lacks in timeliness (The Wall Street Journal began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health and the relationship between Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s Musk documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.

Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling. X has blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the Musk ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.

Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is a longtime Donald Trump supporter and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year. Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.

What sets Fielder’s You Can See Everything apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison, and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that she defrauded Theranos investors. Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.

That central tension turns You Can See Everything into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of her recent PR campaign, and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.

It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or seen in Hulu’s The Dropout. Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes You Can See Everything feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.

Tech.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”

As pointed out by users on Reddit, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.

Google’s SynthID detector flagged it as made or edited with OpenAI’s tools. Screenshot: Emma Roth / The Verge

The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.

Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself, while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

Tech.title: Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social
Tech.content: Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. In an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider said to think of Attie as “social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

Tech.title: Withings now charges $100 per year to sync your data to other apps
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you’re a new user of Withings’ fitness-tracking smartwatches or smart scales and want to sync and access your health data through third party apps like Apple Health or Google Health it’s now going to cost you.

According to a discussion on Withings’ support forums spotted by MacRumors, new Withings accounts created from October 13th, 2026, and onwards will require a Withings Plus subscription to use the “automatic sync to third-party apps” feature. The subscription costs $9.95 per month or $99.50 per year but Withings’ devices come with a free one month trial that includes the option to sync their data to third-party apps. When the trial is over the syncing is paused but the data in those apps isn’t deleted.

Existing users who already have a Withings account created on or before October 12th, 2026, will continue to have access to automatic third-party app syncing for free, according to official comments shared by a member of Withings’ support team. And because the feature is tied to an existing users’ account and not a specific device, the third-party syncing will continue to be available without a subscription if they buy and register new watches, scales, or other Withings hardware.

Tech.title: Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta announced the Muse Spark Open AI model today, claiming that it’s the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” But the company also says that it’s the “the first model in its class” that can “run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.”

Meta and Apple, typically rivals, worked together on the launch and are publicly supporting each other.

“Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on X.

“Congrats to the team!” new Apple CEO John Ternus said in a reply. “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”

“We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said to Axios, who also noted that the companies have been collaborating over several months.

The new model is a “natively multimodal model” with 816 billion total parameters that “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” according to Meta. Apple also published a new technical post about MLX, an “array framework” for ML tasks on Apple Silicon, Muse Spark Open, and two other open models.

Tech.title: Sony made a $5,900 gold-plated Walkman MP3 player
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell.

All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD (Direct Stream Digital) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise.

The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference.

What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated.

This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

Tech.title: Volvo will use Nvidia’s tech for hands-free, point-to-point driving
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised).

Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan, said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge.

Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future.

By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt.

Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars.

“Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.”

Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead, including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality.

Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.”

Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

Tech.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it
Tech.content:
Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product.

Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure.

“You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.”

Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down.

“I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.”

Image Credits:Kimberly White / Getty Images

He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure.

“Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.”

Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles.

“It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.”

Tech.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
Tech.content:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.

Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”

The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.

Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.

Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

Tech.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
Tech.content:
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.

Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee, Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.

“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”

By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.

“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.

Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.

These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.

Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.

“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”

The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.

“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.

“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”

Tech.title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network
Tech.content:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt, explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.

“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”

Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.

Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.

The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”

Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.

“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”

Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.

“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

Tech.title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
Tech.content:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.

The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.

“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”

Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.

Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.

METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.

“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.

METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.

Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

Tech.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more
Tech.content:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.

The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform, which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.

These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.

Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.

Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.

Image Credits:Bluesky

“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”

When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.

To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.

“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”

That network today has 47 million registered users, though it’s seen a decline in engagement, as some users who tested it out later returned to X.

Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.

“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

Tech.title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
Tech.content:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.

Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.

The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.

“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.

Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.

“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”

He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”

While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.

All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.

“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.
